children.translated_text: May the great mother of the fresh creation, resting on the stainless digit, and the father, whose body is filled with the hidden radiance of the five-faced one,
make my heart shine forth as the unsurpassed nectar-lineage, consisting of the emission of being that flashes from the union of those two.
I bow to the goddess <s>Citpratibha</s>, the supreme <s>Bhairava</s>-yogini,
who has made her abode in the trident and lotus whose parts are the knower, the means of knowing, and the knowable.
I bow to the goddess who abides in the body, in the form of dancing <s>Bhairava</s>,
who plays like a streak of lightning in the thick cloud-filled sky of the rainy season.
May the shining trident of knowledge, whose blaze of light has burned up the three bonds of difference,
appear, able to cut away both sound and opposing positions.
The power of freedom, the wish to create sequence, and sequential nature: these are the manifestations of the all-pervading Lord.
May that very triad of goddesses, abiding within, unfold for me my unsurpassed nature.
The goddess's son, <s>Ganapati</s>, alone, whose own state has become lord over the circle of great rays born from that deity's power,

children.text: devīsuto gaṇapatiḥ sphuradindukāntiḥ samyaksamucchalayatān mama saṃvidabdhim ||
children.translated_text: and who shines with the brightness of the moon, may he fully swell the ocean of my consciousness.
He who made manifest on the outer path the net, reddened with passion, strewn into the hollow of the knot,

children.text: kalombhitaṃ bāhyapathe cakāra stānme sa macchandavibhuḥ prasannaḥ ||
children.translated_text: extended and contracted, and raised by the digit: may that lord <s>Macchanda</s> be gracious to me.
Victorious are the former teachers of the lineage called <s>Tryambaka</s>, who possess the special radiance of heaps of fine pearls from <s>Tamraparni</s>,
helmsmen unstained by the play of waves on the ocean of the guru's scripture.

children.text: jayati gurureka eva śrīśrīkaṇṭho bhuvi prathitaḥ
children.translated_text: Victorious is the one guru, renowned on earth as <s>Srisrikantha</s>,
and, as his other embodiment, the blessed <s>Mahesvara</s> and <s>Bhutiraja</s>.
Victorious are the compositions, spread through the quarters,
which issued from the blessed awakening of <s>Somananda</s> and the venerable <s>Utpala</s>, and are fragrant with consciousness.
I praise the bee of the mind of my guru <s>Lakshmanagupta</s>,
expanded by immersion in the fullness of that savor and enchanting through its sound.
May that excellent guru, the venerable <s>Cukhulaka</s>,
who crossed beyond all the meanings of the scriptures and rested in complete bliss, grant me what is desired.
May that one <s>Sambhunatha</s>, together with the goddess, triumph, capable of uplifting the world,
by whose emitted rays of instruction this path of scripture, though deep, has become clear to me.
There are many varied manuals for the distinctions among the streams,
but in the sequence of the meaning of the unsurpassed six-and-a-half, not even one is seen.
Therefore, often requested by good pupils and fellow students,
I compose this procedure, clear and complete in meaning.
The lineage of teachers comes from the pair of lotus feet of the venerable <s>Bhattanatha</s>, and likewise from the pair of feet of the venerable <s>Bhattarika</s>.
<s>Abhinavagupta</s>, made bright by the awakening produced by their worship, which removes the poison of other bonds, makes this work.
There is nothing here that is not taught in the venerable <s>Malinivijayottara</s>,
by the god of gods, either in its own words or by implication.
The teaching of the all-pervading Lord is divided into ten, eighteen, eight, and other divisions;
its essence is indeed the <s>Trika</s> scripture, and the essence of that is the doctrine of the <s>Malini</s>.
Therefore everything is contained here; by the command of our guru-lord,
we make clear what has not been seen by learned men abandoned by the tradition.
This is a work of <s>Abhinavagupta</s>, whose name was proclaimed by his teachers,
as one who gained renown through meditation on the lotus feet of the three-eyed Lord.
O people, examine this lotus-heart of <s>Abhinavagupta</s>,
whose contraction has been removed by the light falling from the sun-like feet of the venerable <s>Sambhunatha</s>, for the sake of worshipping <s>Mahesa</s>.
Here, first of all, it is proclaimed in all the scriptures
that ignorance is the cause of transmigration, and knowledge is the sole cause of liberation.
They regard impurity as ignorance, the cause of the sprout of worldly existence;
so it has been said, and likewise in the venerable <s>Malinivijayottara</s>.
By means of a qualifier, with reference to what stands in the intellect at the time after transmigration,
it rejected the supposition of that and declared liberation in its absence.
The word "ignorance" does not mean absence of knowledge, because that would extend too far;

children.text: sa hi loṣṭādike 'pyasti na ca tasyāsti saṃsṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: for such absence exists even in a clod and the like, but they have no transmigration.
Therefore that very knowledge which consists in the non-manifestation of the knowable reality in its totality
is ignorance, as stated in the <s>Siva Sutras</s>.

children.text: caitanyamātmā jñānaṃ ca bandha ityatra sūtrayoḥ
children.translated_text: In the two sutras, "Consciousness is the self" and "Knowledge is bondage,"
this meaning is shown through the application of combination and separation.
The word "consciousness," ending in an abstract suffix,
states in the ancient sutra pure freedom, without implying any particular qualification.

children.text: dvitīyena tu sūtreṇa kriyāṃ vā karaṇaṃ ca vā
children.translated_text: But by the second sutra, which speaks of either action or instrument,
duality is stated of that whose nature is pure consciousness.
The manifestation of duality is ignorance; because it is insubstantial, it is called bondage.
Therefore it has been explained, by repetition, as something to be cut off completely.
Apart from the free self, nothing at all, whether insubstantial or not insubstantial,

children.text: na mokṣo nāma tannāsya pṛthaṅnāmāpi gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: is called liberation, nor is even a separate name for it accepted.
But knowledge of the true reality of the knowable, consisting in fuller and fuller manifestation,
is progressive knowledge that grants the calming of each corresponding state of worldly existence.
"I am free from the taints of passion and the rest; I am inwardly empty and devoid of agency";
in this way, in brief and in detail, knowledge liberates only to that extent.
Therefore, even one who is liberated from a limitation, while still remaining within another limitation,
is not truly liberated; the liberated one is free from every limitation.
But knowledge of the true reality of the knowable, wholly free from any self-limitation,
By limiting conditions, that ignorance nowhere bestows true liberation.
What has been stated as the nature of knowledge and ignorance, each of these too,
is said in the teaching of <s>Śiva</s> to be twofold, distinguished as pauruṣa and bauddha.

children.text: tatra puṃso yadajñānaṃ malākhyaṃ tajjam apyaya
children.translated_text: There, the ignorance of the person, called mala, and born from that,
has the character of covering his <s>Śiva</s>-nature, whose form is his own full consciousness and activity.
It has the form of contracted seeing and action; for the bound soul it is not conceptually constructed.
That ignorance is not an aspect of the intellect, because determination and the like are absent.
When the intellect, determining, "I know this in this way,"
arises through reflection in the atomic subject produced in the cavern of the six sheaths,
then such knowledge is termed ignorance,

children.text: bauddhaṃ tasya ca tatpauṃsnaṃ poṣaṇīyaṃ ca poṣṭṛ ca ||
children.translated_text: bauddha; and in relation to it, that pauruṣa ignorance is both to be nourished and a nourisher.
But when the latent formation of the bound soul has waned, for the person who has attained the supreme state,
that pauruṣa knowledge unfolds, non-conceptual.
The ascertainment that comes in conformity with knowledge whose nature is unfolded non-conceptuality

children.text: tadbauddhaṃ yasya tatpauṃsnaṃ prāgvatpoṣyaṃ ca poṣṭṛ ca ||
children.translated_text: is bauddha; for one whose pauruṣa knowledge is such, it is, as before, both nourished and nourisher.
There, although pauruṣa ignorance is destroyed by initiation and the like,
nevertheless that knowledge becomes clearly manifest at the end of that body.
But when, through bauddha knowledge, the bauddha ignorance that has expanded
is dissolved, then liberation while living stands in the palm of the hand.
Initiation too, when preceded by bauddha knowledge, is truly liberating;
therefore even there bauddha knowledge has primacy.
This duality concerning knowledge and ignorance has been set forth in the <s>Svāyambhuva</s>, the <s>Ruru</s>,
the <s>Mataṅga</s>, and other scriptures by venerable teachers beginning with <s>Kheṭapāla</s>.
For the attainment of bauddha knowledge whose nature is such ascertainment,
scripture alone is primary, since it reveals the principles that are to be known.
Even when the inner pauruṣa ignorance has melted away through initiation,
because what belongs to the intellect has not ceased, conceptual construction may still occur.
For self-identification remains in the intellect as long as the body exists;
even at the body's end, liberation would not occur merely from the removal of pauruṣa ignorance.
But when bauddha ignorance ceases, because conceptual construction is uprooted,
liberation is certainly then and there; so the creator has said in the venerable <s>Niśāṭana</s>.
One whose mind is joined with conceptual construction goes to <s>Śiva</s> after the fall of the body;
the other does so at that very moment. Therefore scripture is primary here.

children.text: jñeyasya hi paraṃ tattvaṃ yaḥ prakāśātmakaḥ śivaḥ
children.translated_text: For the supreme principle to be known is <s>Śiva</s>, whose nature is luminosity.
Indeed, what is not of the nature of luminosity has neither manifestability nor even objecthood.
Even the non-objecthood of entities is accessible only to a single savoring awareness;
this awareness is not like a wall, since even "this is a non-object" is apprehended.
And what is called luminosity shines everywhere.
Since it cannot be denied, what need is there to construct means of knowledge for it?
Even the means of knowledge that extend life to objects

children.text: teṣāmapi paro jīvaḥ sa eva parameśvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: have as their supreme life that very <s>Parameśvara</s>.
Thus even the disposition that would deny everything functions in this way.
The claim, "knowledge exists for the sake of another self," does not appear valid to me.
In denying or establishing objects, such a principle is first there;
what useful role, then, could belong there to the logical application of means of knowledge?
Therefore it is said in the <s>Kāmika</s>: free from reasoning based on causes,
that god beyond the gods has no dependence on another.
Because the other depends on him, he is established as independent.
For the independent sovereign, the orders of place, time, form, and sequence

children.text: niyatā neti sa vibhurnityo viśvākṛtiḥ śivaḥ
children.translated_text: are not fixed; thus he is the all-pervasive, eternal <s>Śiva</s>, whose form is the universe.
Because he is all-pervasive he is present everywhere; because his being is eternal, he is without beginning or end.
And because his form is the universe, he manifests the diversity of the conscious and the unconscious.
Therefore his manifoldness is stated in the <s>Dīkṣottara</s> and other texts.

children.text: bhuvanaṃ vigraho jyotiḥ khaṃ śabdo mantra eva ca
children.translated_text: World, body, light, space, sound, and mantra,
differentiated as bindu, nāda, and the rest: <s>Śiva</s> is said to be sixfold.
Whatever nature one is firmly established in, one attains that state.
From knowledge of the words beginning with space, supreme liberation arises; there is no doubt.
With regard to the god's having the form of the universe, this too is an indication:
he is established in unlimitedness, and his limiting conditions dissolve.
And it is said in the <s>Kāmika</s>: the god has every form and is without form;
therefore, like water and a mirror, he pervades everything moving and unmoving.
Nor are his properties such as all-pervasiveness mutually distinct.
That single property of his functions by including all the rest.
Therefore the straightforward rule is that he is endowed solely with the power of freedom.
Even his possession of many powers is nothing but inseparability from that very power.

children.text: śaktiśca nāma bhāvasya svaṃ rūpaṃ mātṛkalpitam
children.translated_text: And <s>śakti</s>, power, is the own form of a thing, conceived by the knowing subject.
Therefore he is nondual even when conceived as possessing power.

children.text: mātṛkﾱpte hi devasya tatra tatra vapuṣyalam
children.translated_text: For in the god's various bodies, fashioned there and there by the knower,
what real difference is there, any more than between fire's burning and cooking capacities?
Nor is he, in the highest reality, anything apart from manifestation.
Indeed, nothing exists, and no difference between that and its power or possessor of power is real.
For whatever, by identity with a thing, generates the upsurge of its own power
is the power of that thing; in this way, O <s>Devī</s>, it appears even while having another form.
And <s>Śiva</s>, his greatness undiminished, appears as created
in imagination and the like, by his freedom, in the mirror of the knowing subject that is his own consciousness.
Therefore, by whatever face this partless one shines,
that very reality, as such, is power; the sequence of power and possessor of power is clear.
And in the venerable <s>Kiraṇaśāstra</s>, this is preceded by a question and answer about that matter:

children.text: anubhāvo vikalpo 'pi mānaso na manaḥ śive ||
children.translated_text: 'Experience and even conceptual determination are mental; there is no mind with respect to <s>Śiva</s>.'
And to the question, 'How can <s>dīkṣā</s> (initiation) occur without knowing <s>Śiva</s>?' there is this answer:
Experience such as hunger is certainly not conceptual determination, nor is it mental.
Although taste and the like are not directly perceived, from form alone, as in the case of a tree,
conceptual cognition knows it; in the same way, through <s>nāda</s>, <s>bindu</s>, and so on, it knows <s>Śiva</s>.
Since this many-powered nature of <s>Śiva</s> has been taught, therefore there is a great
expansion of distinctions such as <s>kalā</s>, <s>tattva</s>, city, sound, atom, and station.
Creation, maintenance, concealment, dissolution, grace, and the rest,
and also what is called the fourth state, are unfoldings of the God's many-powered nature.
The states of waking, dream, and deep sleep, and whatever states are other than or beyond them,
these too are the abundant waves of freedom belonging to that Lord.
The Great Lords of Mantra, the Lords of Mantra, and the mantras, with <s>Śiva</s> at their head,
as well as the <s>akala</s> and the <s>sakala</s>, are manifestations of <s>Śiva</s> alone.
The unfailing <s>dharma</s> (essential property) of the entire aggregate of <s>tattvas</s>
is the Self itself, whose nature is selfhood; so it is said in the venerable <s>Triśiromata</s>.
Situated in the heart, present in every body, established in its own nature, extremely subtle,
and as the collected totality of the <s>tattvas</s>, it is designated by the word 'aggregate.'
The Self itself, flooded with the nectar of <s>Śiva</s>, is said to be the <s>dharma</s>.
Knowledge abiding as luminosity, in the midst of being, non-being, and the rest,
is to be known as remaining in its own place; its seerhood is free from covering.
It is pure cognition, spotless, described as a distinct thing.
The activity of the aggregate's <s>dharma</s> has been stated; everything is accomplished for it.
Abandoning the upper region and entering below, he stands in <s>Rāma</s>, moving in the middle region.
Going, standing, dream, waking, opening, and closing,
running and leaping, exertion, and the experience of power,
varieties of intellect, states, names, and actions in many forms:
this is the pervasive <s>Rāma</s> here, <s>Śiva</s>, the supreme cause.
By the mere suppression of memory, in one whose mind has had its impurity exhausted,
the supreme object of meditation, established in the state of coming and going, is meditated upon.

children.text: paraṃ śivaṃ tu vrajati bhairavākhyaṃ japādapi
children.translated_text: Through <s>japa</s> too one reaches supreme <s>Śiva</s>, called <s>Bhairava</s>.
<s>Japa</s> is said to be his own nature, fallen away from the states of being and non-being.
Thus here too, by his own freedom,
distinctions such as far and near are constructed with regard to the freedom of consciousness.
In this way, because he is full of freedom, this supreme Lord performs what is extremely difficult to accomplish.

children.text: kena nāma na rūpeṇa bhāsate parameśvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: In what form, indeed, does he not appear?
He appears without covering, and he appears with his own nature covered.
He appears both covered and uncovered, manifold through the conjunction of difference.
Thus the triad of powers in the Lord, whose other name is freedom,
has been made manifest by the gurus under names such as will and the rest.
For the God is taught through words stated in scripture whose meanings are etymologically apt:
this God <s>Mahābhairava</s>, the Lord, who is supreme <s>Śiva</s>.

children.text: viśvaṃ bibharti pūraṇadhāraṇayogena tena ca bhriyate
children.translated_text: He bears the universe by filling and supporting it, and by that same relation he is borne by it.
Because he is endowed with reflective awareness, has the form of sound, and benefits those afraid of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
because, from the melting caused by fear of <s>saṃsāra</s> and also from reflection born in the heart,
he makes the reflection on the fear of becoming manifest through the descent of power,
and because he is present among those whose minds delight in the absorption that devours Time,
and among the powers that drive the stars and dry up the time-principle,
because the roaring of his own goddesses of the senses terrifies contracted bound beings,
and also that of the fourfold inner and outer groups beginning with the <s>khecarīs</s>,
he is their master, greatly terrifying because he breaks apart the activity of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Thus, with these meaningful derivations, he is praised in scripture by the gurus as <s>Bhairava</s>.
When there is no talk of what is to be rejected or accepted, the surging of one's compact mass of bliss
is play; the wish to abide with utter superiority is freedom.
Even in the undivided Self, practical dealing is the converse that speaks in terms of difference.
His illumination is due to making everything appear, since all praise is directed toward him.
From the attainment of the Self onward, in every duty whatsoever, one is inclined toward him.
His movement is consciousness in essence, made of all action, possessing the qualities of seeing and acting.

children.text: iti nirvacanaiḥ śivatanuśāstre gurubhiḥ smṛto devaḥ
children.translated_text: Through such derivations the God is remembered by the gurus in the <s>Śivatanuśāstra</s>.
Through teaching, restraining, protecting, and ripening, he benefits everything.

children.text: tena patiḥ śreyomaya eva śivo nāśivaṃ kimapi tatra ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the Lord is nothing but auspiciousness-filled <s>Śiva</s>; there is nothing in him that is not auspicious.
Because a form of this kind shines to some extent in <s>Rudra</s>, <s>Upendra</s>, and others,
the qualifier 'supreme great state' has been adopted in order to remove limitation.
Thus the true essence of what is to be known is shown, by the command of <s>Śiva</s>,
by me, according to the sequence of my own awareness, true reasoning, the Lord's scripture, and the <s>Trika</s>.
These are precisely his powers, the three beginning with <s>parā</s>, which shine forth.

children.text: sṛṣṭau sthitau laye turye tenaitā dvādaśoditāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the fourth state, they are thereby declared to be twelve.
To that extent he, whose nature is fullness, is called supreme <s>Śiva</s>.
Therefore the worshippers here are directly established in that very reality.
And the arrangement of distinctions, portions, deficiency, excess, and so on among those powers
is explained in the scriptures only through the force of his freedom.
He is <s>Ekavīra</s>, then <s>Yāmala</s>, three-powered, fourfold in self,
five-formed, sixfold in self, sevenfold, adorned with the eightfold form,
ninefold in self, possessing the power of the ten directions, consisting of eleven <s>kalās</s>,
and the lord of the great wheel with twelve spokes: such is <s>Bhairava</s>.
Thus, even as far as the thousand-spoked wheel, or even in what is beyond number, the Lord
<s>Maheśāna</s>, whose power is the universe, expands within the wheel of the universe.
And even with respect to those wheels, according to the way each follows its own group,
the distinction belonging to a wheel has been explained here and there within unity.
In the doctrine of the <s>Traiśirasa</s>, through the conjunction of the reckoning as four, six, two, and two,
the lordship of the <s>Nātha</s> over the six cakras is taught, for his own form is manifold.
There the names of the cakra-goddesses are given according to the distinctions of their functions,
through meaningful conceptions of yoginīs, their mild and fierce forms, and their meditations.
For the inner flash of intuition is the body of the one Lord who is consciousness;
a mild, or otherwise delimited, circle of waves of consciousness is worshipped.
When one thinks, 'May there be nourishment for this,' that goddess of consciousness, so declared,
through meditation mixed with recitation and also through outward ritual activity,
becomes manifest and shines forth, granting that very fruit to him.
Nourishment is the making of what is dry into something juicy; therefore the water is white.
Following from that, the meditation is extended with that as its dominant feature.

children.text: ye ca svabhāvato varṇā rasaniḥṣyandino yathā ||
children.translated_text: And those phonemes which by nature pour forth sap, as it were,
being mostly dental, labial, and dental, when joined with certain other phonemes,
having reached the condition of seed, make that consciousness clearly manifest.
The utterance, 'Produce nourishment; moisten him greatly with this sap,'

children.text: saṃjalpo 'pi vikalpātmā kiṃ tāmeva na pūrayet ||
children.translated_text: even though a conceptual formulation, would surely fill that same consciousness.
'This is nectar, this is milk, this is ghee that brings strength;
with this I shall nourish his seed': in this way one should complete this rite.
Therefore <s>Viśveśvara</s>, <s>Bodhabhairava</s>, is worshipped
by people who desire enjoyment and liberation, both through limitation and through the absence of limitation.
For this reason the guru taught, 'Even those who are devoted to other deities...',
for those who regard anything apart from awareness as fit to be worshipped,
even they, when they analyze the knowable object, understand it as non-different from awareness.
Therefore no injunction applies to the Self whose nature is the manifestation of I-ness as uninterrupted apprehension,

children.text: svayaṃprathasya na vidhiḥ sṛṣṭyātmāsya ca pūrvagaḥ
children.translated_text: which is self-manifest; and the creative form of this Self comes before any injunction.
For the creation of deities is knowable, and it has arisen from the cause that is śakti (power).
But consciousness in the form of 'I' is eternal and consists in self-manifestation.
Injunction, command, and the threefold bhāvanā (realizing contemplation) are of the nature of prompting.
<s>Indra</s> and the others, established only through that, are indeed deities preceded by injunction;

children.text: ahaṃbodhastu na tathā te tu saṃvedyarūpatām ||
children.translated_text: but I-awareness is not like that. They, however, seeing them as having emerged only into the form of objects of cognition,
though they know that one, do not truly know him.

children.text: taduktaṃ na vidurmāṃ tu tattvenātaścalanti te ||
children.translated_text: Thus it is said: 'But they do not know me in truth; therefore they fall away.'
That falling away is precisely the assumption of a delimited form;
therefore the statement beginning 'Worshippers of the gods go to the gods' was explained.

children.text: nimajjya vedyatāṃ ye tu tatra saṃvinmayīṃ sthitim
children.translated_text: But those who, having plunged into knowability, know there a state made of consciousness,

children.text: viduste hyanavacchinnaṃ tadbhaktā api yānti mām ||
children.translated_text: even if they are devotees of those deities, reach me, the undelimited one.
Everywhere here the word 'I' denotes awareness alone and nothing else.
It is expressed by the words 'enjoyer' and 'lord' as both the one to be worshipped and the worshipper.
It has been taught that the worshipping consciousness itself is what is to be worshipped, and nothing else.

children.text: na tvākṛtiḥ kuto 'pyanyā devatā na hi socitā ||
children.translated_text: No other form from anywhere is meant; such a thing is not the deity intended here.

children.text: vidhiśca noktaḥ ko 'pyatra mantrādi vṛttidhāma vā
children.translated_text: Nor is any injunction stated here, nor any mantra or the like, nor any sphere of activity.
This Self, covering itself, has come to rest and entered the condition of the inert.
As both covered and uncovered Self, it extends from the gods down to immobile things.
In this twofold condition of the inert and the non-inert there is manifold variety.

children.text: tasya svatantrabhāvo hi kiṃ kiṃ yanna vicintayet
children.translated_text: For its state of freedom can conceive whatever it will; what could it not conceive?

children.text: taduktaṃ triśiraḥśāstre saṃbuddha iti vetti yaḥ
children.translated_text: This is said in the <s>Triśiras</s> scripture: 'He knows, "I am awakened."'
For being an object of knowledge is a property of consciousness; its shadow does not cover consciousness itself.
Therefore, in the non-inert portion called pudgala, atom, and so on,
manifold variety exists in the part that belongs to non-covering.

children.text: saṃvidrūpe na bhedo 'sti vāstavo yadyapi dhruve
children.translated_text: Although in the form of consciousness, which is stable, there is no real difference,
nevertheless it is observed because of gradations in the diminishing of covering.
We shall explain that in detail in the determination of śaktipāta (descent of power).
After the supreme state has been completed, it will be discussed in connection with grossness.
Therefore the all-pervading one reveals, to one knowing subject,
his own complete form, and to another through a sequence of parts and subparts.
The manifestation of one's own nature as the single being of all states of the universe
is the supreme knowledge of finite souls; anything other than that is manifold lower knowledge.
And that knowledge, manifesting through a direct means and also through means leading to that means,
is differentiated here by various modes of expression.
Even there, because it is mediated by gateways belonging to oneself and to another, wholly and partially,
much difference proceeds through mediation and non-mediation.
And what is an auxiliary means of knowledge is not called ignorance;

children.text: jñānameva tu tatsūkṣmaṃ paraṃ tvicchātmakaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: rather, that too is subtle knowledge, while the supreme is considered to have the nature of will.
The condition of means and goal is the settling of knowledge into grossness;
and this very kriyāśakti (power of action) is the sole cause of bondage and liberation.
There, in the first self-apprehension, the single abode of the non-conceptual,
whatever shines forth openly and directly is proclaimed to be called will.
Just as, for those whose sight has flashed open, an object is fully clear
even without mental linking, so too, for some, is the state of being <s>Śiva</s>.
That which arrives at reflective awareness through repeated consideration
of the sequence of ascertainment involving conceptual elements is known as jñānopāya (the means of knowledge).
But that which accomplishes an external object fashioned by that conceptual construction
is handed down as kriyopāya (the means of action); here difference is not what brings liberation.

children.text: yato nānyā kriyā nāma jñānameva hi tattathā
children.translated_text: For what is called action is nothing other; it is indeed knowledge itself, precisely so,
and by established usage it has come to fall within yoga, so it is said in the sacred āgamic teaching.

children.text: yogo nānyaḥ kriyā nānyā tattvārūḍhā hi yā matiḥ
children.translated_text: Yoga is nothing else, action is nothing else: the understanding that is grounded in reality,
when directed to the pacification of the impressions in one's own mind, is called action.
In one's own mind are impressions born from karma, impurity, and <s>māyā</s>,
and the understanding, innate to consciousness, that serves as the cause for their pacification,
presiding over the host of external and internal principles beginning with the body,

children.text: kriyā saiva ca yogaḥ syāttattvānāṃ cillayīkṛtau ||
children.translated_text: that alone is action, and that is also yoga, when the principles are dissolved into consciousness.
Even in ordinary life, when the inward flash arises as 'I am going,'
that, entering the body, the place, and also the senses, is the action of motion.

children.text: tasmātkriyāpi yā nāma jñānameva hi sā tataḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore even what is called action
is indeed knowledge itself; thus knowledge alone is properly declared to lead to liberation.

children.text: mokṣo hi nāma naivānyaḥ svarūpaprathanaṃ hi saḥ
children.translated_text: For what is called liberation is nothing else; it is the manifestation of one's own nature.

children.text: svarūpaṃ cātmanaḥ saṃvinnānyattatra tu yāḥ punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the self's own nature is consciousness, and nothing else. As for the powers such as action,
they too are not other than the form of consciousness,
because they cannot have an unconscious nature, and because a bearer of properties could not then be defined.
For in the scripture of <s>Parameśvara</s>, unlike the unseen potency of <s>Kāṇāda</s>,
no separate substrate is taught for powers that have the form of properties.
And if the powers such as seeing, action, and will are held to be distinct,
then the statement '<s>Śiva</s> is one' becomes empty of real content.
Therefore this very condition of being consciousness is that autonomy,
which, when analyzed, comes to rest in many powers.
And since liberation is the manifestation of the self, no such doubt should be raised here:
'An effect does not necessarily follow from a cause; therefore even one who knows may not be liberated.'
For the relation of cause and fruit stated between knowledge and liberation

children.text: na sā mukhyā tato nāyaṃ prasaṃga iti niścitam ||
children.translated_text: is not primary; therefore this consequence certainly does not apply.
Thus action is by nature knowledge alone, yet it bears a kind of grossness in itself;

children.text: yato vahati tenāsyāṃ citratā dṛśyatāṃ kila ||
children.translated_text: therefore, in this action, let its manifold variety be observed.
In the means consisting of action, because subsidiary means are divided into what is grasped and what is external,
and because of the variety of divisions and subdivisions, the internal count is without number.
By this is also refuted the suspicion that some learned men entertained:
that because means differ, there would be difference even in liberation.
Though the causes differ, whether by the destruction of impurity and its power, by disappearance, or by falling away,
there is no difference, as in cases such as the destruction of a pot.
This threefoldness was taught in the scripture called <s>Śrīpūrva</s>,
by the supreme Lady, in determining <s>samāveśa</s> (immersion).
The immersion that arises in one who thinks of nothing at all,
through awakening by the guru, is declared to be <s>śāmbhava</s>.
The immersion one attains while contemplating the reality with the mind alone, without utterance,
is here called <s>śākta</s>.
The immersion that comes about through utterance, instruments, meditation, phonemes, and imaginings of their locations
is properly called <s>āṇava</s>.
The phrase 'of one who thinks of nothing at all' indicates that conceptual construction is of no use,
and by that it shows immediate absorption into the object to be known.
How does that occur? He explains: through an exceedingly weighty guru,
through a cognition turned toward the knowable and endowed with immediate firm establishment.
The suffix <s>tasi</s> is here explained as having the sense of the instrumental case, or else through a difference of syntactic locus.
And immersion, for one who is not autonomous, occurs through sinking into the form of one's own supreme reality.
It is becoming the form of the supreme, the form of <s>Śambhu</s>, the primordial one inseparable from <s>Śakti</s>.
Therefore the meaning of the statement here should be understood as follows: the knowable opens forth by itself,
even without determinate ascertainment, and at once, reflected in the mirror of the cognizing subject,
it subordinates that subject while displaying its own sovereignty.
It abides according to degrees of excellence in the purity of the heart.

children.text: jñeyaṃ dvidhā ca cinmātraṃ jaḍaṃ cādyaṃ ca kalpitam ||
children.translated_text: The knowable is twofold: sheer consciousness and the inert; and the first, too, is conceptually imagined,
while the other is real in that way. This is the division in such a case.
The immersion that occurs with the inert has the form of a reflected image,
whereas immersion with consciousness is simply identity, and nothing else.
Therefore nonconceptual awareness, requiring no cultivation or the like,
having attained identity with <s>Śiva</s>, is here <s>śāmbhava samāveśa</s> (Śaiva immersion).
Later ascertainments may indeed occur here afterward through its grace,
and they may have attained identity, but they do not have the status of means.
The person who says that the nonconceptual is a means of knowledge only in dependence on conceptualization
has already been answered; for what is established is subsequently followed by conceptual construction,
because the manifestation of certainty is quite clear in the thought, 'It has been grasped.'
But from the power of unity with the nonconceptual one understands, 'I grasp,'
and the very flashing forth of the object in self-awareness whose nature is nonconceptual
is attainment, not attainment from conceptualization, which is devoid of dependence on the object.
This is simply the repose of consciousness in purity or in its opposite.
With respect to its own nature, it may be independent of conceptualizations or dependent on them:
even at midnight, a jeweler, when gems are shown for the time of a lightning flash,
picks out the various particular qualities even of many jewels.
And this purity of consciousness comes either from the force of previous practice,
or from the unrestrained will of the Lord; this will be discussed.
The fiftyfold character of this <s>samāveśa</s> has also been described,
because of the clearly intended divisions present in the thirty-six principles.
Among these principles there is the triad whose nature is <s>puṃ</s>, <s>vidyā</s>, and <s>śakti</s>,
because, in order, their divisions are numbered by the conventional number-words 'ocean,' 'direction,' and 'fire,'
for what is called <s>puṃ</s>, <s>vidyā</s>, and <s>śakti</s> is all-pervasive.
Because of those that are non-pervasive, this has indeed been counted by means of that in terms of difference;
and even mutually, from impurity, from being purified, and from purity, it is so differentiated.
The elements are established by direct perception, while cause and effect are inferred;
therefore they are called elements, set apart from the class of the <s>tattvas</s> (principles).
For that which falls within the sphere of the existence present in every cognition is precisely an element,
and the knowers recognize its place here in the fourfold division where there is room for it.
The entry of <s>Rudra</s>'s power is surely discussed as fivefold;
what room, then, could there be for describing possession by elements and the like?
If one says, 'This is only incidental,' this answer is possible;
the world is not something that bends to our own mind, since people's tastes are different.
In dualist scriptures the separateness of the elements and the rest from <s>Parameśa</s> is taught;

children.text: bhūtādīnāṃ yathā sātra na tathā dvayavarjite ||
children.translated_text: but here, in the system free from duality, it is not like that.
Whatever this group of thirty-six is, and whatever else there may be,
all that is the great goddess, the unrestricted power of <s>Rudra</s>.
For that very reason, in this second section,
the universal form of earth and the rest was explained through distinctions such as the fifteenfold division.
Therefore, just as with regard to an object set before one, through qualities and the like as parts and possessors of parts,
there is awareness of its partless nature, so it should be understood here also.
For this very reason, through the powers of nonconceptuality, fixity, lordly force, and majesty,
or through other properties inherent in him because they have the form of <s>śaktis</s> (powers),
they worship that all-pervasive <s>Parameśvara</s>, either wholly or in part,
from the mass of conceptual impressions that have arisen from scripture.
Because of the sharpness of those properties flashing within their own particular concepts,
they enter, as non-different, the bearer of properties, the complete mass of all properties.
For this very reason <s>Śrīvidyādhipati</s> said with reverence:
'If sense-born imagining does not make your nonconceptual nature its object,
our clear experiences, cognitions painted inwardly, would not exist.'
This has been said in the venerable <s>Mataṅga</s> and similar texts: 'consisting of the rays of its own power,'
and 'now the seat of the Lord,' and so on, expressed with qualifying descriptions.
In that heaven, intensely luminous in self, unmoving, and possessed of an immovable form,
that same supreme and subtle limit has the nature of nectar in all directions.
With its coverings destroyed, peaceful, intensely desirous of reality alone,
ceased with respect to beginning and end, auspicious, it is conventionally treated as a form.
Here the ground and purpose of that figurative treatment are this:
through it there is clarity in the bearer of properties, and a swift abiding in identity with it.
Those very properties, called <s>śaktis</s> (powers), are worshipped
through their appropriate forms and shapes, for the attainment of becoming one with them.

children.text: tatra kācitpunaḥ śaktiranantā vā mitāśca vā
children.translated_text: Among them, again, one <s>śakti</s> may imply other powers, whether infinite or limited,
by the rule of whiteness and existence, according to remoteness and nearness.
Thus fullness of nature, luminosity, the character of consciousness,
and <s>Bhairava</s>-hood imply all the powers, because they are pervasive.
But <s>Sadāśiva</s> and the others, since they lack upward pervasion and belong to what is lower,
may imply powers according to the nearness or distance of the worship directed to them.
Since this is so, and since the conceptual path-sequence called <s>Śākta</s>
has been taught here, it is therefore accompanied by concepts corresponding to their opposites.
Having ascended the nonconceptual path, by whatever path one may enter,
from earth up to <s>Sadāśiva</s>, by that very path one becomes <s>Śiva</s>.
In a stainless heart, in the light where the excellent portion of earth shines forth,
consciousness, through that very opening, has the nature of supreme <s>Śiva</s>.
Thus those who dwell at the far limit of right understanding know this good means,
consisting of a portion of the supreme will-power, as the absorption called <s>Śāmbhava</s>.
Now the <s>Śākta</s> is described: thought, intellect, mind, and ego-making are plainly,
because they are conceptual, made of <s>māyā</s>; in reality, will and the rest are so too.
That which proceeds by self-identification, through the sequence of intention and ascertainment,
is <s>Śākta</s>; although it is also a means based on <s>māyā</s>, at its end it is nonconceptual.

children.text: paśorvai yāvikalpā bhūrdaśā sā śāmbhavī param
children.translated_text: Indeed, the nonconceptual ground that is the condition of the bound soul is supremely <s>Śāmbhavī</s>,
but incomplete because of the defectiveness of the knower; when that is removed, it blossoms forth.
Thus the conceptual ground, in the <s>Śākta</s> means, lies in the awareness of agency;

children.text: yasyāṃ sphuṭe paraṃ tvasyāṃ saṃkocaḥ pūrvanītitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: when that is clear, the supreme is present there, but contraction remains in it according to the earlier reasoning.
For one intent on dissolving the whole mass of contraction, however,
that radiant power produces inner appearances exactly as desired.

children.text: nanu vaikalpikī kiṃ dhīrāṇave nāsti tatra sā
children.translated_text: But is conceptual cognition not present in the <s>Āṇava</s> means? It is present there;
here, however, another means has been defined by the absence of <s>uccāra</s> (articulate utterance).
By the word <s>uccāra</s> here are meant the many distinctions beginning with that and ending with the rest;

children.text: śaktyupāye na santyete bhedābhedau hi śaktitā ||
children.translated_text: these are not found in the <s>Śāktopāya</s>, for difference and non-difference are precisely the state of <s>śakti</s>.
The <s>aṇu</s> is what is called manifest difference; its means here is <s>Āṇava</s>,
itself consisting of conceptual certainty, though at the end it is nonconceptual.
But intellect, mind, ego-making, and the individual person would pervade <s>Śiva</s>;
or, because they are situated below, how could such a statement have been made?
The answer is given: in reality, for us, <s>Śiva</s> himself is of that very kind;
self-luminous, having concealed his own nature, he is again just so.
This too is well explained even in dualist scriptures such as the <s>Mataṅga</s>:
that manifestation belongs to <s>Śiva</s> himself, who pervades downward,
by which the supreme state shines even on the level of intellect and mind.
Both of these absorptions proceed toward the ocean of the nonconceptual;

children.text: prayāta eva tadrūḍhiṃ vinā naiva hi kiṃcana ||
children.translated_text: without being firmly established in that, there is nothing whatsoever.
And here no difference in the fruit, consciousness, should be imagined; therefore he said:
'The primacy of conception is indicated precisely here.'
Even one who asserts epistemic validity in dependence on conceptual construction, according to that view,
has non-conceptual status as a means of knowledge taken up through the sequence of that very conceptual construction.
One who at first does not know the true nature of a jewel, through discussion of the means of ascertainment,
when he reaches non-conceptuality without any means, is said to be a knower of jewels.
The means of non-difference alone has been stated here as <s>śāmbhava</s>; <s>śākta</s> is said to be
the means whose nature is difference-and-non-difference, while the means of difference is the <s>āṇava</s>.
At the end, in this knowledge with its means, the whole expanse of ritual action
will be included in a plainly manifest form.
For what is called action is no entity other than cognition; through dependence on a means
it has obtained a sequential nature, and that was earlier called action.
And right knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, whether established in oneself or in another,
since manifestations such as oneself and another are mere constructions.
And when both are equally imagined, the guru in whom the flashing forth of unity occurs

children.text: guruḥ sa tāvadekātmā siddho muktaśca bhaṇyate ||
children.translated_text: is so far said to be one Self, accomplished and liberated.
For as far as his own continuum extends, to that extent it is called the guru;
and because it is made of right knowledge, he is therefore liberated by his own Self.
For that very reason the knower carries across his own continuum;
this is established by reasoning and scripture, since the sage is one to that extent.
Therefore those who raise the objection here, 'But liberation comes from knowledge,

children.text: dīkṣādikā kriyā ceyaṃ sā kathaṃ muktaye bhavet ||
children.translated_text: while this activity, initiation and the like, is action; how can it be for liberation?

children.text: jñānātmā seti cejjñānaṃ yatrasthaṃ taṃ vimocayet
children.translated_text: If it is knowledge in essence, knowledge should liberate the one in whom it is located;
or, if it liberates another, what could fail to be incoherent?'

children.text: iti te mūlataḥ kṣiptā yattvatrānyaiḥ samarthitam ||
children.translated_text: they have been refuted at the root. As for what has been defended here by others:
'Impurity is, they say, a substance, like a film situated in the eye;
the action of <s>dīkṣā</s> destroys it, like the action of collyrium and the like.'
That we shall refute later, as censured by reasoning and scripture,
and we shall show the real status of impurity, <s>māyā</s>, and <s>karma</s>.
Thus, in the knowledge whose means are the three powers, the last of them
is the root; the one beyond it is the middle, and the one beyond that is the first.
Higher even than that is the supreme knowledge, free from means and the like,
resting in the power of bliss; here it is called the unsurpassed, <s>anuttara</s>.
That self-luminous consciousness, whose true being is difficult to obtain
even for <s>Vidyās</s>, <s>Vidyeśvaras</s>, and others, is taught in the <s>Śrīsiddhātantra</s>.
And this is clearly indicated in the eighteenth chapter of the <s>Mālinī</s>,
through the statement, 'and this is not so without the grace of <s>Śaṃkara</s>.'
By this very reading in the <s>Mālinīvijayottara</s>,
this fourfold knowledge, the great rise of accomplishment and liberation,
is set forth by me in this scripture named <s>Tantrāloka</s>.
There, in this matter, whatever is reflected upon inwardly or outwardly,
though its form has not yet been opened out, shines forth first.
So too there is manifestation with an unopened form, as a definable self;
doubt arises when some form has been determined, not otherwise.
In the primary question 'What is this?', a portion of this object is well ascertained;
doubt has a nature in which properties such as existence and non-existence remain unopened.
No further meaning of the word 'what?' comes to light;
rather, it denotes only the very thing whose form has not been disclosed.

children.text: sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti na mukhyo 'styeṣa saṃśayaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Is it a post or a man?' is not this primary doubt;
for that is simply the arising of determination among many classes of properties.
Again, because the twofold form to be reflected upon remains unopened,
doubt lies in the aspect 'what is it?', while conceptual determination is otherwise clear.
Therefore the first presentation, namely the manifestation of being whose self is unopened,

children.text: prathamaṃ sa ihoddeśaḥ praśnaḥ saṃśaya eva ca ||
children.translated_text: is here the statement, the question, and doubt itself.
Likewise, by the path of the expansion of being whose form is unopened,
self-awareness, as it expands, becomes the questioner, taking on the nature of the pupil.
Likewise, because there is concealment whose nature is the certainty of inward reflection,
and although it shares in the rise of contraction born immediately after expansion,
to whatever extent there may be outward expansion whose self is clearly manifest,
to that same extent it, with its form still unopened, is called the questioner.
Awakening itself, in this way, has the form of question and answer;
even in the positions of guru and pupil, this difference of bodies is not ultimately real.
For awareness, because its nature is awareness, makes the many forms established within
appear outwardly at once, as universal and particular.
The production of some property capable of expecting a particular aspect that is to be produced
is the production of the universal; that is of the nature of doubt.
But when the particular aspect that is to be produced comes to a halt,
then there is determination acceptable to the knower, not otherwise, even through tens of millions of constructs.
Then, because of skill in entering the strength of that object's own self,
its opening out through that act gives determinations in the form of definitions and answers.
Again, as they follow behind as many determined portions of properties,
there is repeated examination whose nature is statement and definition.
In perception, inference, comparison, trustworthy testimony, and the like, everywhere
the triad of statement, definition, and examination shines forth for living beings.
The non-conceptual presentation is statement; conceptual construction, again, is definition;
and, in direct perception, examination is a succession of conceptual determinations.
'This is a tree' is the statement; 'because it has smoke, it has fire'
is the definable mark, while the network of knowledge of pervasion and the rest is the examination here.
In comparison, 'this object here' is the prior statement; 'called a <s>gavaya</s>, similar to a cow'

children.text: iti vā lakṣaṇaṃ śeṣaḥ parīkṣopamitau bhavet ||
children.translated_text: is the definition, while the remainder would be the examination in comparison.
In 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice,' 'one who desires heaven' is such a statement, and 'should sacrifice' is its definition.
As for the phrase "with the <s>agniṣṭoma</s> and the like," this examination applies to what remains.
When alternatives are being created, and when one allows for portions agreeable to another's taste,
the creation of an object as being just so is called <s>uddeśa</s> (initial statement).
At that very time consciousness selects just so much as has the character of being created,
for, not delimited by time, it connects what belongs to all times.
The creation of what is being created and the withdrawal of a portion already created,
when a property is being restated, is called the defining mark of consciousness.
The further creations, withdrawals, and rests of portions that follow upon that
are called <s>parīkṣā</s> (examination), fashioned with a boundary according to the knower's inclination.

children.text: prākpaśyantyatha madhyānyā vaikharī ceti tā imāḥ
children.translated_text: First come <s>parā</s>, then <s>paśyantī</s>, <s>madhyamā</s>, and <s>vaikharī</s>; these are those forms of speech.
They are the goddesses <s>parā</s> and <s>parāparā</s>, while the last has the nature of <s>aparā</s>.
This very thing is described as the triad of powers beginning with will.
Animated by this, this whole sphere of practical discourse is extended.
Since, in the <s>Pārameśvaraśāsana</s>, it has the nature of question and answer,
within the fivefold connection it has the form of relation to the supreme.
As is stated in the <s>Ratnamālā</s>: everything is made of the supreme <s>kalā</s>.
The <s>mahā</s>, the <s>nava</s>, the inner, the divine, and the mixed are taught; the mutual one is the fifth.
The unity of the two, the questioner and the speaker, is called
<s>saṃbandha</s> (connection); and its supremacy consists in the manifestation of complete unity.
By this same method another kind of connection too may fully exist,
as what is expressed by scripture, because results and the rest possess completeness.
Thus this consciousness, the goddess, always by its very nature
has the triad beginning with <s>uddeśa</s> as its life and is the very form of all scripture.
There the preliminary <s>uddeśa</s> is taught, divided into what is prior-born and what is subsequent.
The means connected with the division of knowledge is followed by the supreme means as the third.
Then come the <s>śākta</s> means, the human means, and, as the seventh, the means concerning time.
Then there are the arising of the wheel, the path of place, the path of principles, and the division of principles.
There are the path beginning with <s>kalā</s>, the application of the paths, <s>śaktipāta</s>, and concealment.
There are the preliminary undertaking of initiation and initiation in the <s>sāmayī</s> and <s>pautrika</s> rites.
There are the procedure of knowables, subtle initiation, and immediate departure.
Then come <s>tulādīkṣā</s>, remote initiation, raising up the <s>liṅga</s>, and consecration.
There are funeral rites, the arrangement of <s>śrāddha</s>, and the explanation of remaining conduct.
There are worship of the <s>liṅga</s> and occasional rites such as many divisions, festivals, and <s>pavitra</s>.
There are secret conduct, the flood of mantras, the <s>maṇḍala</s>, and the rite of seals.
There are unification, entry into one's own true form, and the bringing together of the scriptures.
There are the statement of future consequence and the determination that the scripture is to be accepted.

children.text: iti saptādhikāmenāṃ triṃśataṃ yaḥ sadā budhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, if a wise person constantly studies this collection of thirty plus seven
<s>āhnikas</s>, he becomes <s>Bhairava</s> directly.
When complete awakening in the thirty-seven makes one <s>Bhairava</s>,
what wonder is it if even limited beings attain <s>Bhairava</s>-hood through his glance?
This is the prior <s>uddeśa</s>; now the subsequent one is being stated.
In the section on the division of knowledge, everything is set forth in order.
In the second section there is the distinction of being beyond the means.
In the supreme means are analyzed the reflection of universal consciousness, the sequence of the arising of reflective awareness,
and the state of being nondifferent in form from mantra and the rest.
The refinement of conceptual construction, the reality of reasoning, and the true nature of the guru,
the uselessness of the limbs of yoga, and disregard for imagined worship and the like,
the arising of the wheel of consciousness, the potency of mantra, and the real nature of recitation and the like,
and the equality of prohibition and injunction are discussed here in the <s>śākta</s> means.
Intellectual meditation, the principle of breath, full utterance, the nature of consciousness,
and utterance as the mark of the path of entry into the inner supreme reality,
as well as the instrument and the principle of phonemes, are explained in the <s>āṇava</s> means.
The imagined construction of the moving measure, the day and night, transitions, and the like,
the manifoldness of withdrawal, and the arising of phonemes are treated in the construction of the path of time.
The division of wheels and the division of mantras and vidyās belong to this arising of the wheel.
Measure, the collection of bodies, and the linking of principles
are set out in the indication of the path of place; two topics belong to the determination of the path of principles.
These are the relation of effect and cause and the explanation of the sequence of principles.
The property of things, the rule of principles, and the explanation of waking and the other states
together with the distinction of cognizing subjects are considered in the division of principles.
The nature of <s>kalā</s> and the construction of principles by one, three, five, and other numbers,
the order of divisions of phonemes, and the explanation of the supporting power of all
are analyzed to this extent within the further inquiry into the path beginning with <s>kalā</s>.
The undisturbed laughter born of the contemplation of non-difference is treated in the application of the paths.
The increase in number of impurities and the like, the reality of them, and the manifoldness of powers,
the establishment of independence, and the manifoldness of concealment
are the extent of what is to be stated in the examination of <s>śaktipāta</s>.
The removal of concealment and fullness through knowledge,
together with the uselessness of departing from the body, are established in the preliminary undertaking of initiation.
In the examination of the disciple's suitability and the like, there is the division of places and the construction of place.
The division of general <s>nyāsa</s> and the vessel for <s>argha</s> are its purpose.
The suitability of substances, worship, and the worship of the outer door follow in order.
There are entry, the nature of the directions, and the purification of body, breath, and the rest.
There are the manifoldness of special <s>nyāsa</s> and the vessel for the special <s>argha</s>.
There are worship of the body and worship through <s>nyāsa</s> on one's own paths of breath, intellect, and consciousness.
There is the surpassing of the groups of other scriptures and worship of the wheel in every respect.
There are the taking of the ritual ground, the five products of the cow, and worship of the earth and <s>Gaṇeśa</s> groups.
There are worship of the weapon, the fire rite, and also the consecrating preparation connected with fire.
There are libation, the preparation of the oblation, and the final rite with the tooth-stick.
Also, the rite of <s>śivahasta</s> and the consideration of preparing the couch,
the occasional rite connected with sleep, and the <s>samayas</s> (initiatory observances): this is the summary.
In this rite of becoming a <s>samayin</s>, in the fifteenth <s>āhnika</s>, there will be
the contemplation of identity with the <s>maṇḍala</s> and an extensive treatment of the animal to be offered.
The satisfaction of the fire, the kindling of one's own nature, and, in the disciple's body,
the rite of installing the paths, together with the variety of what is to be purified, what purifies, and so on,
the divisions of initiation, the supreme installation, the purpose of the reality of mantra,
and the distinction of the <s>yojanikā</s> and the rest are to occur here in the sixteenth <s>āhnika</s>.
The preparation of the thread, the purification of the principles, the burning of the bonds, and then the joining,
and likewise the division of the paths: thus has it been stated in the <s>pautrika</s> rite.
The absence of birth and the rest, and then the clear distinction among mantras:
these are to occur in the eighteenth <s>āhnika</s>, called 'Concise Initiation.'
Examination of the <s>kalās</s>, installation of the dagger and the rest, and the bodily practice of movement,
together with the rite of <s>Brahmavidyā</s>: thus it has been taught in the chapter on immediate ascent.
The examination of eligibility, the inner consecration, and then the rite of the balance:
this whole matter to be spoken of belongs to the twentieth <s>āhnika</s>.
The rite concerning the dead and the living, instruction in the net, the group of consecratory acts,
and consideration of strength and weakness: this is the procedure in the twenty-first <s>āhnika</s>.
Hearing, authorization, purification, the removal of sin,
and the cutting away of doubt are what is clearly to be spoken of in the sequence of extracting the <s>liṅga</s>.
Examination, making one an <s>ācārya</s>, his vow, and the removal of wrong understanding,
its divisions, and the status of being a <s>sādhaka</s>: this much belongs to the rite of consecration.
Then the eligible person, the consecration, and its purpose:
this is what is to be discussed in the twenty-fourth <s>āhnika</s>, called the final sacrifice.
The purpose, through the granting of enjoyment and liberation, and here the rite itself are clear.
In the twenty-fifth <s>āhnika</s>, the illumination of <s>śrāddha</s>, there is a collection of the subject matter.
The purpose of the remaining observance, daily worship, the supreme worship on the altar,
the nature of the <s>liṅga</s> in many forms, and the definition of the rosary:
the divisions of worship are to be stated in the illumination of <s>liṅga</s>-worship.
Next come the division of occasional observances and the rule concerning their purpose,
the distinctions of festival days, their particular features, the discussion of the <s>cakra</s>, and its worship,
and the analysis of the purpose of worship on days beginning and ending with the guru and the rest.
The examination of death, and likewise the rites such as the assembly of the <s>Yoginīs</s>,
the method of explanation, the rule concerning what has been heard, and the rule of guru-worship: this much
is contained in the twenty-eighth <s>āhnika</s>, also called the illumination of occasional rites.
The distinction of the eligible self, the sequence concerning the perfected wife and the family,
the rite of worship, the rites of the messenger, and the sequence of the secret <s>Upaniṣad</s>,
initiation, consecration, and awakening: these are in the twenty-ninth <s>āhnika</s>.
The nature of mantra and its potency are explained in the thirtieth.
The distinctions of the trident and lotus, and the analysis of <s>Vyomeśa</s>, the <s>svastika</s>, and the like,
are to be expounded at length in the thirty-first <s>āhnika</s>.
Distinctions of what is subordinate and what is principal, the nature, and the discussion of potency,
and the distinction of <s>kalās</s>: these are stated in the illumination of the <s>mudrās</s>.
Since, beginning with the thirty-two principles and with what is called <s>Īśa</s>, it is quite clear
that there is no difference, that other outline has therefore not been stated here.
And because they are chiefly to be known, the sequence of another authority section
has been stated as an outlining method, for the sake of easy comprehension.
Now their characteristics and examination are explained in order.

children.text: ātmā saṃvitprakāśasthitir anavayavā saṃvidityāttaśaktivrātaṃ tasya svarūpaṃ sa ca nija mahasaśchādanādbaddharūpaḥ
children.translated_text: The self is the abiding radiance of consciousness, consciousness without parts; the mass of powers taken on by it is its nature, and it has the form of a bound being because of the concealment of its own splendor.

children.text: ātmajyotiḥsvabhāvaprakaṭanavidhinā tasya mokṣaḥ sa cāyaṃ citrākārasya citraḥ prakaṭita iha yatsaṃgraheṇārtha eṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Its liberation comes through the method of manifesting its nature as the light of the self; and this, variegated because it assumes variegated forms, is the meaning set forth here in brief.

children.text: mithyājñānaṃ timiramasamān dṛṣṭidoṣānprasūte tatsadbhāvādvimalamapi tadbhāti mālinyadhāma
children.translated_text: False knowledge, like darkness, produces unequal defects of sight; because of its presence, even what is stainless appears as an abode of impurity.

children.text: yattu prekṣyaṃ dṛśi parigataṃ taimirīṃ doṣamudrāṃ dūraṃ rundhet prabhavatu kathaṃ tatra mālinyaśaṅkā ||
children.translated_text: But when the object to be seen, having entered vision, wards far away the mark of the defect caused by darkness, how could any suspicion of impurity prevail there?

children.text: bhāvavrātahaṭhājjanasya hṛdayānyākramya yannartayan bhaṅgībhirvividhābhirātmahṛdayaṃ pracchādya saṃkrīḍase
children.translated_text: By forcefully entering people's hearts through the multitude of entities, making them dance with many different gestures, and concealing your own heart, you play.

children.text: yastvāmāha jaḍaṃ jaḍaḥ sahṛdayaṃmanyatvaduḥśikṣito manye 'muṣya jaḍātmatā stutipadaṃ tvatsāmyasaṃbhāvanāt ||
children.translated_text: The dull person, badly trained in his self-image as a connoisseur, who calls you dull: I think his dullness is worthy of praise, because it suggests similarity to you.
Here gurus who have shed impurity, who know the higher and the lower, and who consist of the reality of <s>Śiva</s>, are authorized
for thorough inquiry; therefore the request for the removal of the stain of hatred toward that is fruitless.
That first word there, whose form is the uninterrupted cognition of the unsurpassed,
I begin this second section in order to determine it.

children.text: anupāyaṃ hi yadrūpaṃ ko 'rtho deśanayātra vai
children.translated_text: For the reality whose nature is <s>anupāya</s> (meanslessness), what purpose could instruction have here?
There may be instruction once; afterward it is called meanslessness.
If this principle is meansless, how could it be so without a means?

children.text: svayaṃ tu teṣāṃ tattādṛk kiṃ brūmaḥ kila tānprati ||
children.translated_text: But for those for whom it is of just such a kind by itself, what indeed can we say to them?
That fourfold form of all-pervading consciousness which has been stated

children.text: svabhāva eva mantavyaḥ sa hi nityodito vibhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: is to be regarded as its very nature, for it is all-pervading and eternally arisen.
By so many countless natures through which it shines forth,
some enter it by a portion of a portion, while others enter without parts.
Even there, because of relation to difference depending on means such as subsidiary means,
the variety even of the means cannot be denied, since it is other than that.
Among them, those whose selves are stainless, [approach] their own consciousness as <s>Bhairava</s>
For those who abide in <s>nirupāya</s> (the path without means), its procedure is now set forth.
There, first of all, the yoga of action cannot deserve the status of a means,
for, on the contrary, it is understood to have arisen from that.
If it is said, 'It would indeed be a means for cognition,' then cognition is explained as
luminosity; and how could that come from another, when it is self-luminous in itself?
Who, then, needs arguments for this: that the reality of consciousness is self-luminous?
If that were absent, the universe, being inert, would not illuminate anything.
Whatever means there may be, whether external or also some internal one,
all of it looks toward that; how could it possess the status of a means in regard to that?

children.text: tyajāvadhānāni nanu kva nāma dhatse 'vadhānaṃ vicinu svayaṃ tat
children.translated_text: Give up acts of attention. Come now, where indeed do you place attention? Examine that for yourself.

children.text: pūrṇe 'vadhānaṃ na hi nāma yuktaṃ nāpūrṇamabhyeti ca satyabhāvam ||
children.translated_text: Attention is certainly not appropriate in the full, and what is not full does not attain true being.
Therefore, for visualization and the like, whose very life is attention, on the supreme path,
the <s>Bhairava</s> path, how could there be direct instrumentality as a means?
Even those who seek to discern that form by a direct means
are surely dull people who want fireflies for perceiving the sun.
Moreover, whatever this is that is accepted as an external or internal means,
is merely the nature of luminosity, the own body of <s>Śiva</s> alone.

children.text: nīlaṃ pītaṃ sukhamiti prakāśaḥ kevalaḥ śivaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Blue,' 'yellow,' 'pleasure': the light alone is <s>Śiva</s>.
In that supreme nonduality whose nature is luminosity, what other thing could there be?
Could there be a relation of means and object to be attained? For he is only luminosity.
This difference consisting of duality, and also the statement 'this is nonduality,'
this <s>Parameśvara</s> shines as a body of luminosity alone.

children.text: asyāṃ bhūmau sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ bandho mokṣaścitirjaḍaḥ
children.translated_text: On this level, pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, consciousness, and the inert,
like the words 'ghaṭa' and 'kumbha' for a pot, have one meaning; they too are one alone.
For how could a non-luminous part within luminosity ever come to be luminous?
Or, if that is illumined, then the dualities relative to it are abolished.
Or, if it is not illumined, how can substantial reality be asserted of it?
Therefore its being a particular form of luminosity is not established.
Therefore, when this thesis, 'this is one luminosity,' is well established,
those who maintain differentiated cognitions are truly warded off from afar.
Mere luminosity is stated because non-luminosity is denied;
but the meaning of the word 'one' is not number, which involves difference among individual consciousnesses.
This is not the great goddess <s>Śakti</s>, because it is not dependent on another;

children.text: na caiṣa śaktimāndevo na kasyāpyāśrayo yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: nor is this the powerful god, because it is no support for anything.
This is not to be meditated on, because there is no state of meditator; nor is it a meditator, since what is to be meditated on is absent.
It is not worshipful, because there is no worshipper; nor a worshipper, because there is no worshipful object.

children.text: na mantro na ca mantryo 'sau na ca mantrayitā prabhuḥ
children.translated_text: The Lord is not a mantra, nor something to be empowered by mantra, nor a user of mantra;

children.text: na dīkṣā dīkṣako vāpi na dīkṣāvānmaheśvaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Maheśvara</s> is neither initiation, nor an initiator, nor one who has received initiation.
Here there is no place, seat, restraint, oblation-water, conjunction, invocation, and the rest,
ending with dismissal, since agent, object, and action have been abandoned.
It is not existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor that which is devoid of both.
For that state is hard to know: it is somehow this unsurpassed <s>anuttara</s>.
For any entity that appears as 'this' has a delimiting nature;

children.text: sa eva ghaṭavalloke saṃstathā naiṣa bhairavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that alone is established in the world like a pot, but this <s>Bhairava</s> is not so.
Non-being and non-luminosity have no usefulness anywhere;
the universe's life is real, and he consists of luminosity alone.

children.text: ābhyāmeva tu hetubhyāṃ na dvyātmā na dvayojjhitaḥ
children.translated_text: For these two very reasons, he is not of two natures and not devoid of the two.

children.text: sarvātmanā hi bhātyeṣa kena rūpeṇa mantryatām ||
children.translated_text: For he shines in every way; in what form could he be treated by mantra?
In the venerable <s>Triśiras</s> it is taught as the nature of supreme knowledge:
the supreme state, pregnant with power, through the power dwelling within the womb.

children.text: na bhāvo nāpyabhāvo na dvayaṃ vācāmagocarāt
children.translated_text: It is neither being nor non-being nor the two, because it is beyond the range of speech;
it has ascended to the inexpressible path, abiding in power and devoid of power.
Thus those who are purified by the ultimate reality of firmly established consciousness
and are established on the path of the unsurpassed are not constrained by means.
For them this whole circle of entities shines forth on every side,
standing directly before them, dissolved in the fire of consciousness-<s>Bhairava</s>.
For these people, imaginings of portions of pleasure and pain, doubt, and anxiety
have come to have only complete immersion in the non-conceptual supreme as their remainder.

children.text: eṣāṃ na mantro na dhyānaṃ na pūjā nāpi kalpanā
children.translated_text: For them there is no mantra, no meditation, no worship, and no conceptual imagining,
no repose of any kind extending from the <s>samayin</s> and the rest up to the teacher.
They have the nature of a chisel that cuts through the whole apparatus of restraints;
in their remaining activity, nothing beyond grace has any purpose.

children.text: svaṃ kartavyaṃ kimapi kalayaṃlloka eṣa prayatnānno pārārthyaṃ prati ghaṭayate kāṃcana svapravṛttim
children.translated_text: This person in the world, calculating some duty of his own, through efforts does not direct any activity of his toward another's good;

children.text: yastu dhvastākhilabhavamalo bhairavībhāvapūrṇaḥ kṛtyaṃ tasya sphuṭamidamiyallokakartavyamātram ||
children.translated_text: but for one whose every impurity of becoming has been destroyed and who is full of the state of <s>Bhairava</s>, this much is plainly his task: only the duty of the world.
Those who see him, through the gradual taking on of his form, become stainless in consciousness;
they too become of that form; to that extent alone is his nature as grace.
This knowledge of reality is called the principal sacrifice and the like,
up to initiation, by the Lord in the venerable <s>Siddhayogīśvarīmata</s>.
Higher than the ritual ground is the <s>tūra</s>; higher than the <s>tūra</s> is the cloth;
higher than the cloth is meditation; then the object meditated on; after that there would be the higher fixation.
Higher even than that is the form born of yoga; higher even than that is knowledge;
for by knowledge the yogin becomes a great accomplished <s>Yogīśvara</s>.
Even he, by the abode of his own freedom, if he wishes to bestow grace
on those whose consciousness is not pure, should resort to the procedure intended for that.
And that grace is said to be varied according to those who are to be favored,
because of the distinctions produced by its mixture with the streams of means beginning with the supreme and the non-supreme.
For that very purpose, even for this one whose nature is <s>Parameśvara</s>,
there is attentive regard for hearing and studying the scriptures and teachings concerning those means.

children.text: nahi tasya svatantrasya kāpi kutrāpi khaṇḍanā
children.translated_text: For nowhere is there any impairment of that independent one;
but grace toward a person whose mind is not pure is not without a means.
In the venerable great scripture called <s>Ūrmimahāśāstra</s>, which has the form of the lineage of siddhas,
this was said; likewise it was taught by venerable teachers beginning with <s>Somānanda</s>.
From the guru's words, or through the cleansing produced by arranging a mass of reasonings, or from confidence arisen toward scripture, or from what has been taught,

children.text: vilīne śaṅkābhre hṛdayagaganodbhāsimahasaḥ prabhoḥ sūryasyeva spṛśata caraṇāndhvāntajayinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: when the cloud of doubt has dissolved, touch the feet of the Lord, whose radiance shines in the sky of the heart, like the sun, conquering darkness.
This daily section, discerning the unsurpassed abode and free from what is suitable to means, has been composed.
Now the supreme means-related teaching is set forth: the unsurpassed state itself of the great Lord.
The mere light which has been called the supreme <s>Bhairava</s> radiance:
there, mere freedom is further analyzed.

children.text: yaḥ prakāśaḥ sa sarvasya prakāśatvaṃ prayacchati
children.translated_text: That which is light grants luminosity to everything;
and the universe does not exist apart from it, whether it is real or merely appears.
Therefore that supreme Lord, unobstructed in the sky of his own Self,
displays this vast spectacle of creation and withdrawal.
Just as earth, water, and the rest shine in a spotless mirror,
unmixed, so the activities of the universe shine in the one Lord of consciousness.
A similar form appears in the eye, in a mirror, in the sky, and in water;
for in a pure form, it is form alone that appears.
A woman secretly in love, touching a mirror made beautiful by the reflection of her lover
with her pitcher-like breasts, still is not satisfied.

children.text: na hi sparśo 'sya vimalo rūpameva tathā yataḥ
children.translated_text: For his touch is not there; because the mirror is pure, it is only form in that way.
And purity is an extremely close, single conjunction with what is of the same kind.
The capacity to show within oneself, because of non-difference, what is different,
without abandoning one's own luminosity: that is purity, as taught by the gurus.
Primary purity belongs wholly to the one Lord of consciousness;
elsewhere, something is pure in some respect through the relation of part and whole, according to his will.
The body of entities that offers resistance is indeed made of <s>māyā</s>;
but those very entities also have a non-resistant form made of <s>sadvidyā</s>.
Thus, illuminating appearance as having both forms,
the boon-giving Lord shines in all things in the manner of image and reflection.
But someone who says, 'The rays of the eyes rebound strongly from a clear surface,

children.text: viparyasya svakaṃ vaktraṃ gṛhṇantīti sa pṛcchyate ||
children.translated_text: turn back, and apprehend one's own face,' should be questioned.
The light that is apart from the body belongs to the self that presides over it;

children.text: tenaiva tejasā jñatve ko 'rthaḥ syāddarpaṇena tu ||
children.translated_text: if cognition occurs by that very light, what purpose would there be for a mirror?
And if the rays, turned back and having assumed the nature of an apprehender,

children.text: rūpaṃ dṛśyeta vadane nije na makurāntare ||
children.translated_text: were to see the form, it would be seen on one's own face, not inside the mirror.
This form on my own face would shine as mine, like touch;
but it does not do so as something different from the tangible and whose nature is purely knowable.
That reflected object is only the configuration of visible form;
it is connected with touch, smell, taste, and the rest only as subordinated.
Their subordination is because they are not apprehensible; their absence follows from the lack of a valid means of knowledge.
That lack follows from absence of contact with the object, and that too follows because the object is not located in the mirror.
For this very reason properties such as heaviness are not observed in it.
For it is not situated in the mirror; in seeing it, the mirror is the means.

children.text: tasmāttu naiṣa bhedena yadbhāti tata ucyate
children.translated_text: Therefore this does not shine as something separate; because it shines from that,
that is called the support. There the means are, in order, lamp, sight, and consciousness.
Because lamp, eye, and acts of awareness lack hardness,
and because they are pure on every side, they do not appear separately like a mirror.
And this has been shown by the God of gods for the increase of understanding.
For the deluded it becomes a real object, but even beyond that it is not sufficient elsewhere.

children.text: pratīghāti svatantraṃ no na sthāyyasthāyi cāpi na
children.translated_text: It is not resistant, not independent, and it is neither permanent nor impermanent;
this is the greatness of some clear reality, as stated by the compassionate one.

children.text: na deśo no rūpaṃ na ca samayayogo na parimā na cānyonyāsaṃgo na ca tadapahānirna ghanatā
children.translated_text: There is no place, no form, no conjunction with time, no measure, no mutual contact, no removal of that, and no density;

children.text: na cāvastutvaṃ syānna ca kimapi sāraṃ nijamiti dhruvaṃ mohaḥ śāmyediti niradiśaddarpaṇavidhiḥ ||
