children.translated_text: nor is there unreality, nor any essence of its own. Thus, surely, delusion would cease: so he taught the method of the mirror.
When the path of reflection has been shown there in this way,
that which is a reflection of sound is called an echo.

children.text: na cāsau śabdajaḥ śabda āgacchattvena saṃśravāt
children.translated_text: And that sound is not a sound born from sound, since it is heard as coming,
and also because people far away do not hear the sound from that same speaker.
When there is contact with openings distinguished by covered portions of hollows and the like,
because this sound is variegated, it is a reflection, like a face and so on.
It appears as, 'This is the form of another object of knowledge,'
just as in a mirror: 'I hear what has been spoken by someone.'
Because a reflection is necessarily turned toward its image,
perceivers situated between them hear the echoed sound.
Even without apprehending the primary object, there may be apprehension of the reflection;
one may see a beloved standing behind oneself, her form imprinted in a mirror.
And such facing is spoken of because it is established as non-different from the mirror.
Therefore it is reflected in the hollow space of a well and the like...
The space of the mouth, accompanied by sound, shines forth as real, like that other mouth.
And just as one who stands behind a mirror does not perceive the face,
so one who stands behind a space of that kind does not perceive the sound.
A sound that has not become manifest certainly is not reflected.
Its manifestation and its hearing occur at the same time in the second moment.
But in a moment, its being a reflection and its hearing are simultaneous.
For the ascertainment of the hand and of its shadow-form is not simultaneous.
When, in this way, the true nature of reflection has been shown there,
we state the matter at hand: there, sound is capable of being reflected.
Sound in space is beautiful, in the delightful domain of touch.
Another touch too, arising from a hard blow, from pain, cold, and the like,
though located in another, because it is a reflection, causes hair to rise on one's own body.
And this is not primary, because it does not disclose the succession of its effects.

children.text: evaṃ ghrāṇāntare gandho raso dantodake sphuṭaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, smell in another nose and taste in the saliva are clear.

children.text: yathā ca rūpaṃ pratibimbitaṃ dṛśorna cakṣuṣānyena vinā hi lakṣyate
children.translated_text: And just as a reflected form is not perceived by the two eyes without another eye,

children.text: tathā rasasparśanasaurabhādikaṃ na lakṣyate 'kṣeṇa vinā sthitaṃ tvapi ||
children.translated_text: so taste, touch, fragrance, and the like, though present, are not perceived without the sense faculty.

children.text: na cāntare sparśanadhāmani sthitaṃ bahiḥspṛśo 'nyākṣadhiyaḥ sa gocaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor, when it is situated within in the domain of touch, is it the object of external contact or of cognition by another sense.
Therefore, when this has been effected by the inner organs whose purpose is one's own such sense faculty standing near it,

children.text: tadā tadāttaṃ pratibimbamindriye svakāṃ kriyāṃ sūyata eva tādṛśīm ||
children.translated_text: then the reflection received by that sense organ gives rise to its own action of just that kind.

children.text: na tu smṛtānmānasagocarādṛtā bhavetkriyā sā kila vartamānataḥ
children.translated_text: But that action would not arise in the present merely from a remembered object within the range of the mind.

children.text: ataḥ sthitaḥ sparśavarastadindriye samāgataḥ sanviditas tathākriyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the excellent touch, standing in that sense organ and having arrived there, is known and has such an action.

children.text: asaṃbhave bāhyagatasya tādṛśaḥ sva eva tasmin pratibimbitastathā
children.translated_text: When such an externally situated thing is impossible, that same excellent touch, reflected there from itself,

children.text: karoti tāṃ sparśavaraḥ sukhātmikāṃ sa cāpi kasyāmapi nāḍisaṃtatau ||
children.translated_text: produces that blissful action, and it too does so in some continuum of <s>nāḍīs</s>.
Thus, depositing the universe as itself in the mirror of consciousness,
it proclaims the stainless universal form of that Lord.
And just as smell, form, touch, taste, and the rest, when reflected,
shine through the coloring of their support, like a face and so on in a sword-blade,
so this universe, reflected in awareness, assumes
the broad expanse of qualities beginning with luminosity and freedom.

children.text: yathā ca sarvataḥ svacche sphaṭike sarvato bhavet
children.translated_text: And just as, in a crystal that is transparent on every side, there would be reflection from every side,
so too in awareness, which enjoys transparency on every side.
That extreme transparency is the non-appearance of its own shape;

children.text: ataḥ svacchatamo bodho na ratnaṃ tvākṛtigrahāt ||
children.translated_text: therefore awareness is most transparent, not a jewel, since a jewel retains a shape.
A reflection is bestowed by an original image situated outside.
If that very image too has the nature of a reflection, what original image could remain?
Or if some cause is consecrated as the original image,
that too becomes a reflection in awareness; otherwise it would be unreal.
Thus this, guarded by the weapon of firm reasoning based on self-awareness,
the sovereignty of reflection alone expands throughout the whole universe.

children.text: nanu bimbasya virahe pratibimbaṃ kathaṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: But, in the absence of an original image, how could there be a reflection?

children.text: kiṃ kurmo dṛśyate taddhi nanu tadbimbamucyatām ||
children.translated_text: What can we do? For it is seen. 'Then let that be called the original image.'
Not so, because it lacks that definition. What, indeed, is called an original image?
A face, for example, appearing as existent, independent, and unmixed with another.
Without abandoning its own nature, resemblance to another form
is called the state of being a reflection, as on the surface of a sword-blade, mirror, and the like.
And it has been said by the <s>Saugatas</s>: even when there is an external thing, cognition is one, yet because it cognizes many,
it has forms resembling many existent things, but it is not itself many.
But if this is so, what is the definition of reflection? It is stated:
Because it cannot be mixed with another, and because its difference cannot appear,
they call it a reflection, like a face in a mirror.
Since this is mixed with awareness and cannot appear as different from awareness,

children.text: paratattvādi bodhe kiṃ pratibimbaṃ na bhaṇyate ||
children.translated_text: why should supreme reality and the rest not be said to be a reflection in awareness?
If it is asked, 'Whence comes this fixed application of the definition? Let it be called the original image,'

children.text: prājñā vastuni yujyante na tu sāmayike dhvanau ||
children.translated_text: the wise are concerned with the thing, not with a conventional word.

children.text: nanu na pratibimbasya vinā bimbaṃ bhavetsthitiḥ
children.translated_text: But a reflection cannot have existence without an original image.

children.text: kiṃ tataḥ pratibimbe hi bimbaṃ tādātmyavṛtti na ||
children.translated_text: What follows from that? For in a reflection the original image exists by identity, does it not?
And therefore, when that is impossible, there is no damage to this definition as stated;
the question comes to rest merely on the cause.
There too it concerns the cause called the occasioning cause, and in no way the material cause.
And occasioning causes sometimes occur somewhere.
For this very reason, in a light present before one, by an occasioning cause such as memory,
let the form of the beloved be transferred there when that occasion is dense.
Otherwise, why does the beloved, mounted in consciousness and joined with separation,

children.text: kasmādbhāti na vai saṃvid vicchedaṃ purato gatā ||
children.translated_text: not appear when consciousness, going before one, has gone beyond separation?
For this very reason, let there clearly be some internal principle called cognition,
where its appearing with separation occurs in imagination and dream-vision.

children.text: ato nimittaṃ devasya śaktayaḥ santu tādṛśe
children.translated_text: Therefore the powers of the Lord may be the occasioning causes in such a case.
Thus this whole universe, in the clear <s>Bhairava</s>-consciousness-space
of the Lord, is fully a reflection, and certainly not through the favor of another.
That which, for the Lord's being the self of the universe, has no dependence on anything else,

children.text: tāṃ parāṃ pratibhāṃ devīṃ saṃgirante hyanuttarām ||
children.translated_text: they call that supreme goddess, the unsurpassed <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition).
She is rich in the manifestation of <s>kula</s> for this <s>akula</s> Lord.

children.text: kaulikī sā parā śaktir aviyukto yayā prabhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: That supreme power is <s>Kaulikī</s>, by whom the Lord is never separated.

children.text: tayoryadyāmalaṃ rūpaṃ sa saṃghaṭṭa iti smṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: If there is a paired form of those two, that is remembered as <s>saṃghaṭṭa</s> (coalescent union).
It itself is called the power of bliss, since from it the universe is emitted.
This goddess is called the reality beyond the supreme-and-non-supreme.

children.text: tatsāraṃ tacca hṛdayaṃ sa visargaḥ paraḥ prabhuḥ ||
children.translated_text: That is its essence, that is its heart; he is the supreme <s>visarga</s> (emission), the Lord.
In the <s>Devīyāmalaśāstra</s> she is described as <s>Kālakarṣiṇī</s>.
Likewise, she is taught in the rite of the <s>Mahāḍāmara</s> and at the head of the <s>Śrīparā</s>.
In the <s>Śrīpūrvaśāstra</s> she is described as the true being of the Mothers.
In this <s>saṃghaṭṭa</s>, because it has the nature of consciousness, the reflective awareness of what is there
is the will-power, the supreme mistress of the <s>Aghorā</s> powers.
If she herself becomes agitated in form, she comes into being as the ruling power.

children.text: tadā ghorāḥ parā devyo jātāḥ śaivādhvadaiśikāḥ
children.translated_text: Then the fierce supreme goddesses are born, instructresses on the Śaiva path.
The self-reflective awareness that previously existed as the single hero,
having the nature of the unfolding of the knowable universe, stands as the power of knowledge.

children.text: iyaṃ parāparā devī ghorāṃ yā mātṛmaṇḍalīm ||
children.translated_text: This is the goddess <s>Parāparā</s>, who creates the fierce circle of Mothers,
unceasingly, as the one lamp for the pure and impure paths.
When the knowable portion, unfolding, reaches agitation because of its predominance,
then, within the state of mere consciousness, an appearance of deficiency arises.
That, once established, is called the beginning of the stability of the class of knowables.
This establishment is the ocean of awakening assuming manifold forms.
This is the seed of that arrangement of seeds; yogins discern it.
The will-power is said to be twofold: agitated and unagitated.
For she takes what is desired into herself through the twofoldness of the object.
Through a power flashing with sudden brilliance and having the form of fire,
there is attainment of what is desired, and then, through steadiness, through the earth-nature.
Although this knowable is present in abundance within the power of unfolding,

children.text: tathāpi vibhavasthānaṃ sā na tu prācyajanmabhūḥ ||
children.translated_text: nevertheless she is the place of manifestation, not the earlier birthplace.
Therefore they declare the fourfold form of the will-power to be the supreme nectar.
Because no further agitation exists, this is not the seed of anything.
Being an agitator is seedhood; being the support of agitation is wombhood.
The agitating form of consciousness both becomes agitated and also agitates.
Agitation is its taking on the character of the knowable; causing agitation is the externalization of that.
The desire to emit the portion of the single seed, non-different from the universe standing within,
is agitation; when it wills what is other than that, they know the manifestation of the will toward reality as causing agitation.
When, having attained union with that, that will becomes effective,
the pupils of glorious <s>Somānanda</s> call this the support of agitation.
That bare knowable, whose distinctions such as observing in consciousness have not yet emerged,
is the seed; through its conjunction, seedhood belongs to the phoneme.

children.text: tasya bījasya saivoktā visisṛkṣā ya udbhavaḥ
children.translated_text: Of that seed, this very desire to emit, which is its arising, is said to belong to it.
For from it this graspable object is to be manifested as if different from consciousness.
This is agitation; causing agitation, however, is the forceful displacement of the other subject, become silent,
from its portion of indifference by the power of consciousness.
Although that desire to emit has arisen, because of union with another reflective awareness,
it becomes fulfilled; this is here proclaimed as the support of agitation.
Then that inner knowable seeks the condition of being imagined as different.
Therefore, from the seed of the universe, the whole external image will unfold.
I have shown the true nature of the relation between the agitated and the agitator,
by the grace of my teacher, the venerable <s>Maheśvara</s>, as he taught it.
Let us return to the matter at hand: this seed is not the tetrad of phonemes,
nor is it a womb, since it does not attain the condition of being the support of agitation.
And because it rests only in itself, it is therefore called nectar-natured.
Thus that pentad which was stated before, mutually
surging in various forms through intermixture with one another,
namely the unsurpassed supreme vibration and bliss as it surges up,
through the collision of will and unfolding, attain extreme variegation.
When unsurpassedness, bliss, and consciousness are placed in the will-power,
they call that the triangle, beautiful with the delight of <s>visarga</s>.
When the powers of unsurpassedness and bliss have reached establishment there,
through conjunction with the pair of triangles they pass into the state of the six-spoked one.
Those very powers, even in conjunction with unfolding, again become identical with it,
and the manifest form of the action-power is made clear mutually.
The agitation situated in will and unfolding that was mentioned, even through that movement,
consists of those same powers sharing that form; they do not remain otherwise.
Objection: But unsurpassedness and bliss are by nature devoid of division;
how have they taken such great variegation into themselves?
Listen, then: this Lord of consciousness has an immeasurable nature,
the master of the phases of dissolution and arising in the manifoldness of infinite powers.
If <s>Maheśvara</s> were to remain with a body of a single form,
he would give up being <s>Maheśvara</s> and being consciousness, like a pot and the like.
For limited luminosity is indeed the defining mark of the insentient.
Since awareness is unlike the insentient, it is not delimited.
Therefore the own powers of the great ocean of awareness, surging forth,
assume, like waves, the variegation of collision within their own self.
The mutual variegation of the powers' collision within the self

children.text: etadeva paraṃ prāhuḥ kriyāśakteḥ sphuṭaṃ vapuḥ
children.translated_text: is precisely what they call the supreme manifest body of the action-power.
In this fourteenth abode, where the three powers have become manifest,
therefore the Teacher in the <s>Śrīpūrvaśāsana</s> called it triśūla-hood.
And this has been taught as stainless by teachers who see reality.
For the possessor of power is colored or marked, but <s>śakti</s> is never marked by anything.
Will, knowledge, and action: whatever is marked out separately in this way,
that very thing is plainly the possessor of power, through its own respective objects of desire and the like.
But when this triad shines forth in unity,
then it cannot be treated as a limiting adjunct by anything, because each would contradict the others.
Therefore the triad of powers, having become fluidly fused, is that trident.
By swift immersion in it, the yogin becomes stainless.
Thus, beginning from the supreme nectar-state, this kind of octad
plainly becomes a set of eight octads through differentiation into the forms beginning with <s>Brāhmī</s>.
Here that <s>Anuttara-śakti</s>, even while making her own body openly present,
is of the form of <s>bindu</s>, because of the impurity of the knowable <s>kalā</s>.
When the power of action has arisen as the abode of moon, sun, and fire,

children.text: avibhāgaḥ prakāśo yaḥ sa binduḥ paramo hi naḥ ||
children.translated_text: the undivided light is indeed, for us, the supreme <s>bindu</s>.
And in the ordinance for protecting reality, this has been taught by <s>Parameśin</s>:
standing within the circle of the heart-lotus, composed of person, power, and <s>Śiva</s>,
the <s>bindu</s>, the stainless deliverer, should be known according to the distinction of dissolution.
That sound, whose nature is <s>nāda</s>, is present in all living beings;
it abides inactive through the division into lower and upper.
The variety consisting of delight, sharpness, and the like, and also of white, red, and so on,
that light itself is independent of them. And the teacher says:

children.text: yanna sūryo na vā somo nāgnirbhāsayate 'pi ca ||
children.translated_text: It is not illuminated by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by fire either;
nor do the sun, moon, and fire have any splendor of their own apart from its light.

children.text: kimapyasti nijaṃ kiṃ tu saṃviditthaṃ prakāśate ||
children.translated_text: Rather, consciousness shines forth in just this way.
Light, joined with the diverse limiting adjuncts that arise through the power of its own freedom,
enters into subordinate variety such as sharpness and the like.
Though the hot-rayed sun is difficult to look at, when it falls on a path of waters
it becomes a delight to the eyes; see the power of the limiting adjunct.
That light in the sun and the rest is muddied by limiting adjuncts;
therefore it depends on the <s>Māheśa</s> light of consciousness.
Mere light, clearly manifest, is plainly called the sun.
That which pours out the essential portion of the object to be illuminated is called the moon.
They call the sun the means of knowledge; they describe the moon as the knowable object.
Although both are autonomous, they stand inseparably joined to one another.
This, whose nature is both experiencer and experienced, has become mutually turned toward itself.
From that, the fire-form of consciousness, blazing, is called <s>Citrabhānu</s>.

children.text: yo 'yaṃ vahneḥ paraṃ tattvaṃ pramāturidameva tat
children.translated_text: This very thing is the supreme reality of fire, the reality of the cognizer.
But consciousness alone is to be known as independent, because it is identical with knowability.
Because of its autonomy it is called the cognizer; because of distinctions in what is known, it is variegated.
It is expanded by the appearance of variety arising from the burnable objects that are portions of the moon.
For that very reason it is called fire, <s>Citrabhānu</s>, by <s>Maheśin</s>.
The state of consciousness itself is independent of the aggregate of means, such as the knowable object and so on;
therefore it is the subject, saying 'I am,' as in the case of one who knows the scripture.

children.text: ajña eva yato jñātānubhavātmā na rūpataḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the knower, as the very self of experience, is ignorant only in that sense, not by nature.

children.text: na tu sā jñātṛtā yasyāṃ śuddhajñeyādyapekṣate
children.translated_text: But that is not the knowerhood in which she depends on a pure knowable object and the rest.
In that condition, knowerhood is spoken of because of its capacity.
Rather, that is instrumentality, imagined by a prior cognizer.
Even while consciousness surges forth, because it is free from temporal sequence,
it is already arisen and complete, having the form of subject, object, and the rest.
But an action such as cooking, because it is delimited by time, is fit for sequence.
Even if it is barren of the final moment, it does not attain the state of being cooked.
Thus the nature of the principle of light as moon, sun, and fire is established;
yet its primary character as mere light is not set aside.

children.text: eṣāṃ yatprathamaṃ rūpaṃ hrasvaṃ tatsūrya ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Of these, the first form, the short one, is called the sun.
Because of agitation and bliss, with repose in the long vowel, it is called the moon.
That which is called the supreme protracted vowel, standing beyond the bliss of the moon,
is said by those skilled in scripture to have the fiery form of light.
Here, when the three abodes are present, that which is mere light
is taught in scripture as <s>bindu</s>; that is regarded as the <s>Śiva-bindu</s>.
This is distinct from the letter <s>ma</s>, though it bears only its shadow,
just as <s>ra</s>, <s>la</s>, and <s>ha</s> are established in the form of the inert and visarga letters.
Just as the vowel <s>i</s> itself is another vowel through the shadow of a portion of <s>repha</s>,
so too, from a slight trace of <s>ma</s> and <s>ha</s>, it is another, though it is a vowel in two ways.
Within it, that impulse to emit, which has been called the supreme <s>Kaulikī</s>,
because of agitation surely assumes the nature of <s>visarga</s>.
And it is said in the <s>Triśiras</s> scripture, in the discussion ending with the pervasion of <s>kalā</s>:
Therefore the seventeenth <s>kalā</s>, whose form is made of nectar,
has spread out through the movement of the <s>bindu</s> as the own forms of the higher and the lower.
It is the manifestation of all objects; but she is without <s>visarga</s>.
She is called <s>Śakti-kuṇḍalikā</s>, and likewise <s>Prāṇa-kuṇḍalikā</s>;
at the boundary-region of <s>visarga</s>, she is also called the supreme <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>.
She is called the <s>Śiva</s>-space, the supreme abode of the <s>brahman</s>-self.
The mere <s>visarga</s> of the Lord is the play of creation and dissolution.
The casting of the self, by the self, into the self is the natural state of emission.
When <s>visarga</s>, emitted in this way, has reached a condensed state,

children.text: haṃsaḥ prāṇo vyañjanaṃ ca sparśaśca paribhāṣyate ||
children.translated_text: it is defined as <s>haṃsa</s>, breath, consonant, and contact-letter.
The unsurpassed supreme abode is what is called <s>akula</s>.
The <s>visarga</s> of that Lord is called the <s>Kaulikī śakti</s>.
And her state as <s>visarga</s> (emission), since it proceeds by the arising of bliss,
is an upsurging condition that reaches as far as the clearly manifested power of action.
Thus <s>visarga</s> itself, when what is other has been drawn into it, has this much as its nature:
the ocean has just so much form as its endless succession of waves.
Therefore this <s>visarga</s>, whose essence is the unmanifest <s>ha</s>-phase,
is called the principle of <s>kāma</s> (desire) in the venerable <s>Kulaguhvara</s>.
That imperishable, unmanifest one, established in the throat of the beloved,
has the form of sound, is without deliberate willing, and is free from meditation and concentration.
Fixing the mind there, one should bring the world under control all at once.

children.text: ata eva visargasya haṃse yadvatsphuṭā sthitiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as the position of <s>visarga</s> is clear in <s>haṃsa</s>,
so too is the position of <s>anuttara</s> and the rest, extending from <s>ka</s> to <s>sa</s>.
From <s>anuttara</s> there is plainly the birth of the fivefold <s>ka</s>-class,
because its nature as the five powers is evident in each individual letter.
From the power of desire, established in its own nature, there is unity of form.
The <s>ca</s>-class, consisting of the five powers, has the nature of sequential manifestation.
That power has been said to take on the impurity of the knowable through swift movement.
From that twofold power there arose the two classes beginning with <s>ṭa</s> and <s>ta</s>.
But from opening out arises the <s>pa</s>-class, since through it the universe is completed.
For this form of the knowable clearly extends up to the twenty-fifth principle.
Because it is knowable, this much, as manifest, is taught as the form of the contact letters.
And the power of desire is twofold, according as it is agitated or unagitated.
When it turns toward a portion of a heterogeneous power, it passes into the state of <s>ya</s>.
That same power, more quickly taking on and being colored by the impurity of the knowable,
goes, through its orientation toward the heterogeneous, into the states of <s>ra</s> and <s>la</s>.
Likewise the power of opening is twofold; when it goes to a heterogeneous power,
it assumes the state of <s>va</s>, pouring forth the essence of creation.
Desire itself, having gone to <s>anuttara</s> and bliss through conjunction with swiftness,
is called wind; fire is so called because it makes manifest, and earth because of stability.
For this reason this tetrad is called internal,
because it is included within desire and the other powers, and because it rests in their completion.
The combining of homogeneous powers such as desire and the rest
is called by teachers an agitation, even though those powers have both agitated and unagitated natures.
When there is homogeneity with <s>anuttara</s>, there are two possible courses.
If the single <s>anuttara</s> present there is able to give birth to bliss,
then, through its conjunction, the conjunction is plainly of the nature of agitation.
But if even the second <s>anuttara</s>-abode is not sufficient for birth,
then, without agitation at all, there is the state whose essence is <s>anuttara</s>.

children.text: icchā yā karmaṇā hīnā yā caiṣṭavyena rūṣitā ||
children.translated_text: The desire that is devoid of action, and that which is colored by what is to be desired,
assumes a threefold condition, divided by swiftness and stability:
unopened, opening, and fully opened; such is the established order.
What is desired is threefold within this power, because it has not fallen away from identity with that form.
That very thing, by its own heat, whose nature is the impulse of its own freedom,
is clearly cast outward as something to be externalized, and stands as the triad <s>śa</s>, <s>ṣa</s>, and <s>sa</s>.
For that very reason the universe shines clearly in this letter <s>sa</s>.
Yogins declare that same thing to be the nectar and the supreme abode.
And in the cessations at the beginning and end of agitation, that alone is the supreme nectar.
In the absorptions and samādhis consisting of the real presence of the pleasure of the sighing sound,
that alone is declared to be the supreme <s>brahman</s>, undivided.
The Blessed One himself said this in the venerable <s>Kulaguhvara</s>,
where the meaningful designation is obtained through the unity of power and the possessor of power:
Having the shape of the hollow of a crow's beak, free from meditation and concentration,
the principle of <s>viṣa</s> (poison), called vowel-less, has been revealed to you out of affection.
The fullness of <s>kāma</s> is perceived as a principle in conjunction.
And the principle of <s>viṣa</s> is nectar when the covering of the limited soul has fallen away.
For the pervading power is <s>viṣa</s>, since it covers the radiance of that which is not pervading.

children.text: nirañjanaṃ paraṃ dhāma tattvaṃ tasya tu sāñjanam ||
children.translated_text: Its stainless supreme abode is the principle; its state with stain is the conditioned form.
Because from that the universe, whose nature is the power of action, flashes forth,

children.text: icchā kāmo viṣaṃ jñānaṃ kriyā devī nirañjanam ||
children.translated_text: desire is <s>kāma</s>; <s>viṣa</s> is knowledge; action is the stainless goddess.
The immersion of these three is called <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Bhairava</s>.

children.text: atra rūḍhiṃ sadā kuryāditi no guravo jaguḥ ||
children.translated_text: Our teachers have said, 'One should always become firmly established here.'

children.text: viṣatattve sampraviśya na bhūtaṃ na viṣaṃ na ca
children.translated_text: Having entered into the principle of <s>viṣa</s>, one should shine forth with the contemplation,
'There is no element, no poison, and no possessing force; I alone am pure.'
But, one may object, birth has here been stated from the six neuter letters; by that they would have neuter status.

children.text: kathaṃ syāditi cedbrūmo nātra ṣaṇṭhasya sotṛtā ||
children.translated_text: How can this be so? If this is asked, we answer: here the neuter is not the begetter.
For so it is: that power of desire which is said to abide there
itself gives birth to its own task, internal and formed as its own desired object.
But what stands here as the cause of coloring is the object to be desired; therefore,
from that part there is no birth. The impurity born from it, and its body, are that.
They know the collective form, joined with the coloring of the knowable,
as neuter, because it lacks the condition of being an agitator and an unagitated abode.
Because of the shining of this tetrad of letters by its own heat,
the stainless <s>Bhairava</s> has taught the name 'heat' for it.
The wise say that this series from <s>ka</s> through <s>ha</s> is the support of agitation.
And when even that is joined in the form of the womb, it goes to another agitation.
Through connection with that indication, it becomes the fiftieth letter.
It is well established, as before, in the ground designated by the set of twenty-five.

children.text: catuṣkaṃ ca catuṣkaṃ ca bhedābhedagataṃ kramāt
children.translated_text: And tetrad and tetrad, in sequence, pass into difference and non-difference.
The first tetrad is skilled in joining distinctions within consciousness.
Another tetrad is the single cause by which distinction becomes established in non-difference.
In this way, whatever class of phonemes there is, all of it was originally made of vowels.
Through connection with manifestation it becomes a consonant, since its vital breath is surely the vowel.
Here, in the continuum of phonemes, the set of six vowels alone is the root.

children.text: ṣaḍdevatāstu tā eva ye mukhyāḥ sūryaraśmayaḥ
children.translated_text: Those very six are the deities, the principal rays of the sun.
For within the solar rays there are the lunar digits.
Therefore here the triad of long vowels is clearly the lunar body.

children.text: candraśca nāma naivānyo bhogyaṃ bhoktuśca nāparam ||
children.translated_text: And what is called the moon is nothing other than the enjoyed; it is not separate from the enjoyer.
The enjoyer alone, through twofoldness, is arranged as the enjoyed.

children.text: ghaṭasya na hi bhogyatvaṃ svaṃ vapurmātṛgaṃ hi tat ||
children.translated_text: For a pot's being enjoyed is not its own form; that is indeed something belonging to the knowing subject.

children.text: ato mātari yā rūḍhiḥ sāsya bhogyatvamucyate
children.translated_text: Therefore the establishment that occurs in the subject is called its being enjoyed.
The <s>anuttara</s> (unsurpassed reality), because of the relation of what is apprehended and the apprehender,
has attained the form of a conjunction; likewise the enjoyed is will and the rest.
When will and the others, born from <s>anuttara</s> and bliss, have entered the state of the enjoyed,
the arising of the sandhi letters is said to be the form of the enjoyer.
The god made of <s>anuttara</s> and bliss is said to be the enjoyer alone.
Will and the rest are only the enjoyed; for that very reason they are his powers.

children.text: bhogyaṃ bhoktari līnaṃ ced bhoktā tadvastutaḥ sphuṭaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If the enjoyed is dissolved in the enjoyer, then the enjoyer is clearly that reality.
Therefore, of the six, the triad is the essence, consisting of consciousness, will, and opening.
They call that very triad the supreme splendor of <s>Bhairava</s>.
That triad is proclaimed as the full power of <s>Parameśa</s>.
Since the universe is implied by it, therefore, when this is worshiped,
worship has been performed toward the power of the universe, barren of limitation.
Thus, 'this greatness is only so much' cannot be said even to that extent.
Who could impose a limit on the power of one whose power is unlimited?
Therefore the unsurpassed god, through freedom and unsurpassedness,
and because he is joined with the power of <s>visarga</s> (emission), becomes possessed of the form of the universe.
Thus <s>Maheśvara</s>, whose power is full with the fifty apprehensions,
is one alone, whose nature is reflective awareness; the other powers are established here alone.
The goddess of eighty-one padas will indeed be included here.
When its nature is a single apprehension, that mass of speech is <s>Bhairava</s>.
By connection with the shadow of what is apprehended, she herself is power and <s>Mātṛkā</s>.
Because of the conjunction of the mass of speech, she, having distinct wombs, is <s>Mālinī</s>.
As before, by a ninefold apprehension, she has the form of the separate classes of phonemes.
But when she is established in each single apprehension, she has the nature of fifty.
Thus, through penetration by <s>nāda</s> (resonance), <s>Śiva</s>, whose nature is apprehension,
stands everywhere in the universe as the agent in the form of mother and father.
This <s>visarga</s> itself is śākta; again, as <s>Śiva</s>'s bindu,
with the infinite universe held within it as an embryo, it assumes the nature of <s>anuttara</s>.
The apprehension belonging to the Lord in his own self, whose inner essence is the unlimited universe,
is said to be marked by the attainment of the pair.
In the Lord, whose self is the nondual <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Śakti</s>, <s>anuttara</s> and <s>visarga</s>,
apprehension, because of its fullness, is called 'I'.
The expansion beginning with <s>anuttara</s> is the power-form called <s>hāntā</s>.
Retracted into <s>anuttara</s> with the whole universe, it dissolves there.
This universe is situated within power, in the supreme <s>anuttara</s>.
The truth that it belongs to her is an enclosing by the all-pervading Lord.
Therefore, in the venerable <s>Triśikāśāstra</s>, the power has an enclosed form.

children.text: saṃvittau bhāti yadviśvaṃ tatrāpi khalu saṃvidā
children.translated_text: Whatever universe shines in consciousness, there too it shines indeed through consciousness.
This triad, through the conjunction of paired terms, has become an aggregate:
the single supreme form of <s>Bhairava</s>, whose nature is the 'I'.
The power of <s>visarga</s> belonging to <s>Śambhu</s> operates everywhere in this way.
From that alone arises all this play of the savor of bliss.

children.text: tathāhi madhure gīte sparśe vā candanādike ||
children.translated_text: For example, in a sweet song or in a touch such as sandal paste,
when neutrality has disappeared, that pulsation in the heart
is called the power of bliss; for this reason a person is <s>sahṛdaya</s> (sensitive-hearted).
First, after casting everything to be done into the fire of emptiness,
there is what is called repose of the mind; immediately afterward, it is the āṇava mode.
The turning, within one's own consciousness, toward that object which has been seen, heard, or otherwise perceived
is called the awakening of the mind, whose nature is fullness with the unfolding of <s>Śakti</s>.
There, from the conjunction of that orientation and that object, when the object
is rooted in the heart, through entry into fullness, and from the dissolution of the limited mind in <s>Śiva</s>,
because limitedness, implied by a future orientation as before, dissolves,
that is called the dissolution of the mind; it is the supreme śāmbhava <s>visarga</s>.
Therefore, in the procedure for preserving the tattvas, <s>visarga</s> is taught as threefold.
The conjunction of the two is accepted as standing in the middle of the cup of the heart-lotus.
That internal <s>visarga</s> is said to have the characteristic of repose of the mind.
The second <s>visarga</s> has the characteristic of awakening of the mind.
Here this moving and unmoving universe shines as become one.
When some distinction of the grasped and the grasper is accepted here,
then it is called sakala; through union with <s>Śiva</s>, it is niṣkala.
The third <s>visarga</s> consists in complete grasping through the cessation of the grasped and grasper.
That <s>visarga</s> has the characteristic of dissolution of the mind.
It is subtle, whose nature is unification, consisting of consciousness, and satisfied in itself.
This meaning has been explained in the venerable <s>Siddhayogīśvarīmata</s>.
There, <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s> is the seed, the living principle, whose nature is consciousness.
From that is born the triad called fixed will and opening forth; and then again come the phonemes.
Beginning with the vowel <s>a</s>, and so on, up to the phase belonging to <s>visarga</s> (emission).
The letters from <s>ka</s> through <s>sa</s> arise from <s>visarga</s>, and that <s>visarga</s> is fivefold:
outside, inside, in the heart, in <s>nāda</s> (resonance), and then in the supreme station.
The <s>bindu</s> (point) is in the self; it pervades from the heart to the crown of the head.
For mantras lacking beginning and end would be like autumn clouds.
This much is the mark of a guru: he should know the beginning and the end.
Such a knower is to be worshiped like myself, as <s>Bhairava</s> whose nature is deity.
Therefore whatever there is, whether verse, gāthā, or the like, joined with beginning and end,
because of that, one who knows in this way sees everything precisely as mantra.
The power of <s>visarga</s> has been explained as the cause of the universe,
at length by the supreme Lord in the Vedānta called <s>Aitareya</s>.
What is red is fire; what is seed has the form of sun and moon.
The letter <s>a</s> is the supreme <s>brahman</s>, whose nature is the arising from their conjunction.
And beyond even that, its potency consists of the phases of the five elements,
and, as something to be enjoyed, it has the form of food and the nature of sound, touch, and taste.
Sound too is sweet because it causes the increase of potency.

children.text: taddhi vīryaṃ paraṃ śuddhaṃ visisṛkṣātmakaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: For that potency is regarded as supreme and pure, having the nature of the wish to emit.

children.text: tadbalaṃ ca tadojaśca te prāṇāḥ sā ca kāntatā
children.translated_text: That is strength, that is vigor, those are the vital breaths, and that is beauty.
From that potency come offspring; and that same potency is spoken of in rites.
In sacrifices and the like, it is present in rain, then in good herbs; and those again
are in seed, and that is in offspring. Thus in <s>visarga</s> there is universal form.

children.text: śabdarāśiḥ sa evokto mātṛkā sāca kīrtitā
children.translated_text: That same reality is called the mass of sound, and it is praised as <s>mātṛkā</s> (the matrix of letters).
Because it enters into the states of what is stirred and what stirs, they call it <s>Mālinī</s>.
Beautiful through the union of seed and womb and the arising of <s>visarga</s>,
<s>Mālinī</s> has been determined to be the supreme power, whose form is the universe.

children.text: eṣā vastuta ekaiva parā kālasya karṣiṇī
children.translated_text: In reality she is one alone, the supreme one, drawing forth time.
Through association with the distinction between power and possessor of power, she assumes the state of a pair.
His reflective awareness, complete and having the form 'I',
by its freedom within itself, causes division to appear.
And when division appears, its body is taught as threefold:
<s>paśyantī</s>, <s>madhyamā</s>, and the gross one called <s>vaikharī</s>.
Each of these too has a threefold form, as gross, subtle, and supreme.
Among them, that which is a lovely sequence of vowels and has the form of <s>nāda</s>
is indeed the gross <s>paśyantī</s>, because there is no division into letters and the like.
Undivided single-formness is called sweetness, the power.
But the manifest clarity that arises from the friction of places of articulation, breath, and the like is harshness.
In this speech whose form is <s>nāda</s>, because it occurs near consciousness,
through similarity, the becoming identical with that is perceived immediately.
Those for whom this becoming identical does not occur do not know immersion in the body and the like.
Their awareness remains sunk as a mere measure, and they are called without heart.
But whatever sound there is in instruments covered with hide and the like,
because it is both clear and unclear in form, is <s>madhyamā</s> in its gross form.
And because in the middle one there is the presence of an undivided portion, there is pleasing coloration.
Where undivided vowel-nature is present, that is what charms deeply.
For undividedness brings delight; let this be seen from the recitation of rhythm.
Indeed, in that playing, one is pleased by its indistinct sound.

children.text: yā tu sphuṭānāṃ varṇānāmutpattau kāraṇaṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: But that which becomes the cause in the production of distinct letters

children.text: sā sthūlā vaikharī yasyāḥ kāryaṃ vākyādi bhūyasā
children.translated_text: is the gross <s>vaikharī</s>, whose effect is for the most part sentences and the like.
In this gross triad, whatever reflective tracing there is, as before,
that separate threefold tracing is called the subtle triad.

children.text: ṣaḍjaṃ karomi madhuraṃ vādayāmi bruve vacaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'I make the <s>ṣaḍja</s> sweet; I play; I utter speech':
indeed, three distinct acts of reflective awareness are experienced separately.
Of this triad also, the first form, which is without limiting adjunct,
is the supreme triad; there <s>Śiva</s> has the nature of supreme consciousness.
And in the manifestation of division, the chief powers here are three:
<s>Anuttarā</s>, supreme will, and that which is established as both supreme and non-supreme.
The power of opening, called knowledge, is said to be the non-supreme.
Again, from their form as agitation, six stainless consciousnesses are taught.
From the entry of these very ones, arising as the power of action,

children.text: saṃvido dvādaśa proktā yāsu sarvaṃ samāpyate
children.translated_text: twelve consciousnesses are declared, in which everything comes to completion.
This much is the principal wheel of powers of the God of gods.
With this much, the God of gods, <s>Bhairava</s>, is complete in power.
Because they consist of reflective awareness and are joined with the projection of <s>visarga</s>,
and because their measure is calculated through knowledge, they are sometimes called <s>Kālikās</s>.
And in the venerable <s>Sāraśāstra</s> too it is said: in the center one should worship the supreme one-syllabled goddess,
called <s>Bhairavātman</s>, encircled by twelve <s>Yoginīs</s>.
From those very ones, the wheel of powers extends up to sixty-four.
Beginning from the letter <s>e</s>, it proceeds to the thousand-petalled one.
And their names, according to differences of function, are many in the <s>āgamas</s>.
Their worships too take dualistic, nondualistic, and mixed forms.
This has also been told at great length in the venerable <s>Traiśirasa</s>.
It has not been written here because of fear of prolixity and because it is not useful here.

children.text: tā eva nirmalāḥ śuddhā aghorāḥ parikīrtitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those same powers are called stainless, pure, and <s>Aghorāḥ</s>.
And because they are the sources of the <s>Ghorāḥ</s> and the <s>Ghoratarāḥ</s>, they have their nature as well.
In creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and in the transcendence of those three limiting adjuncts,
the form belonging to those very powers is divided in many ways.
The form beyond limiting adjuncts is said by the teachers to be twofold.
Or because the limiting adjuncts do not flash forth, and because of the practice of pacification,
pacification is twofold: through quiescence, and through the sequence of forced ripening.
Enough has been said of what is called the savor of devouring, whose nature is constant blazing.
And that third pacification by forced ripening
is fit for instruction, since it burns up the fuel of differentiation.
All entities, forcibly offered into the belly-fire born of one's own awareness,
abandon the divisions of difference, as they kindle that fire by their own power.
When, by forced ripening, the differentiated form of entities has been dissolved,
the goddesses of consciousness eat the universe, which has become nectar.
Satisfied, they rest in identity upon their own self, full and lying in the innermost heart,
the god <s>Cidvyomabhairava</s>, without difference.
Thus, because of the entrance of acts and rites and because of the multiplicity of worship by name,
the manifold form of these goddesses appears, even though there is no difference.
And through the application and withdrawal of these very goddesses,
there is an extension of difference through one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and further numbers:
<s>Rudra</s>, the twelve suns, other digits, hosts, and so on.
Enough of much else; now the matter at hand is taken up.
This entire class of entities, expanded as the world,

children.text: pratibimbatayā bhāti yasya viśveśvaro hi saḥ ||
children.translated_text: shines in the self of consciousness as a reflection; he in whom it does so is indeed the Lord of the universe.
For the one in whom such a nonconceptual awareness of the self is always arising,
that very reflective awareness is stamped as the <s>śāmbhava</s> means.
This reflective awareness of full I-ness has been explained for him;
apart from it there are no mantras, mudrās, rites, or worships here.
Again and again resorting to this nonconceptual immersion,
one reaches the state of <s>Bhairava</s>, whose other name is liberation while living.
From this point onward, this liberation while living is examined,
where even this construction of means and goal exists only by way of schematic statement.
But in the preceding chapter there was not even any conception of difference at all;

children.text: tenānupāye tasminko mucyate vā kathaṃ kutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: therefore, in that non-means, who is liberated, or how, or from what?
In the nonconceptual reflective awareness called the <s>śāmbhava</s> means,
the wise person should apply the fiftyfold division previously outlined.
Seeing earth itself, without conceptualization, as reflected in one's own self,
one attains the state of <s>Bhairava</s>; this same procedure applies also to water and the rest,
up to the supreme principle at the end, beyond all coverings,
all-pervading, autonomous, omniscient, which is conceived as <s>Śiva</s>.
Seeing even that reflected in the noble mirror of unconceived consciousness,
free from conceptual construction, one oneself becomes <s>Bhairava</s>-like.
Just as, when seeing red before one with nonconceptual awareness,
one is firmly established, through that particular doorway, in the partless single awareness of a pot,
so too, from each aggregate and totality beginning with earth,
one touches one's own self and appears as full alone.
'This has arisen from me; it is reflected in me alone;
and it is not different from me': such is the threefold <s>śāmbhava</s> means.
This is the schematic account of creation, persistence, and dissolution,
and the <s>Spanda</s> teaching states where it is established and whence it comes.
By just this much the supreme sovereignty of consciousness has been made known,
and also its nature as the all; what other characteristic need be stated?
Revealing the universe within oneself alone, in the space of consciousness, with the awareness 'I am the universe,'
one's identity with <s>Bhairava</s> is manifest as the creator, whose nature is the universe.
The whole complex of the six <s>adhvan</s>s is reflected in me alone;
with the clear awareness 'I am the maker of persistence,' this is the form of the universe.
In the self bristling with the flames of great awareness that is ever arisen,
one grows peaceful by seeing, 'This universe melts away in me.'
From the house of the dream of saṃsāra, pregnant with endless varied forms,
the blazing fire rises, thinking, 'I myself am <s>Śiva</s>, the burner of it.'

children.text: jagatsarvaṃ mattaḥ prabhavati vibhedena bahudhā tathāpyetadrūḍhaṃ mayi vigalite tvatra na paraḥ
children.translated_text: The whole world arises from me in many ways through differentiation; nevertheless, this is firmly rooted in me, and when I dissolve, there is no other here.

children.text: taditthaṃ yaḥ sṛṣṭisthitivilayam ekīkṛtivaśād anaṃśaṃ paśyetsa sphurati hi turīyaṃ padam itaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus one who, by unifying creation, persistence, and dissolution, sees them as without parts, from this point shines as the fourth state.
In this supreme means, radiant with <s>śāmbhava</s> nonduality,
only some come to confidence, having been formed by the Supreme Lord.
Bathing, vows, bodily purification, concentration, the application of mantra,
the arrangement of the <s>adhvan</s>, the rule for sacrifice, oblations, recitation, and samādhis:
no such construction at all is applicable here as something distinct.
The capacity to bestow grace upon others is clearly established for one who abides here.
If a person fit for such grace approaches the teacher,

children.text: athāsau tādṛśo na syādbhavabhaktyā ca bhāvitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: but that teacher is not of such a kind, though inspired by devotion to existence,
and if he worships that teacher, moved by the wish for such grace,
then the learned teacher should instruct him in the varied procedure beginning with initiation.
For even the future forms of worship come to completion here alone,
and, having attained identity with this, the supreme <s>Śiva</s> is directly discerned.
Thus this supreme self-knowledge, the <s>śāmbhava</s> means, has been explained in full detail.
Now, for the sake of the consciousness of the supreme self, we shall explain the circle of the <s>śākta</s> means.
In this supreme lordly nature taught in the immediately preceding chapter,
one who wishes to enter conceptualization should at once carry out its refinement.
A refined conceptualization gives rise to a conceptualization refined by its own self,
one like itself; that too gives rise to another, and that too to another of similar nature.
The refinement that occurs successively in just four conceptualizations
At first it is indistinct; then, becoming clear and bursting forth, it has the nature of what has opened.
Then it becomes clearer and clearer, until at the end it becomes most clear.
And even in the conception that begins from indistinctness there is also an intermediate differentiation.
Then consciousness, enlarged by the abundant identity of utmost clarity,
attains the stainless state whose nature is free from conceptual construction.
Therefore that <s>Bhairava</s>-radiance, whose own nature is consciousness,
for those who reflect upon it again and again, comes to have a clear nature.
But, one may object, consciousness is herself the agent of reflective awareness, made of <s>parāmarśa</s> by nature.

children.text: parāmṛśyā kathaṃ tāthārūpyasṛṣṭau tu sā jaḍā ||
children.translated_text: How can she be an object of reflection? In producing such a form, would she not be inert?
The answer is: awareness of one's own self is full by its very nature.
In it there is nothing to be removed and nothing to be added; this was stated earlier.
But because of its stainless freedom, which can accomplish the impossible,
<s>Parameśvara</s> is expert in the play of concealing his own self.
The Lord's self-concealment, even though his own form is not covered,
is itself <s>māyā</s>; for from it comes just this much differentiation, operating as the universe.
It is merely his appearing in that way; this is called the duality of the Great Lord.
By removing those two, this is called <s>parāmarśa</s> (reflective awareness).
The learned cut the root of this tree, which is hard to split,
with the sharp axe of <s>sattarka</s> (true reasoning); this is certain.
The wise call this contemplation one that milks forth all desires,
for it makes an object clear even when it has gone beyond the range of wishful thought.
In the venerable <s>Pūrvaśāstra</s> that is stated: reasoning is the highest limb of yoga.
Because it examines what is to be rejected and the rest, effort in that matter is praised.
When the mind has become steady on the path, even toward what is to be rejected, through desire for an object,

children.text: prerya tena nayettāvad yāvat padam anāmayam ||
children.translated_text: one should impel it by that and lead it onward until it reaches the stainless state.
Here the path is the means to liberation; what is to be rejected is what is taught in another scripture.
The desire that particularizes and binds is connected with limitation.
What is meant by that is the <s>rāga-tattva</s> (principle of attachment); by it one becomes attached there,
just as, after seeing the enjoyment of sovereignty, or even without seeing it, one may become attached to a low enjoyment.
So too a foolish person becomes attached even to liberation because of <s>rāga</s> (attachment).

children.text: sa evāṃśaka ityuktaḥ svabhāvākhyaḥ sa tu sphuṭam ||
children.translated_text: That very thing is called a portion; it is called innate nature, and it is plainly
an auxiliary to attainment, but the learned say it is an obstruction to liberation.
For this very reason, even while knowing the greatness of the teaching of <s>Śiva</s>,
a fool, colored by attachment, becomes attached to Vaiṣṇava and other systems.
For to that extent the sovereign power in him, called <s>Vāmā</s>,
unfolds as Pāñcarātrika, Vairiñca, Saugata, and the like.
Some childish people are seen denouncing the enjoyment of sovereignty,
but not from contentment, since they set blessings in motion for their own enjoyments.
In this same way there are people whose minds are intent on denouncing immersion in <s>Cidbhairava</s>,
because they have been cast down by extremely terrible powers.
Therefore, even while knowing the greatness of the <s>Śāmbhava</s> teaching, if one is confident in another doctrine,
one should not suppose that by that he has crossed beyond the great ocean of differentiation.
And this is plainly stated in the venerable <s>Kāmikā</s>, in the section on the bonds:
Those who know the <s>Veda</s>, <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, and <s>Purāṇa</s>, and those devoted to the <s>Pāñcarātra</s>,
whatever steadfast sages are devoted to other scriptures,
Buddhists, Jainas, and the like--all of them are colored by attachment to vidyā.
Because they are bound by the bond of <s>māyā</s>, they do not obtain initiation into <s>Śiva</s>.
And by the word <s>rāga</s> is meant the regulating <s>rāga-tattva</s>.
Since it belongs to the māyīya order, it confines that person to that scripture.
Even the liberation of Vaiṣṇavas and others, imagined according to their own conception,
whether union with supreme Prakṛti or even the state of bliss,
or mere purity of mind, or the extinction of continuity like a lamp,
is a condition of pralaya-ākala, whose self is still bound up with what is knowable and unknowable.
Even after attaining it for a long time, when the enjoyment of those experiences has been consumed,
at the end of the dissolution of that principle, having entered the creation above it,
he reaches the state of a mantra through the awakening devised by <s>Ananteśa</s>.
We shall elaborate this later; for now let that matter rest here.
Therefore one who is deluded by reports fashioned by ignorant people,
and whose consciousness is fixed on a false guru, is colored by the bond of <s>māyā</s>.
Even he, through the yoga of <s>sattarka</s> (true reasoning), is led toward the true guru.
<s>Sattarka</s> is pure knowledge itself, and that is the will of the Supreme Lord.
Therefore it is said in the venerable <s>Pūrvaśāstra</s>: one who wishes to go, by the will of <s>Śiva</s>,
is led to the true guru for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation.
There, however, this <s>śaktipāta</s> (descent of power) proceeds gradually.

children.text: sthitvā yo 'sadgurau śāstrāntare vā satpathaṃ śritaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One who, after remaining with a false guru or in another scripture, has resorted to the true path,
has, in this matter, a distinguishing factor regarding truth or falsity in guru and scripture.
The variety of <s>śaktipāta</s> will be analyzed ahead.
This is stated in the <s>Svacchandaśāstra</s>: <s>māyā</s> bewilders all
proponents such as Vaiṣṇavas, while they desire liberation in what is not liberation.
But one who, though established there, is skilled in the rising <s>parāmarśa</s>,
purified by <s>śaktipāta</s> through the greatness of pure knowledge,
does indeed ascend the true path, free from obstructions.
For such a person, sometimes reasoning arises of itself.

children.text: sa ca sāṃsiddhikaḥ śāstre proktaḥ svapratyayātmakaḥ
children.translated_text: And this is called innate in scripture, consisting in one's own conviction.
What is also said in the <s>Kiraṇā</s> is: from the guru, from scripture, and from oneself.
There the later one is more important than the earlier, while each earlier one is a means.
He in whom this <s>sattarka</s> (true reasoning) arises of itself is qualified in every respect.
He is consecrated by the goddesses who are his own consciousness, and he is initiated.

children.text: sa eva sarvācāryāṇāṃ madhye mukhyaḥ prakīrtitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He alone is proclaimed the chief among all teachers.
In his presence, authority does not belong to other appointed teachers.

children.text: sa samastaṃ ca śāstrārthaṃ sattarkādeva manyate ||
children.translated_text: And he understands the whole meaning of scripture from sound reasoning alone.

children.text: śuddhavidyā hi tannāsti satyaṃ yadyanna bhāsayet
children.translated_text: For there is no real thing that <s>śuddhavidyā</s> (pure knowledge) does not make manifest.
And knowledge of the meanings of all scriptures arises in him unexpectedly.
Thus, in the venerable <s>Pūrva</s> passage, by the word "unexpectedly,"
a cause not commonly known in the world is called "unexpected."
And this is the expansion of the <s>śuddhavidyā</s> of the supreme Lord.
Its divisions are many: without a support and having a support;
all-pervading and present in a part; and that too rests in a principal or secondary part.
A support means dependence on another; the higher support is insight, and then its activity.
Even if he has not seen the <s>maṇḍala</s>, anyone who knows in this way in truth

children.text: sa siddhibhāgbhavennityaṃ sa yogī sa ca dīkṣitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: always becomes a sharer in siddhi; he is a yogin, and he is initiated.

children.text: evaṃ yo vetti tattvena tasya nirvāṇagāminī
children.translated_text: For one who knows thus in reality, an initiation leading to nirvāṇa
would take place: so it is taught in the venerable <s>Triṃśakaśāsana</s>.
The unappointed guru is to be known as one who is naturally perfected.
But he who, without that supreme state, through contemplation whose nature partakes of that form,
knows the scripture, is called in the scripture an unappointed appointer.
Of him too there are divisions according to superior, middling, inferior, and other means.
By cultivation, or else by meditation, recitation, dream, vow, or oblation,
a great-minded person obtains the noble unappointed consecration.
In the venerable <s>Vājasanīya</s>, in <s>Śrīvīra</s>, in the venerable <s>Brahmayāmala</s>,
and in the venerable <s>Siddhā</s>, this was clearly stated by <s>Dhātṛ</s>, and elsewhere too.
Because it proceeds by his own will, an infinitude of causes is accepted.
Sometimes it is by the yoga of devotion, by ritual action, or also by knowledge;
by instruction in knowledge and dharma, or by mantras, or also by initiation.
By these and many other modes, the supreme Lord
shows grace to the being in saṃsāra, the Lord of the whole universe.
Through awakening by the circle of Mothers, through consecration, or through tapas, dear one,
through meditation, yoga, recitation, knowledge, mantra-worship, or vow,
the general knowledge of the Kula, which gives Kaulika siddhi, is to be obtained.
Wherever the object to be accomplished, whose nature is knowledge of reality, is seen,

children.text: sa eva hi gurustatra hetujālaṃ prakalpyatām ||
children.translated_text: there indeed he is the guru; let a network of causes be posited.
In the <s>Brahmayāmala</s>, there is no other defining mark apart from knowledge of reality.
And there too it is said: when service has been performed without wavering,

children.text: sādhakasya na cetsiddhiḥ kiṃ kāryamiti codite
children.translated_text: if siddhi does not come to the practitioner, and it is asked, "What should be done?"
there is his own self-initiation through a sequence of self-recognition.
For the sake of establishing manifestness; after that, the goal to be accomplished is accomplished.
By this, self-knowledge as the means that brings about manifestness
has been stated as primary, if the teacher should not be vividly manifest.
And again in that same text, in the ritual of worship of <s>Raktā</s>,
one who always performs the prescribed rite is called an ācārya in a month;
in a fortnight he is a sādhaka, in half of half that time a putraka, and likewise a samayin.
The goddess <s>Raktā</s> initiates through the yoga of recitation, in due sequence.
When the stated guru cannot be obtained, one should perform this rite.
And in the doctrine, concerning the study of vidyā from a book, such a fault
as is stated there means that, when that fault is absent, this is not forbidden.
When it is asked, "What is the result when mantras, materials, and the like are kept secret?"
those whose vidyā is learned from books, and who lack initiation and samaya,
are tamasic and abundantly practice injury to others and acts of subjugation.

children.text: na ca tattvaṃ vidustena doṣabhāja iti sphuṭam ||
children.translated_text: And they do not know reality; therefore it is clear that they incur fault.
The previous pair of words should be explained as mutually cause and effect.
But he who, without scripture, does not attain the consciousness called <s>śuddhavidyā</s>,

children.text: guroḥ sa śāstram anvicchus taduktaṃ kramamācaret
children.translated_text: should seek scripture from the guru and follow the procedure taught by him.
By whatever means, having worshiped the guru with devotion,
he then understands the meaning of scripture through connection with that procedure of initiation.

children.text: abhiṣekaṃ samāsādya yo bhavetsa tu kalpitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having obtained consecration, the one who becomes such is appointed,
yet he is skilled in removing the entire mass of bonds.
He who, through connection with the proper sequence, in some scriptural matter
comes to a sudden understanding is both appointed and unappointed.

children.text: tasya yo 'kalpito bhāgaḥ sa tu śreṣṭhatamaḥ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Of him, the unappointed part is remembered as the very highest.
For excellence is caused by gradation in the portions of <s>śuddhavidyā</s>.
Just as, because of difference, liberated <s>Śivas</s> are lower than <s>Śiva</s> who is perfect from the beginning,
so those whose knowledge is acquired are inferior to those whose knowledge is naturally perfected.
In their presence those others have no authority, just as beings of the nature of liberated <s>Śivas</s> do not.
Rather, they should remain silent, or else follow whatever action is to be done.
But one who, though unappointed in nature, for the sake of strengthening corroboration,
has received consecrating formation from another is directly <s>Bhairava</s> as guru.
For, from the sequence of scripture and from cultivating the insight of a guru who knows that,
knowledge made certain for oneself, because of its fullness, becomes <s>Bhairava</s>-like.
Therefore what is taught in the venerable <s>Kiraṇa</s>, "from the guru, from scripture, and from oneself,"
that this knowledge has three grounds of certainty, and what is taught in the <s>Niśāṭana</s>,
appears in that way through their combination, reversal, and separation.
Because of the diversity of the instrument, people make that very act of cutting diverse:

children.text: kartuṃ vāsīṃ ca ṭaṅkaṃ ca krakacaṃ cāpi gṛhṇate ||
children.translated_text: to cut, they take up an adze, a chisel, and also a saw.
And so far there is indeed one cutting off, just as was intended at the beginning;

children.text: itthameva mitau vācyaṃ karaṇasya svakaṃ vapuḥ ||
children.translated_text: in just this way, with respect to measuring knowledge, the instrument's own form must be stated.

children.text: na svatantraṃ svato mānaṃ kuryādadhigamaṃ haṭhāt
children.translated_text: A means of knowledge is not independent, nor would it by itself force cognition;
for cognition is said to extend as far as the knower's assurance.
And that assurance is varied, likewise according to the descent of <s>śakti</s>;
therefore, even when a thing has been known, there is clearly scope for means of knowledge.

children.text: dṛṣṭvā dṛṣṭvā samāśliṣya ciraṃ saṃcarvya cetasā
children.translated_text: Seeing again and again, embracing, and long savoring her in the mind,

children.text: priyā yaiḥ parituṣyeta kiṃ brūmaḥ kila tānprati ||
children.translated_text: those by whom the beloved would be satisfied: what indeed can we say to them?
Thus, even in a plunge of the mind, there is no recourse to what has not been apprehended;
nor is there uselessness, infinite regress, or mutual dependence.

children.text: evaṃ yogāṅgamiyati tarka eva na cāparam
children.translated_text: Thus the limb of yoga goes this far: <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) alone, and nothing else;
it is for the surpassing sharpness of inward and ever more inward reflective awareness.
Non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession:
these five restraints are not directly useful for consciousness itself.
And the observances beginning with austerity, and whatever posture is taught,
and the breath-controls too: all this is an external expansion.
And in the venerable <s>Vīrāvalī</s> it is said: In mere awakening, whose nature is <s>Śiva</s>,
when the moon and sun have dissolved through the bond of the mind's dissolution,

children.text: prāpte ca dvādaśe bhāge jīvāditye svabodhake
children.translated_text: and when the living sun, self-illuminating, has reached the twelfth part,

children.text: mokṣaḥ sa eva kathitaḥ prāṇāyāmo nirarthakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that alone is declared liberation; breath-control is pointless.

children.text: prāṇāyāmo na kartavyaḥ śarīraṃ yena pīḍyate
children.translated_text: Breath-control, by which the body is afflicted, should not be performed;

children.text: rahasyaṃ vetti yo yatra sa muktaḥ sa ca mocakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: whoever knows the secret wherever he is, he is liberated and he liberates.
And this so-called withdrawal is that withdrawal of the sense-cognitions from objects;
it is, supposedly, the fastening inward of a bond for what is not bound.
The binding of the mind to some object is of the nature of <s>dhāraṇā</s> (fixation);
a stream of knowledge similar to that is meditation, and beyond that, when it has set,
when identity with the knowable itself arises in consciousness,
this emptiness of the duality of grasped and grasping is <s>samāhiti</s> (absorption).
This triad of fixation, meditation, and absorption
has no usefulness at all with regard to supreme consciousness.
But the status of yoga-limb is described for the restraints and the rest, ending in absorption,
because each earlier one is a means to the following one and because they are useful for the final <s>tarka</s>.

children.text: antaḥ saṃvidi rūḍhaṃ hi taddvārā prāṇadehayoḥ
children.translated_text: For what is rooted inwardly in consciousness is to be placed, through that gateway, in breath and body,
or in the intellect, by practice; but this reasoning does not apply to consciousness itself.
Or rather, in our view, because breath, intellect, body, and the rest are plainly all-formed,
practice situated there too is an exclusion of what is other.
The body, from eagerness for rising up because it has the property of leaping and falling,
is made to leap, because the fear of falling toward its opposite has been removed.
When one's own reflection, resembling reflection on the guru's word,
has awakened, the rejection of its opposites occurs in recitation and contemplation.

children.text: nahyasya guruṇā śakyaṃ svaṃ jñānaṃ śabda eva vā
children.translated_text: For the guru cannot implant in him his own knowledge, or even the word,
in the intellect; therefore one's own sequence of awakening is certain.

children.text: ata eva svapnakāle śrute tatrāpi vastuni
children.translated_text: For this very reason, when in dream a thing has been heard there too,
the discipline of imagining identity with that thing is not said to be fruitless.
When convention is disregarded, reflection fixed on the word is recitation;
when convention is respected, its meaning should be discussed as contemplation.
In that nondual consciousness, practice has no usefulness;
it serves only to root out the suspicion of the impurity of duality.
And doubts of duality are examined by <s>tarka</s>; this has been explained.
For the accomplishment of that <s>tarka</s>, however, the restraints and the rest also have the status of means.

children.text: uktaṃ śrīpūrvaśastre ca na dvaitaṃ nāpi cādvayam
children.translated_text: And it is said in the venerable <s>Pūrvaśāstra</s>: There is neither duality nor nonduality;
after beginning, by <s>Śambhu</s>, with 'worship of the liṅga and all the rest,'
everything here is either enjoined or else prohibited;

children.text: prāṇāyāmādikair aṅgair yogāḥ syuḥ kṛtrimā yataḥ ||
children.translated_text: for yogas with limbs such as breath-control are artificial.
Therefore they are not worth even a sixteenth part of this unmade reality.
But this, O goddess, is enjoined here as a rule:

children.text: tattve cetaḥ sthiraṃ kāryaṃ tacca yasya yathāstviti
children.translated_text: the mind must be made steady in the principle; and let that be for each person in whatever way it may be.
Thus, for the destruction of dualistic reflective awareness, the supreme Lord
sometimes remains constantly reflecting on the stainless nature.
Whatever reflection on one's nature there is, through means such as sense-objects,
or without them, whether turned toward that or in another way, it is a conceptualization of that through freedom.
And that is clear, shining in the jewel of the transparent and autonomous self;
in the flood of entities, what joins together difference is called the darkness of one's own self.
But that very same conceptualization, whose single object is the self full of all things,
has the nature of <s>śuddhavidyā</s> (pure knowledge): 'All this indeed am I.'
This conceptualization, in the form of <s>śuddhavidyā</s>, has a manifest nature;
here it counteracts the <s>māyīya</s> conceptualization that produces differentiation.
But the reflective awareness that is <s>śuddhavidyā</s> is itself manyfold:
through bathing, purification, worship, oblation, meditation, recitation, and the like,
having entered this whole universe, filled with the savor of one's own consciousness, with savor,
one, being purified, should satisfy the entire circle of the <s>adhvan</s> (cosmic path).
In the white ash that has arisen from the fuel of the universe burned by the blazing fire of awakened consciousness,
the immersion of the body is called bathing.
And thus, having performed the prescribed bathing and satisfied the infinite deities,
thereafter one should purify the principles that begin the formation of the body.
Even in these, though they have the nature of <s>Śiva</s>, the cognition that separates them
is declared impurity; purity is the crushing down of that cognition.
Thus one's own body is a vessel of awareness alone, with differentiation melted away.
Seeing it as nothing but consciousness, the Lord stands in freedom.
Whatever delights the mind, in whatever sensory condition it may be,
is to be yoked to the real abode of <s>Brahman</s>; for that is an implement of worship.
What is called worship is the conjunction even of the flood of differentiated states
with the self of pure, infinite, autonomous <s>Bhairavī</s>-consciousness.
For thus this very consciousness, as inner, outer, and both,
is manifesting by its own freedom, being of the nature of reflective awareness.
And that is twelvefold there, since everything is included within it.

children.text: sūrya eva hi somātmā sa ca viśvamayaḥ sthitaḥ
children.translated_text: For the sun itself has the nature of the moon, and it stands as consisting of the whole universe.
It is itself composed of twelve kalās; that, in ultimate reality, is consciousness.

children.text: sā ca mātari vijñāne māne karaṇagocare
children.translated_text: And it always shines in a fourfold form: in the knower, in knowledge,
in the means of knowledge as the sphere of the instrument, and in the object known.
In the first, it is made of pure consciousness; in knowledge, it has the form of sound.
In the instrument it has the form of apprehension; hence, in the venerable <s>Yogasaṃcāra</s>,
it is said: 'In the white circle of the eye, in direct perception, O <s>Parameśvarī</s>,
there is the supreme wheel there, with sixteen spokes and twelve spokes.
The red circle outside that, like a defensive enclosure, is called

children.text: dvitīyaṃ madhyage ye te kṛṣṇaśvete ca maṇḍale ||
children.translated_text: the second; and the two circles in the middle, black and white,
set within that, pure and shining like split collyrium,

children.text: caturdale tu te jñeye agnīṣomātmake priye ||
children.translated_text: should be known as four-petalled and as having the nature of fire and moon, dear one.

children.text: mithunatve sthite ye ca cakre dve parameśvari
children.translated_text: And the two wheels that stand in paired form, O <s>Parameśvarī</s>,
cause contraction and expansion in one another.
Just as the yoni and the liṅga, through union, pour forth nectar,
so, from the union of nectar and fire, those two melt and flow; there is no doubt.
From the pressing of that wheel at night, a light appears, belonging to sun and moon.

children.text: tāṃ dṛṣṭvā paramāṃ jyotsnāṃ kālajñānaṃ pravartate ||
children.translated_text: On seeing that supreme moonlight, knowledge of time begins to arise.
The thousand-spoked wheel is situated above those two.
From that wheel arises what is called the brahmāṇḍa, the cosmic egg.
The moon, kindled by fire, releases the stream situated there.
In this way it creates the whole world, endless, within each self.
From the sixteen- and twelve-spoked wheels, then into all the eight-spoked ones,
in this sequence, throughout all the wheels, the highest nectar
flows as soma, as far as the fivefold sequence of wheels extends.

children.text: tatpunaḥ pibati prītyā haṃso haṃsa iti sphuran ||
children.translated_text: Then the <s>haṃsa</s> drinks it with delight, flashing forth as '<s>haṃsa</s>, <s>haṃsa</s>'.
One who has heard it even once is not stained by merits or sins.
Then, being transformed in the five-spoked wheel by the nectar flowing from soma,
that all-pervading one runs through the secret wheels that are three and six-spoked,

children.text: yato jātaṃ jagallīnaṃ yatra ca svakalīlayā ||
children.translated_text: from which the world is born and into which it is dissolved by its own play.
There is the bliss of all, and the brahmacārin is intent upon that.

children.text: tatra siddhiśca muktiśca samaṃ samprāpyate dvayam ||
children.translated_text: There both siddhi and liberation are obtained together alike.
From there it again goes upward until it reaches the state whose nature is <s>Brahman</s>.
There fire and moon are emitted in equal measure, from self into self.
The moon, heated while abiding there, is arranged in two parts in the shanks.
Fire should cast it downward, and nectar flows in an instant.
Clearly in the ankles, knees, and the rest, kindled by the crooked sun,
that heated śakti again produces the sequence beginning with the five-spoked wheel.
In this way it is to be understood also in the ear, extending as far as the sphere ending in the feet,
beginning from the big toe and continuing up to the vision of the brahmāṇḍa.
Not knowing this, he is no yogin; knowing it, he becomes lord of the universe.
That supreme Lord, as though blazing, is seen by <s>Brahmā</s> and the others.
Here, in summary, a fourfold sequence has been taught in the sense faculty.
Since there is one in each, its twelvefold nature has thereby been stated.
But it has not been explained by dividing it in detail, because it is extremely secret.
In the object known too the goddess abides, having the form of the months, zodiacal signs, and so on.
Therefore this consciousness is established as inner, outer, and both.
Manifesting itself, it shines there as though making something else shine.
And then, being previously pure and eager for such manifestation,
the goddess brings about creation; by that name she is called āgama.
Likewise, turned outward, she colors the portion of the object that has been manifested,
and fully brings it about together with the wheel of her own activity.
This alone is the persistence of an entity. When, from the savor of inward-turning,
she wishes to withdraw it, bringing about the destruction of that persistence, she is so described.
Then too, when the savor of withdrawal is complete, she herself produces

children.text: śaṅkāṃ yamātmikāṃ bhāge sūte saṃharate 'pi ca ||
children.translated_text: an obstructing doubt, having the nature of restraint, in one portion, and she also withdraws it.
Having withdrawn doubt, or else an entity in the field of experience apart from the object doubted,
she brings about withdrawal precisely by dissolving it in the fire of her own self.
And that withdrawal of the mass of entities into herself, whose nature is dissolution,
she directly reflects upon, so that it flashes forth: 'This has been swallowed by me.'
For the limiting adjunct to be withdrawn by her is the own nature of consciousness itself,
which sets in the unconditioned, perfectly pure form of consciousness.
Even when the mass of entities has been dissolved, at that very moment she may congeal
some entity that remains as doubt, in the form of a latent impression.
As auspicious or inauspicious, this will generate the abundance of its result.
For this doubt remains either before enjoyment or afterward.
Even something else that has congealed she may liquefy at that very moment,
through rites such as expiation, just as in the case of acts such as brahma-homicide.
Thus consciousness brings about form through obstruction and liquefaction.
One should indeed melt even that away; and then one should also make that congeal again.
Thus, when even the object of enjoyment has been enjoyed, then also its instruments
