are withdrawn; she counts them as precisely twelve within the self that is “I.”
For the group of organs of action, intellect, and sense organs, ending with the intellect, is twelvefold;
because it illuminates, it has the nature of the sun and expands toward differentiated objects.
But egoity is the instrument whose sole means is appropriation as “mine” and “I”;
because it apprehends without interruption, that egoity is dissolved there by that very means.
Just as a differentiating instrument such as a sword or noose
is dissolved into one’s own undifferentiated hand, so too is this procedure.
Therefore the goddess of consciousness herself should contemplate the solar orb that is the mass of the senses,
because of her freedom, as imagined within the self consisting of egoity.
That very one is the supreme sun, the thirteenth, complete in its fullness;
because it is an instrument, it plainly undergoes dissolution into the agent.
And the agent is taught as twofold, consisting of the imagined and the unimagined.
The imagined agent is described through limitation by body, intellect, and the like.
In the scriptures this agent is technically designated <s>Kālāgnirudra</s>.
He is called Time because he is connected with limitation, and Fire because he is remembered as the enjoyer.
Because, as lord, he restrains and dissolves by the formation and unformation of saṃsāra,
egoity, whose state as a bound soul has not ceased, is dissolved there.
He too, because his activity is imagined, is dissolved into the great Time,
which expands, consists of “I and this,” and is adorned by the sole non-difference of the universe.
In this awareness of one’s own self, “all this is I, the all-pervading one”;
consciousness shines forth with just such a fully unfolded form.
Then consciousness, colored by the enjoyment of the state of all selves contained within it,
though already complete, is dissolved into the <s>Akula</s> abode.
The class of knowers, the multitude of means of knowledge, and the many established objects of knowledge,
the entire multitude of knowables: all this here is consciousness alone.
That independent freedom, depending on nothing, of one’s own consciousness
as it assumes this much diversity of form, is the supreme <s>Parameśvarī</s>.
These previously stated phases of articulation are now explained as her expansion:

children.text: kṣepo jñānaṃ ca saṃkhyānaṃ gatirnāda iti kramāt ||
children.translated_text: projection, knowledge, enumeration, movement, and sound, in that order.
Projection is the differentiation of one’s own self; knowledge is the nonconceptual apprehension
of what has been differentiated; enumeration is conceptual determination, because it differentiates one thing from another.
Movement is the rising into one’s own form, like a reflection;
sound is the remaining trace of self-apprehension when that has been effaced.
Performing this fivefold articulation, the supreme

children.text: devī kālī tathā kālakarṣiṇī ceti kathyate ||
children.translated_text: goddess is called <s>Kālī</s> and also <s>Kālakarṣiṇī</s>.
Because of that she is called “the real being of the Mothers,” for among knowers
knowership becomes manifest in consciousness extending this far.
In the venerable <s>Niśisaṃcāra</s> she is taught by the word <s>Vāmeśvarī</s>.
Thus consciousness, standing twelvefold among the Mothers of the universe,

children.text: ekaiveti na ko 'pyasyāḥ kramasya niyamaḥ kvacit
children.translated_text: is one alone; therefore there is nowhere any fixed rule of sequence for it.
Because sequence is absent, it is not simultaneous; and because simultaneity is absent, sequence too is not.
The reality of consciousness is utterly pure, beyond talk of sequence and non-sequence.

children.text: tadasyāḥ saṃvido devyā yatra kvāpi pravartanam ||
children.translated_text: Wherever this goddess-consciousness proceeds,
there, through union in identity with her, worship is indeed complete.
Because her nature is reflective apprehension, the resonance that is itself

children.text: sadoditaḥ sa evoktaḥ paramaṃ hṛdayaṃ mahat
children.translated_text: ever arisen is taught as the supreme, great heart.
That self-awareness in the heart, which has melted the whole universe,
and which exists up to the limit of the apprehension of entities and the rest, is called the universal.
In the scripture it is called spanda, whose nature is a surging within oneself.
It is only this slight movement, for it is the flashing of nothing other.
This is a wave of the ocean of awakened consciousness; without it, there is no consciousness.
For the state of being an ocean is precisely the condition of being waveless, wavy, and so on.
This is the essence of everything: the inert world has consciousness as its essence.
Because its establishment depends on that, that essence is the great heart.
For so it is: this existent, called the brahma-root or the māyā-egg,
is not called existent at all without the ascent of will, knowledge, and action.
Because of the ascent of that triad of powers in the <s>Bhairava</s>-like self of consciousness,
it is emitted from that; or rather, it is emitted outward.
Thus the very nature of existence of these existing things is their being composed of the three powers.
Drawing emission back into supreme awakening, it remains just so.
That very existent, outward in form, previously dissolved by the fire of awakening,
then fully remains as the residue of an inwardly sounding reflective awareness.
It has attained simply the nature of space, within the sphere of the triad of powers.
Having become of the nature of sentience, it is dissolved into the self of withdrawal.

children.text: idaṃ saṃhārahṛdayaṃ prācyaṃ sṛṣṭau ca hṛnmatam ||
children.translated_text: This is the heart of withdrawal, and in creation it is regarded as the prior heart.
The uncontrived and stainless reflective awareness whose form is this
is called “I”; this alone is the luminosity of illumination.
This power, whose nature is the heart, belongs to all mantras.

children.text: vinānena jaḍāste syurjīvā iva vinā hṛdā ||
children.translated_text: Without it, they would be inert, like living beings without a heart.
Whatever one established in this uncontrived heart may do,

children.text: prāṇyādvā mṛśate vāpi sa sarvo 'sya japo mataḥ ||
children.translated_text: whether he breathes or touches, all of that is regarded as his japa.
Whatever, through his own will and by the natural condition of creation,
is fashioned outwardly or inwardly, that is his meditation in the highest sense.
For although the abode of consciousness is formless and yet consists of all forms of the universe,
for those who desire results, only some particular form is established as the object to be meditated upon.
For example, although the reality is full through non-difference, someone bringing water
asks for a jar for the sake of liquid, by excluding other forms.
In just the same way, through the unfolding of the supreme Lord's unrestricted freedom,
some particular form gives rise to some particular conception of a result.

children.text: yastu sampūrṇahṛdayo na phalaṃ nāma vāñchati
children.translated_text: But one whose heart is complete does not desire anything called a result.
For him the goddess is the form of the whole universe, and she is so because she is free from limitation.
In the Kula, for a yogin who is intoxicated by the overflowing supreme liquor of <s>Bhairava</s>,

children.text: ghūrṇitasya sthitirdehe mudrā yā kācideva sā ||
children.translated_text: whatever bodily state he has while reeling is itself a <s>mudrā</s> (ritual seal).
Without ever depending on a store of inner fuel,
the fire blazes, its fierce flames spreading through the whole mass of the senses.
When objects enter such a fire of awareness, they increase his true radiance
and come to serve as the occasion for the act of oblation.
He should place before himself anyone purified by the descent of the supreme Lord's power,
and remain there by himself; as stated, that person is initiated.
Although in each individual rite, from recitation and the rest up to oblation,
a supreme settled conviction arises, nevertheless the matter has been explained in this way.
For just as a horse, in various terrains with level places, hollows, heights, and the like,
when being driven, goes along a course fashioned merely by the rider's will,
so consciousness, by varied modes, peaceful, more terrible, and the like,
causes duality everywhere to be abandoned and becomes <s>Bhairava</s>-like.

children.text: yathā puraḥsthe mukure nijaṃ vaktraṃ vibhāvayan
children.translated_text: Just as, when one sees one's own face in a mirror placed before one,

children.text: bhūyo bhūyas tad ekātma vaktraṃ vetti nijātmanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: again and again one recognizes that face, identical with oneself, as one's own self,
so, in the mirror of conceptual construction whose nature is meditation, worship, and adoration,
seeing the self as <s>Bhairava</s>, one soon becomes identical with that.
What is called becoming identical with that is attainment, in the unsurpassed self,

children.text: pūrṇatvasya parā kāṣṭhā setyatra na phalāntaram ||
children.translated_text: of the supreme limit of fullness; here there is no other result.
Every result is imagined here and there only when there is incompleteness.
When fullness is not imagined but real, what other result can be spoken of?

children.text: eṣa yāgavidhiḥ ko 'pi kasyāpi hṛdi vartate
children.translated_text: This is a certain method of <s>yāga</s> (worship), present in the heart of some rare person,
whose wheel of consciousness is quickly pleased, one for whom there is no later birth.
Having reached firm establishment in this worship, he attains <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation),
even while being seen by people and remaining in the condition of bodily bondage.
Here the Lord taught the conduct in the eighteenth chapter:
"Here there is no purity and no impurity, and no consideration of what may be eaten and the like.

children.text: na dvaitaṃ nāpi cādvaitaṃ liṅgapūjādikaṃ na ca
children.translated_text: There is no duality, nor even nonduality; there is no worship of the <s>liṅga</s> and the like,
nor any abandonment of that, nor possessionlessness,
nor possession either, nor the assumption of matted hair, ashes, and the like,

children.text: tattyāgo na vratādīnāṃ caraṇācaraṇaṃ ca yat ||
children.translated_text: nor the abandonment of them, nor the performance or nonperformance of vows and so forth,
nor entry into sacred places and the like, nor the observance of <s>samaya</s> rules and so on,
nor another's form, emblem, name, lineage, and the like.
In this practice nothing at all is enjoined, nor is anything prohibited.
Everything here is enjoined, and also everything is prohibited.
But this alone, O goddess, is enjoined here as a fixed rule:
the yogin, with a very tranquil mind, must make his thought steady in the reality.

children.text: tacca yasya yathaiva syātsa tathaiva samācaret
children.translated_text: And in whatever way that is possible for someone, he should practice in just that way.
But one whose mind is unwavering in the reality, even while enjoying sense objects,
is not touched by faults, like a lotus leaf by water.
Just as someone fortified with mantras and the like that remove poison, even while eating

children.text: viṣaṃ na muhyate tena tadvadyogī mahāmatiḥ
children.translated_text: poison, is not stupefied by it, so too is the great-minded yogin.

children.text: aśuddhaṃ hi kathaṃ nāma dehādyaṃ pāñcabhautikam ||
children.translated_text: How indeed could the body and the rest, made of the five elements, be impure?
Apart from luminosity, what purity or impurity can there be in things?

children.text: aśuddhasya ca bhāvasya śuddhiḥ syāttādṛśaiva kim ||
children.translated_text: And could the purification of an impure entity itself be of that same kind?
For in this way there would be mutual dependence, futility, and infinite regress.
Earth would be purified by water, and water likewise by earth.
This would be mutual dependence; and even if impurity is assumed, this sequence follows.
If earth were purified by impure water, that would be pointless.
Water by air, air by fire, that by something else:
the many-formed mantras are purifying, and from their purification there is purity in those things.

children.text: mantrāḥ svabhāvataḥ śuddhā yadi te 'pi na kiṃ tathā
children.translated_text: If mantras are pure by their own nature, why should those things not be so as well?

children.text: śivātmatā teṣu śuddhiryadi tatrāpi sā na kim ||
children.translated_text: If their purity consists in being of the nature of <s>Śiva</s>, why should that not be present there too?
One might say: "The nonrecognition of their <s>Śiva</s>-nature is not in mantras as it is in earth and the rest;

children.text: te tena śuddhā iti cettajjñaptistarhi śuddhatā ||
children.translated_text: therefore they are pure." Then the cognition of that is purity.

children.text: yoginaṃ prati sā cāsti bhāveṣviti viśuddhatā
children.translated_text: And that exists for the yogin with regard to all entities; therefore there is complete purity.
But, one may object, determination of purity, impurity, and the like is made by scriptural injunction.
Let it be so. Even so, this injunction too has been spoken by <s>Śiva</s>.
If it is asked, "How can it be valid?", this has been elaborated elsewhere.

children.text: vaidikyā bādhiteyaṃ cedviparītaṃ na kiṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: If this injunction is said to be invalidated by the Vedic one, why should the reverse not occur?
If you think correctly, invalidation should occur because the subject matter is specific:
an exception must apply to a rule enjoined generally.
Purity and impurity are enjoined generally, but in a person who knows the reality

children.text: puṃsi te bādhite eva tathā cātreti varṇitam
children.translated_text: they are both invalidated; so it has been explained here.
Nor can there be suspicion of mere <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogistic statement) and the like in a Maheśvara sentence.

children.text: abuddhipūrvaṃ hi tathā saṃsthite satataṃ bhavet
children.translated_text: For such suspicion may continually arise with respect to what is established unintentionally,
in a Veda that has the form of space and the other elements, concerning whether it has false meaning.
But the god, abundantly filled with the manifoldness of unbounded consciousness,

children.text: śāstrātmanā sthito devo mithyātvaṃ kvāpi nārhati ||
children.translated_text: standing as the very self of scripture, can never deserve falsity anywhere.
As the Lord, endowed with will, wishes to stand in the form of entities,
so, wishing to stand by the expression of their own nature, he stands in that way.
Even an <s>arthavāda</s> looks toward another injunction or the like as its basis.

children.text: tatrāstvasatyaḥ svātantrye sa eva tu vidhāyakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, even if it should not be true independently, in its freedom that very thing is nevertheless what lays down the rule.
When it passes into another injunctive sentence, or else into the status of an ancillary element,
this is not simply meaningless merely because of proximity, as in the case of the syllables ga, ja, da, and the like.
And its communication of its own meaning shines by its own awareness itself.
Can a denial of that be made in the case of injunctions and prohibitions?
There is reasoning here in the sentences, and self-awareness too is unobstructed,
for it determines the reality that is like the jewel of the whole meaning.
As for the impurity that is declared in a dead body or in what arises from the body,
let it be understood that this is not so elsewhere: what has fallen away from awareness is impure.
Everything that has attained identity with awareness is therefore established as pure.
And in the venerable <s>Vīrāvalī</s> it is said, in the determination of purity and impurity:

children.text: sarveṣāṃ vāhako jīvo nāsti kiṃcid ajīvakam
children.translated_text: The living soul is the bearer of all; nothing at all is non-living.
Know that whatever is devoid of living awareness is impure.
Therefore whatever is not very far from awareness brings about purity.
Even sages became so, with an undifferentiated disposition.
But for the protection of the world, that reality was concealed by them.

children.text: bahiḥ satsvapi bhāveṣu śuddhyaśuddhī na nīlavat ||
children.translated_text: Although things exist externally, purity and impurity are not like blue color.
This is a property of the knower, because it is known as unity or non-unity with consciousness.
Or, even if it is a property of the object, it is grounded in dependence on the measurer.
In the <s>Sautrāmaṇī</s>, liquor is pure for the <s>hotṛ</s>; for another it is the opposite.
By this, the cancellation of injunctions even by their own sentences
has been shown in some cases, as with injunction and prohibition concerning the killing of a brahmin.
The injunctions about what may be eaten and the like are also discussed by relying on this principle.
And in the <s>Sarvajñānottara</s> and other texts <s>Maheśvara</s> has spoken:
What is proclaimed by men, seers, gods, <s>Druhiṇa</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, and others,
because of the greater excellence of each later one, cancels each earlier one.
The Śaiva teaching is never to be cancelled by Vaiṣṇava statements.
One should likewise consider that a Vaiṣṇava teaching is not cancelled by statements sprung from <s>Brahmā</s>, and so on.
Whoever cancels in the reverse order is deluded and becomes a sharer in sin.
Therefore, chiefly, O <s>Skanda</s>, one should not follow worldly dharmas.
Nor, in one's own stream, should one practice what is prescribed by another scripture.
For although the god has expounded even the Veda and the rest,
still, because of the difference between the presence and absence of contracted condition,
knowledge belonging to the bound soul is said to exist by gradations of contraction.
But the knowledge of the Lord, by gradations of expansion, is what cancels it.
This is duality, this is not: through mutual negation
that would be something constructed by Māyic differentiation; how could it apply to what is not imagined?
And in the <s>Bhargaśikhā</s> it is said that death, time, kalā, and the rest,
arising from the alternatives of duality and non-duality, are swallowed by one whose understanding has been formed.
In the <s>Siddhānta</s>, worship of the liṅga is taught for knowing the universe as made of all the paths.
In the Kula and related systems, it is forbidden for the sake of knowing the body as universal selfhood.
Here, in what is all-formed, why should there be injunction and prohibition concerning that?
It is through the entry of restriction, for the sake of realization of identity.
In the Kaula system there is abandonment of matted hair and the like, because an easy means is taught.
And vow-conduct is for the realization of identity with the meaning of the mantra.
But its prohibition is for the realization of the mantra's meaning as the self of all.
Entry into kṣetras, pīṭhas, and upapīṭhas is taught for the pacification of obstacles.
And then, for the worshipper of mantra and the rest, it is prescribed for the attainment of that.
The rule of not going to kṣetras and the like, however,
is also described as being for the knowledge of fullness in one's own self through universal form.
The presence of samaya and ācāra is taught as something to be guarded.
Since difference is their very life, by abandoning each of them there is purification of reality.
But prohibition of samaya and the rest is stated in the scriptures of the Mata
so that one may understand one's own awareness as unbounded and complete.
This form belongs to another; this, however, is to be meditated on as my own.

children.text: jvālādiliṅgaṃ cānyasya kapālādi tu me nijam
children.translated_text: A liṅga of flame and the like belongs to another, but skulls and the like are my own.
By the word 'and the like' are meant austerity-conduct, time, guesthood, and so forth.
The name ending with Śakti, Śiva, and the rest belongs to this one of mine, not otherwise.
And the gotra is the lineage of gurus, called maṭhikā and kula.
The venerable lineage is called <s>Tryambaka</s>; half of it is designated <s>Amarda</s>.
In this way there are three and a half maṭhikās here in the Śaṅkara sequence.
In the sequence of the ages, the succession of siddhas runs from <s>Kūrma</s> and the others down to <s>Mīna</s>.
And by the word 'and so on' are meant the house, the village, the pīṭha, and the upapīṭha.

children.text: mudrā chummeti teṣāṃ ca vidhānaṃ svaparasthitam
children.translated_text: Mudrā and chummā are included; and their rule is established with respect to one's own side and another's.
For the realization of identity, one should rely on one's own lineage.
One should eat and worship the circle with one of one's own lineage, not with one belonging to another lineage.
And this is prohibited in the scriptures of the Mata because it causes fragmentation.
Even in the supreme reality, though it is unfragmented, this distinction comes into being.
Thus, from entry into kṣetras and the like up to the restriction of lineage,
nothing is prescribed in this system, for it is not directly useful with respect to Śiva.

children.text: na tasya ca niṣedho yanna tattattvasya khaṇḍanam ||
children.translated_text: Nor is it prohibited, since it is not a fragmentation of that reality.
For the Lord whose self is the universe, in his own form,

children.text: vidhirniṣedho vā śaktau na svarūpasya khaṇḍane ||
children.translated_text: injunction or prohibition is imagined in Śakti, not for fragmenting his own nature.
But in entering the supreme reality, whatever means a person knows to be near at that time

children.text: upāyaṃ vetti sa grāhyastadā tyājyo 'tha vā kvacit ||
children.translated_text: is then to be adopted, or in some case to be abandoned.
No compulsion is to be made here: so it is declared in the venerable Trika scripture.
The equality of all deities, and of the ovallī, mantra, and phoneme, is taught.

children.text: āgamānāṃ gatīnāṃ ca sarvaṃ śivamayaṃ yataḥ
children.translated_text: For everything in the scriptures and in the paths is pervaded by <s>Śiva</s>.
He indeed beholds the <s>śivatattva</s> (reality of Śiva) as undivided real being.
For one who approaches the reality of the self as undivided real being,

children.text: ketakīkusumasaurabhe bhṛśaṃ bhṛṅga eva rasiko na makṣikā
children.translated_text: only the bee, not the fly, is a connoisseur of the strong fragrance of the ketakī flower.
In the worship of the supreme nondual <s>Bhairavī</s>, some rare person delights, impelled by <s>Maheśa</s>.
For those who find rest in this yoga, the display of worldly becoming
melts away of itself, like snow in the height of summer.
Enough of excessive digression, with the matter already elaborated at length.
A certain wise <s>Abhinavagupta</s> is fit for this rite of worship.
Thus, in the unfolding of the word <s>Anuttara</s>, the śākta means has now been distinguished.

children.text: āṇavena vidhinā paradhāma prepsatāmatha nirūpyata etat ||
children.translated_text: Now this is set forth by the āṇava method for those who seek the supreme abode.
When the conditioning of <s>vikalpa</s> (determinate cognition) has become free of opposition,
attainment of the desired object is certain, whether for enjoyment or for liberation.
For some, <s>vikalpa</s> becomes quite firm through the freedom of the self alone,
precisely through being separated from dependence on another means.
But for another, that <s>vikalpa</s>, with respect to the refinement of the self,
depends on another means; in that case the preceding method has been taught.
Although <s>vikalpa</s> is established as having the nature of consciousness alone,
nevertheless, as certainty, it connects the limited individual with freedom.
This certainty is of many kinds, and there the means are differentiated.
They are called by the word <s>aṇu</s> because of distinctions of remoteness and nearness.

children.text: tatra buddhau tathā prāṇe dehe cāpi pramātari
children.translated_text: There, in the intellect, likewise in the breath, in the body, and also in the knowing subject,
the ultimate reality shines forth, even though this locus is not ultimate in itself.
For, because of luminous consciousness alone, breath and the rest are not separate from it;
yet, because of its own freedom, its form is twofold, inert and conscious.
This too was taught in the <s>Triśiras</s> by the crescent-crested Lord to the goddess:

children.text: jīvaḥ śaktiḥ śivasyaiva sarvatraiva sthitāpi sā ||
children.translated_text: The living being is the very power of <s>Śiva</s>; though she is present everywhere,
she becomes established in the recognition of her own form and is higher than the unfolding of knowledge.
Because her nature as consciousness is real, there is the manifestation of the freedom of the self.
Seeing the portion that consists of inertness and concealing it, one becomes nondual.
Or there, through the vision of freedom, as with the image of a face in a mirror,
one determines one's own consciousness as pure and as not having the nature of that.
Consciousness, forcefully determined to be distinct from intellect, breath, and the rest,
would in truth be non-different from them, because they are not mutually separate.
Its non-difference from the form of the universe arises from its very purity.
For the fixed, single, flashing form is incompatible with any other form.
Although everything exists inwardly in consciousness, if it were otherwise in the intellect,
why would it pass into breath or body, and by what means or in what way?
Even so, in this nonconceptual state there is no <s>vikalpa</s> without that.
Even when something has been seen, it is as though unseen; certainty comes through <s>vikalpa</s>.
Thus supreme lordship is quickly established in intellect, breath, and body.
In the knowing subject, whose form is emptiness, there is no conceptualizing of an object to be conceptualized.
There the intellect consists of meditation, and the breath has the nature of articulation.

children.text: uccāraṇaṃ ca prāṇādyā vyānāntāḥ pañca vṛttayaḥ
children.translated_text: Articulation consists of the five functions, beginning with <s>prāṇa</s> and ending with <s>vyāna</s>.
The first, called breathing, is of the nature of supreme articulation.
The body is established as a compact mass made of the senses and their objects.
There, first, what consists of meditation is here called <s>Anuttara</s>.

children.text: yaḥ prakāśaḥ svatantro 'yaṃ citsvabhāvo hṛdi sthitaḥ
children.translated_text: This autonomous light, whose nature is consciousness and which abides in the heart,
is said to consist of all the <s>tattvas</s> (principles); this too is taught in the <s>Triśiromata</s>.
The knower of reality sees it within the heart, shaped like the sheath of a plantain,
with outer, inner, and intermediate spaces, like a flower there.
There, with mind fixed on nothing else, he should meditate on the conjunction of moon, sun, and fire.
From the churning of the fire-sticks of that meditation, the great <s>Bhairava</s>, eater of oblations,
blazing in the great fire-pit called the heart, grows expansive.
Of that possessor of power, whose expanded power is the splendor of <s>Bhairava</s>,
one should contemplate the triad called knower, means of knowledge, and object known as non-different from the abode.
That very triad is the triad of the powers of fire, sun, and moon.
These are <s>Parā</s>, <s>Parāparā</s>, and <s>Aparā</s>, ever arisen.
Through creation, maintenance, and dissolution, each of them is threefold.
And each has a fourth form, unbounded and unconstructed.
Thus those twelve goddesses are established like the disk of the sun.
Each one of them illumines fire, sun, moon, and the stillness beyond.
This <s>ānuttara</s> wheel goes forth from the heart through the eye and the other organs,
through the spaces, into the sphere of each corresponding object.
By the rays of that wheel, in that object, according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution,
a form whose nature is the radiance of moon, sun, and fire becomes established.
Thus, with respect to sound and the other objects, through the path of the spaces such as the ear and the rest,
one should contemplate identity with this wheel as it alights.
By this sequential yoga, wherever that wheel alights,
being all-inclusive, it is like a sovereign lord of that very domain.
In this way the whole expanse of the cosmic path dissolves without effort
in the great <s>Bhairava</s> wheel, surrounded by consciousness.
Then, when even the universe has been dissolved through mere residual conditioning,
one should visualize the great wheel turning as it surges up from one's own self.
Then, after the dissolution of what is to be burned and the exhaustion of that residual conditioning,
one should contemplate the wheel as becoming tranquil, then stilled, and then as peace itself.
By this yoga of meditation, the universe is dissolved into the wheel.
Then, in that consciousness, consciousness itself shines forth with its objects dissolved in it.
Thereafter, because consciousness is naturally so, creation again occurs, since consciousness is the great goddess.
In this way, at every moment dissolving the universe into his own consciousness
and then emitting it again, one should constantly attain the state of <s>Bhairava</s>.
Thus, beginning with the trident and proceeding through the sequence of wheels having four or five spokes,
up to a wheel of fifty spokes, the yogin should contemplate the wheel.
Or he may contemplate a wheel with one hundred and sixty-four spokes, or even a thousand-spoked one,
or a wheel with innumerable thousands of spokes, with mind fixed on nothing else.
For the great god, the lord of consciousness, whose consciousness expands,
there is no limiting calculation at all of the universal power belonging to the great lord.
His powers are the entire world, while the possessor of power is <s>Maheśvara</s>.
So in the auspicious scripture <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s> explained it.
Thus he set forth this meditation as the form of the first means.
<s>Śrī Śambhunātha</s>, pleased with me, taught it to <s>Śrī Sumatiprabhu</s>.
Following this same direction, one should also resort to other meditations
which reach the burden of the <s>anuttara</s> (unsurpassed) means without a sequence.

children.text: atha prāṇasya yā vṛttiḥ prāṇanādyā nirūpitā
children.translated_text: Now the activity of prāṇa, beginning with breathing, has been explained;
we shall describe, as its means, the full unfolding of the <s>anuttara</s>.
First, situated in the heart, in one's own bliss, merely in the aspect of the knowing subject,
one should contemplate the state without bliss, because it rests only in emptiness.
At the rise of prāṇa, in the object known, one should contemplate the supreme bliss;
there one is satisfied by the apāna that fills the infinite aspects of what is knowable.
Established in supreme bliss, one should remain adorned by the moon of apāna.
Then, completely satisfied by the impact of the endless mass of flashing knowables,
having reached the ground of samāna, one becomes filled with the bliss of brahman.
After that too, intent on swallowing the conceptual division of the mass of measure and measured,
resting in the fire of udāna, one should contemplate the great bliss.
Having attained rest there, in this great flame, it becomes pacified.
Then there is the great all-pervasion without limiting adjuncts, free from the adjunct called vyāna.
At that time indeed there is the bliss of consciousness, not augmented by the inert.
For here there is no distinct fixed condition belonging to what has the form of the inert,

children.text: yatra ko 'pi vyavacchedo nāsti yadviśvataḥ sphurat ||
children.translated_text: where there is no delimitation at all, since it flashes as the whole universe.
That is the unstruck consciousness, strengthened by the supreme nectar,

children.text: yatrāsti bhāvanādīnāṃ na mukhyā kāpi saṃgatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: where meditation and the like have no principal connection at all.
This alone is the bliss of the universe that <s>Śambhu</s> has taught to us.
There rest is to be placed through the yoga of the heart's articulation.
The complete rest there is the condition composed of the <s>anuttara</s>.
Thus, although this heart and the others have one single nature in their own abode,
their form born from the six articulations of prāṇa is now stated through pervasion.
By applying the staff of prāṇa, through the equalizing of what is before and after,
one should resort to the mansion of <s>Lambikā</s>, resting on the four-petaled lotus.
Then, crossing the trident-ground connected with the triad of channels,
the wise one should enter into the equality of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
Again he should resort to the single expanding one, unconstricted and fully expanded,
the garland of stairways formed by the power up to the eyebrow-point, bindu, nāda, and end of nāda.
There, on the ground of the upward <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>, beautiful with the belly of vibration,
<s>visarga</s> (emission) should rest there, assuming the condition of a fish's belly.
Just as a female donkey or mare, entering the mansion of the bliss of its own abode,
made of expansion and contraction, rejoices in the heart,
so too one should resort to her who is abundantly full of hosts of states that are repeatedly dissolved and created,
the <s>Bhairava</s>-couple established in the form of expansion and contraction.
In the heart, whose great root, trident, and emission are unified,
one reaches rest in the supreme through the yoga of filling everything.
Here, precisely by the full activity of that, one remains pervaded by the whole universe.
In the self-rest of illumination, it should be seen simply as "I."
In the reflective awareness of the <s>anuttara</s>, initially devoid of activity and the like,
the first-rising supreme I-maker, the reflective awareness of consciousness, shines forth.
Then, by the sun whose nature is twelve digits and which is intent on exertion,
one should illuminate the existent, fill it, and then worship it.
Then the moon, consisting of sixteen digits and slow because it swallows <s>visarga</s>,
flashing, emits the life-giving nectar into the fire of awakening.
Its tip reaches the subtle aperture of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
In this way, that divine nectar gives satisfaction among the goddesses of consciousness.
If this much nectar of <s>visarga</s> is emitted into the fire-eater called awakening,
then everything, the sixfold maṇḍala of the paths, has been offered as oblation.
For the <s>visarga</s> of the lord of the <s>anuttara</s> is the mistress of the <s>kula</s>.
Her agitation is the series from ka to ha; its expansion is the pathway of the tattvas.

children.text: aṃa iti kuleśvaryā sahito hi kuleśitā
children.translated_text: "A" and "a" together with <s>Kuleśvarī</s> constitute the lordship of the <s>kula</s>.
The supreme separation of <s>visarga</s> is said to be the universe consisting of that.
This life-giving digit, made of consciousness, prāṇa, qualities, body, and inner and outer substances,
one should worship, offer into, and meditate upon in this way.
Standing attentive to the vibration of the pair of channels of bliss,
one attains this mansion-ground flowing with the outpouring of <s>visarga</s>.
In the agitation of <s>Śakti</s>, in the entry into <s>kula</s>, in the field at the tips of all channels,
in pervasion and in the contraction of everything into the self, the wise one should enter the heart.
Through the mutual friction of the network of lunar and solar digits,
in the abode whose nature is fire and soma, the bliss of <s>visarga</s> opens forth.
Enough of speaking about the secret; this is hidden by its very nature.
There, resting in the heart of the Yoginīs, the wise adept becomes accomplished.
Having become established in the mode of giving up, taking up, and rejecting,
one should see the universe, through the mode of non-difference, as the wonder of <s>citi</s> (consciousness).
Abandoning the wretchedness of needing practical results, in the self that is both outer and inner,

children.text: kharūpe nirvṛtiṃ prāpya phullāṃ nādadaśāṃ śrayet ||
children.translated_text: and gaining repose in the form of <s>kha</s> (space), one should resort to the fully expanded state of <s>nāda</s> (resonant sound).
By that inward state one should fully open the face of consciousness;
then the circle of rays capable of consciousness becomes non-different from what is to be known.
That knowable is dissolved by the fire called consciousness;
when dissolved, it is dissolved in this triangle, in the fire of <s>śakti</s> (power).
There, perfectly reposed in the being of the exalted point of awareness,
resting in the seed of withdrawal, the yogin becomes composed of the supreme.
Within, without, or in both, beautiful in the universal and the particular,
the <s>spanda</s> (vibration) of consciousness has the three powers as its nature, and possesses contraction and expansion.
Even where there is expansion without contraction, it is so through that manifestation;
with the inner as his object and his sight turned outward, he attains the supreme state.
Then, in the manifold form of effective action fashioned by freedom,
reflective awareness is the distinct <s>spanda</s>, called outward readiness.
There he should come to rest, in that power which is within the circle of mantras,
for the attainments beginning with peace arise from identity with each corresponding form.
And this divine aggregate of sense-powers, called the freedom of awakening,
while remaining unclosed, makes this world consist of its own self.
All his modes of activity are dissolved through union with the great audacity;
he stands completely filled within the massed flood of his own rays.
There, thinking of nothing at all and seeing clearly, he reaches consciousness,
whose sparks alone are the cause that burns the ashes of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
This was said by the Supreme Lord in the <s>Triśirobhairavāgama</s>:
Listen, goddess; I shall explain entry into the ground of mantra.
The upward movement of the central channel is marked by obtaining its nature;
it is beyond the state ending in <s>visarga</s>, and is defined as the furthest limit.
Through the blocking of the downward flow and the avoidance of an upward thrust,
it grants the manifestation of knowledge in which the great light arises.

children.text: anubhūya pare dhāmni mātrāvṛttyā puraṃ viśet
children.translated_text: Having experienced it in the supreme abode, one should enter the city through the movement of the measure;
that single movement, descended without waves, has <s>Śiva</s> as its nature.
It is radiant with the sixfold set of cakras, multiplied by four, six, two, and two;

children.text: tatsthaṃ vicārayet khaṃ khaṃ khasthaṃ khasthena saṃviśet ||
children.translated_text: established there, one should contemplate space by space, and by what stands in space enter what stands in space.

children.text: khaṃ khaṃ tyaktvā khamāruhya khasthaṃ khaṃ coccarediti
children.translated_text: Abandoning space after space, mounting into space, one should utter the space that stands in space;
by the authority of occupying space, the rays of consciousness stand in the word.
One should contemplate the entity that abides within; standing in the entity, one is free from desire for the entity.
Restraining the courses of entity and non-entity, one sees the obstruction of entity and non-entity.
The roots are self, the atomic subject, the kula, and also <s>śakti</s>, manifestation, consciousness, and delight;
the triad of powers is colored by seer and seen, and also free from them.
This <s>kha</s> is taught as tenfold, characterized by utterance and non-utterance:
standing in the abode, standing in the middle of the abode, and enclosed in the womb of the abode.

children.text: dhāmnā tu bodhayeddhāma dhāma dhāmāntagaṃ kuru
children.translated_text: By the abode one should awaken the abode; make the abode go to the end of the abode.
That abode, by the motion of the abode, is to be pierced as the inner end of the abode.
Through division into difference, subdivision, and further difference, the division is to be made from the middle.
Thus this means of entry has been proclaimed as <s>āṇava</s> (individual-based).
It was declared to me by venerable <s>Maheśvaranātha</s>, who abides in my heart;
and in the venerable <s>Brahmayāmala</s> it is said: the splendid <s>rāva</s> (resonant cry) is tenfold.

children.text: sthūlaḥ sūkṣmaḥ paro hṛdyaḥ kaṇṭhyastālavya eva ca
children.translated_text: It is gross, subtle, supreme, in the heart, in the throat, and in the palate;
and it is all-pervading everywhere, granting the state of pervasiveness.
The great yogin who has conquered <s>rāva</s> may pass into another body;

children.text: parāṃ ca vindati vyāptiṃ pratyahaṃ hyabhyaseta tam ||
children.translated_text: and he attains supreme pervasion. He should practice it every day,
until the resonant power, from <s>rāva</s>, dissolves into soundlessness.
Here, for one who desires to enter the supreme path through contemplation and through means belonging to the body,
beforehand bliss arises from contact with fullness.
Then, too, in the bodiless abode, like the fall of lightning,
from a moment of <s>samāveśa</s> (immersion), emergence appears clearly as a floating up.
Because the practiced unity of consciousness and body is lost, as with water and dust,
through the forceful onset of his own power and through the slackening of the body, he obtains tremor.
When certainty of identity with the body has melted away, because of inwardness,
he becomes sleep-like for a while, so long as he is not yet firmly established in the self of consciousness.
Then, established in the true state, experiencing consciousness as the self of the universe,
he reels within consciousness; for <s>ghūrṇi</s> (whirling) is remembered as great pervasion.
So long as there is the notion of non-self in the self, precisely in what is not the self,
the identification of the self with the body and the like is bondage; liberation is the dissolution of that.
When at first selfhood in the non-self has dissolved and one's own self has been attained,
and when non-selfhood in the self is destroyed, great pervasion begins.

children.text: ānanda udbhavaḥ kampo nidrā ghūrṇiśca pañcakam ||
children.translated_text: Bliss, emergence, tremor, sleep, and <s>ghūrṇi</s>: this is the pentad.
This has been stated; therefore, in the venerable <s>Mālinīvijayottara</s>,
when this pentad beginning with bliss has been manifested,
then the yogin, entering, forcibly attains lordship over each corresponding cakra.
Just as a body, though pervaded by the cognition that rules all,
is sometimes able to perform one particular act, the awareness of form through the eye,
so too, through entry into a certain cakra, some particular attainment may occur.
The bliss-cakra is at the fiery corner; the <s>kanda</s> (bulb) is called emergence.

children.text: kampo hṛttālu nidrā ca ghūrṇiḥ syādūrdhvakuṇḍalī ||
children.translated_text: Tremor is at the heart and palate; there is sleep, and <s>ghūrṇi</s> is the upward <s>Kuṇḍalī</s>.
And this has been stated quite clearly in the venerable <s>Traiśirasa</s> teaching.
Thus the supreme heart, the repose of the displayed <s>uccāra</s> (utterance), has been shown.
That is the unmanifest <s>liṅga</s> (mark), in which man, <s>Śiva</s>, and <s>Śakti</s> are undivided.
Here this whole universe is understood as dissolved and as standing within it.
This is the defining mark of the <s>Bhairava</s>-consciousness possessed of complete power.
But the clear <s>samāveśa</s> (immersion) that occurs when the bodily path unfolds
is veiled by I-ness, arises outward, and is joined with the state of this-ness.
This manifest-unmanifest <s>liṅga</s> is the potency of mantra, both supreme and non-supreme.
It unfolds as man and <s>Śakti</s>, differentiated from the form of <s>Śiva</s>.
That which has subordinated immersion in <s>Śiva</s>'s I-ness is marked by differentiation.
That manifest <s>liṅga</s>, consisting of consciousness, has the form of a particular vibration.
From the manifest comes the production of accomplishments; from the manifest-unmanifest come both accomplishment and liberation.
From the unmanifest comes the primordial strength; but in the <s>anuttara</s> (unsurpassed) this discussion does not apply.
When one offers the universe into the manifest called the self, that human <s>liṅga</s>,
then, when the manifest-unmanifest has melted away from that, it is the unmanifest.
Therefore this self-<s>liṅga</s> rests in the supreme unmanifest, whose nature is <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Śakti</s>, and the atomic individual.
But this discussion does not apply to one who has gone to the abode of the <s>anuttara</s>.
This is the threefold arrangement of distinction belonging to one single vibration.
One should always remain in this <s>liṅga</s>, intent upon repose in worship.
This <s>liṅga</s> is the heart of the yoginī, beautiful with bliss.
Through the union of seed and womb it gives birth to a certain consciousness.
Here, without effort, that whole host of deities
abides in the bliss-filled abode, consisting of ever-arisen consciousness.
Here the power of <s>Bhairava</s>-Lord, which contracts and expands,
shines forth as difficult to accomplish, from him who is without contraction and expansion.
Sprinkled by the stream of emission-bliss belonging to attainment of this <s>liṅga</s>,
that very true universe becomes ever new again and again.
In the <s>anuttara</s>, no means is taught here, precisely because of identity with that form.

children.text: jvaliteṣvapi dīpeṣu gharmāṃśuḥ kiṃ na bhāsate ||
children.translated_text: Even when lamps are lit, does the sun not shine?

children.text: artheṣu tadbhogavidhau tadutthe duḥkhe sukhe vā galitābhiśaṅkam
children.translated_text: With suspicion fallen away in regard to objects, the mode of enjoying them, and the pain or pleasure arising from them,
even without entering them, those whose minds are immersed know inwardly the happiness of the cessation of mental activity.

children.text: satyevātmani citsvabhāvamahasi svānte tathopakriyāṃ tasmai kurvati tatpracāravivaśe satyakṣavarge 'pi ca
children.translated_text: When the self truly exists as the great light whose nature is consciousness, when the inner mind likewise performs service for it, when the group of senses truly exists, driven by its activity,

children.text: satsvartheṣu sukhādiṣu sphuṭataraṃ yadbhedavandhyodayaṃ yogī tiṣṭhati pūrṇaraśmivibhavas tattattvam ācīyatām ||
children.translated_text: and when objects, pleasures, and the like exist, the yogin abides with an arising plainly barren of difference and rich in the power of complete rays; let that reality be accumulated.
Thus the method of <s>uccāra</s> has been stated; now <s>karaṇa</s> (instrumental practice) is analyzed.
And this has been spoken by <s>Parameśa</s> in the supreme <s>Triśiraḥśāstra</s>.
By pervasion of the knowable, the knower, and consciousness, and by abandonment, projection, and placement,
they call <s>karaṇa</s> sevenfold practice, preceded by awakening.
When projection is preceded by that pervasion, <s>karaṇa</s> consists in being established in oneself.
Although <s>karaṇa</s> is clear, it should be learned from the mouth of the guru.
Nevertheless, for the sake of preserving the scripture, it will be described further on.

children.text: ukto ya eṣa uccārastatra yo 'sau sphuran sthitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In that <s>uccāra</s> which has just been described, that which stands there as a throbbing sound
and is almost an imitation of the unmanifest is called <s>varṇa</s> (phoneme).
They know the seeds of creation and withdrawal to be its principal body.
Through the force of practicing it, the yogin gradually reaches the state of being consciousness itself.

children.text: tathā hyanacke sācke vā kādau sānte punaḥpunaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For whether without vowels or with vowels, in the series beginning with ka and ending with sa, again and again,

children.text: smṛte proccārite vāpi sā sā saṃvit prasūyate
children.translated_text: when it is remembered or uttered aloud, that particular consciousness is produced.
Even sounds such as 'pot' and the like, which depend on convention regarding external objects,
can create contemplation of their meaning in the self, like a fantasy.
This has been said by <s>Parameśa</s>: '<s>Bhairava</s> is all-pervading in everything.'
Thus, from continuous utterance of the word <s>Bhairava</s>, one becomes <s>Śiva</s>.
It is also said in the venerable <s>Triśirasa</s>, before the extraction of mantra:
Memory, that is, recollection, is in reality prior among all states.
The nature of mantra connects one with attainment of the nature of what is to be contemplated by it.
Memory generates one's own nature and colors all states.
By means of a form of many aspects, present everywhere,
the attainment of one's own nature is, in the highest sense, consciousness.

children.text: vyaktiniṣṭhā tato viddhi sattā sā kīrtitā parā ||
children.translated_text: Know therefore that it rests in manifestation; that existence is called supreme.

children.text: kiṃ punaḥ samayāpekṣāṃ vinā ye bījapiṇḍakāḥ
children.translated_text: How much more, then, those masses of seed-syllables which do not depend on convention?
Since they set consciousness vibrating, would they not lead one to the condition of a means to consciousness?
Because there is no object to be denoted, and because consciousness vibrates indifferently from its own abode,
there is fullness in the seed-clusters through the expansion and restraint of the vital breath.
There is the first consciousness of true, complete equilibrium, marked by the sigh of pleasure.
For experience is the first contact with <s>anuttara</s>-consciousness.
It unfolds intensely within the three abodes of heart, throat, and lips.
The fourteenth entry is one whose nature is unified with that.
Then, in the aspect of <s>visarga</s>-utterance, on both paths of the <s>dvādaśānta</s>,
the practitioner devoted to japa brings them into unity with the heart.
Through the process from the bulb, heart, throat, and tip of the palate up to <s>Kuṇḍalinī</s>,
one should bring the seed as vibration within the central channel of bliss.
The seed of withdrawal is <s>kha</s>, placed in the heart; the labial one, opened, is at its own crown.
The triangular fire stands at the palate and throat, and the <s>bindu</s> is in the upper station.
By this method, the wise person devoted to repetition of the phonemes
would soon enter the supreme, unsurpassed abode.
By the word <s>varṇa</s> are meant blue and the other colors, or, alternatively, as in the <s>Dīkṣottara</s>.
One should contemplate the fires and winds of dissolution, joined with the <s>Rudra</s>-bindu.
Then, being filled with that, in the heart, after seven days he should see the object of meditation,
variegated with blue, yellow, red, and other colors, like fire full of sparks.
It blazes in the lotus of the heart, awakened by the lamp of the seed.
The bindu, kindled like a lamp, shines like a dense sun.
Through this self-luminous selfhood, the mind fixed on nothing else attains identity
with <s>Śiva</s>, just as copper pierced by mercury becomes gold.
And this is an indication; one should observe it in all mantras.
For whatever network of phonemes, arisen from conceptual resolve, is material,
because of the predominance of consciousness it stands as though non-material.
Therefore, established in a form of that kind, one rises in consciousness,
where the mind is serene, its form unobscured and without limiting adjunct.
In blue, in yellow, in pleasure, and in pain, the form of consciousness is unbroken.
Therefore the gurus have declared variety among the means.
By these articulations, instruments, meditations, and phonemes has been shown
the procedural order of the subsidiary means for attaining the <s>anuttara</s> state.

children.text: akiṃciccintanaṃ vīryaṃ bhāvanāyāṃ ca sā punaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thinking of nothing is the potency in cultivation; and that cultivation, again,

children.text: dhyāne tadapi coccāre karaṇe so 'pi taddhvanau
children.translated_text: is in meditation; that too is in articulation, in the instrument, and that too is in that sound.
That sound is in the imagining of places; thus one should resort to the external sequence.

children.text: laṅghanena paro yogī mandabuddhiḥ krameṇa tu
children.translated_text: The supreme yogin proceeds by leaping over it, but one of dull intellect proceeds by sequence.

children.text: vīryaṃ vinā yathā ṣaṇṭhastasyāpyastyatha vā balam
children.translated_text: Just as a eunuch lacks potency, though perhaps even he may have strength,
so this imagining of outer and inner would be like a dead body.
Thus, in the āṇava mode, the external method that is the subsidiary means to <s>anuttara</s> has been stated by a clear path.
Now the external subsidiary means, manifest as what is called the construction of places, is distinctly analyzed.
The division of place is said to be threefold: in prāṇa, in the body, and also outside.
Prāṇa is fivefold; in the body it is twofold, by being external and internal.
A maṇḍala, a sthaṇḍila, a vessel, a rosary, together with a book,

children.text: liṅgaṃ tūraṃ paṭaḥ pustaṃ pratimā mūrtireva ca ||
children.translated_text: a liṅga, a musical instrument, a cloth painting, a manuscript, an image, and also an embodied icon:
thus the external is elevenfold; again, that may become manifold.
Among these, the procedure resting on prāṇa is taught first.
This whole <s>adhvan</s> (path), even though sixfold and exceedingly extensive,

children.text: yo vakṣyate sa ekatra prāṇe tāvatpratiṣṭhitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: which will be taught, is first established in a single prāṇa.
The measuring of the <s>adhvan</s>, just as it is, is established as sequence and non-sequence.
For sequence and non-sequence are the variegated and the single measuring in the sphere of entities.
And time, whose nature is sequence and non-sequence, exists in supreme consciousness.

children.text: kālī nāma parā śaktiḥ saiva devasya gīyate ||
children.translated_text: The supreme power named <s>Kālī</s> is praised as that very power of the God.
That very consciousness, outside itself, has made sequence and non-sequence pregnant within itself,
and, revealing them through sprouting, is established as the activity of prāṇa.
For what is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is illumination,
when it has cast away the measurable from itself, appears distinct as space.
That very thing is sung as the void-form of consciousness.

children.text: neti neti vimarśena yogināṃ sā parā daśā ||
children.translated_text: Through the reflective discernment 'not this, not this,' it is the supreme state of yogins.
That very self as space, when this object of knowledge is differentiated, turns toward appropriation;
falling and rising up, it is called the wave of the vibration of prāṇa.
Therefore they say that consciousness first became transformed into prāṇa,
and likewise, for the principle of the internal organ, came to have wind as its support.
This is that power of breathing, granting the impulse toward inner exertion;
it is regarded as <s>spanda</s> (vibration), flashing forth, repose, jīva, and the heart's intuition.
That activity of prāṇa, through the five forms beginning with prāṇa, makes its own
the body; consciousness makes it complete, and because of that this body appears.
The deluded therefore see bodily action born from a body pervaded by consciousness identified with the activity of breathing,
and they think, 'There is nothing else.'
Making authoritative that very cognition, which is held by knowers mostly consisting of children, fools, and women,
the <s>Cārvākas</s> are seers of reality.

children.text: teṣāṃ tathā bhāvanā ced dārḍhyameti nirantaram
children.translated_text: If such cultivation for them continually comes to firmness,
when that body breaks apart they would be asleep until that kind of impression is exhausted.
But when that impression is exhausted, another impression of theirs, not exhausted,
awakened from somewhere, produces a varied abundance of fruits.
Because of suspicion of lack of firmness, because the previous impression remains as it was,
because of slackness in what else should be done, and because latent residue is possible,
because it abolishes the duty of other people who are not firmly established in that,
they call this impression of atheism more sinful than sin.
Enough of what is irrelevant; now the subject at hand is analyzed.
As much as this entire <s>adhvan</s> is established in prāṇa,

children.text: dvidhā ca so 'dhvā kriyayā mūrtyā ca pravibhajyate
children.translated_text: that <s>adhvan</s> is divided twofold, by action and by form.

children.text: prāṇa eva śikhā śrīmattriśirasyuditā hi sā ||
children.translated_text: Prāṇa itself is the crest-lock, for that is declared in the glorious <s>Triśiras</s>.
During ritual and the like she is bound; because she is without parts, she has the nature of <s>Śiva</s>.
For within a day and night her movement is twenty-fourfold.
With the hundreds called the apertures of the projection of prāṇa, she gives varied results.

children.text: kṣapā śaśī tathāpāno nāda ekatra tiṣṭhati ||
children.translated_text: Night, the moon, and likewise apāna and nāda stand together in one place.
The living sun does not rise; such is a twilight lasting half a tuṭi.
The sun and moon face upward; fire faces downward within.
The midday sandhyā bestows liberation, when the sun is situated in the middle of space.
For its essence is unsetting, awakening the circle of living beings.
The bindu, prāṇa, day, and the sun stand together in one place.
But the third, the great twilight, is established as having a supremely peaceful nature.
Where the <s>śikhā</s> (crest) is bound in this way, it assigns each respective result.
Therefore this whole <s>adhvan</s> (course) rests and remains in consciousness.
Because consciousness is formless, all-pervading, and inactive,
its appearing as form and action is itself the <s>adhvan</s> of the great Lord.
The <s>adhvan</s>, which must be traversed in sequence, is the cause for attaining the state,
because it has the nature of what is enjoyed for dualists, and because it is consumed by the awakened.
Here, everywhere, one should discuss words according to their meaning,
for in the venerable <s>Niśācāra</s> it is said that designation is regarded as threefold here:
causal, established by usage, and also another kind, technical convention.
Or, when something is prior, it may be primary; therefore one should include it there.
Thus this etymology of the word <s>adhvan</s> has been stated; even if it has not been expressly taught,
in some cases it too should be inferred by one's own understanding, for how much can be written in a book?
There, that appearing as action is called the <s>adhvan</s> named time.
Here the threefold <s>adhvan</s> called syllable, mantra, and word is plainly present.
But the portion that appears as form is called the <s>adhvan</s> of place.
Here the triad named <s>kalā</s>, <s>tattva</s>, and <s>pura</s> is included within it.

children.text: trikadvaye 'tra pratyekaṃ sthūlaṃ sūkṣmaṃ paraṃ vapuḥ
children.translated_text: In each of these two triads there is a gross, subtle, and supreme body;
because of that, this whole <s>adhvan</s> is said to be sixfold.
Of the sixfold <s>adhvan</s>, the preceding triad just mentioned, again,

children.text: eṣa eva sa kālādhvā prāṇe spaṣṭaṃ pratiṣṭhitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is precisely that <s>kālādhvan</s> (course of time), clearly established in <s>prāṇa</s>.
This time is said to be other than the time that stands among the <s>tattvas</s>.
For this time is the action-power of the deity, bringing about the manifestation of the universe,

children.text: kriyāśaktiḥ samastānāṃ tattvānāṃ ca paraṃ vapuḥ
children.translated_text: and the supreme body of all the <s>tattvas</s>.
That is the <s>Īśvara</s>-<s>tattva</s>; it is called the body of <s>Śiva</s>.
For this has the oneness of the universe as its nature, whose activity is abundant enjoyment.
This, indeed, is the condition of being the form of <s>Īśvara</s> in the supreme self.
That, in the knower belonging to <s>māyā</s>, is called the <s>kāla</s>-<s>tattva</s>.
What extends from <s>Śiva</s> through <s>Śuddhavidyā</s> is <s>Śiva</s>'s own body;
that very body, for the individual soul, becomes sheathed from <s>māyā</s> through attachment.
Since the unsupported principle corresponds to <s>māyā</s>, <s>kalā</s>, and knowledge, and <s>Sadāśiva</s>
to <s>Īśvara</s>, time, and necessity, <s>Sadvidyā</s> is called attachment.
The unsupported one is the measurer of emptiness; <s>Sadāśiva</s> is the measurer through intellect.
<s>Īśvara</s> is the measurer through <s>prāṇa</s>, and knowledge is subjectivity identified with the body.

children.text: anāśrayo hi śūnyatvaṃ jñānameva hi buddhitā ||
children.translated_text: For being unsupported is emptiness, and knowledge alone is intellectuality;
being the self of the universe is <s>prāṇa</s>, and in the body there is continuity with the knowable alone.
Therefore this articulation of the universe shines in the path of <s>prāṇa</s>.
In what form this occurs we shall state; let the good attend to it.
Although in this body, whose limit is the <s>dvādaśānta</s>,
<s>prāṇa</s> is everywhere woven warp and woof, still it is not very clear in that way.
Effort, whose nature is mere living, and that which is higher than it, are considered twofold.
It is also divided again in this way as perceptible and imperceptible, in two modes.
One should understand a twofoldness in each case, according to clarity and obscurity.
<s>Prāṇa</s>, beautiful with the effort-vibration called perceptible living,
begins from the bulb; even so, here it is not very clear.
Therefore the arrangement is taught beginning with the support of the bulb.
In the <s>Svacchandaśāstra</s>, this is clear, since the channels are the support of the winds.

children.text: tatrāpi tu prayatno 'sau na saṃvedyatayā sthitaḥ
children.translated_text: Yet even there that effort does not stand as something perceptible.
Because effort is perceptible from the heart, the movement of <s>prāṇa</s> is divided from the heart.

children.text: prabhoḥ śivasya yā śaktirvāmā jyeṣṭhā ca raudrikā
children.translated_text: The power of the Lord <s>Śiva</s> is <s>Vāmā</s>, <s>Jyeṣṭhā</s>, and <s>Raudrikā</s>;
the powers of the lord, the self, and <s>prāṇa</s>, each in turn, bring about effort.
In some cases the lord-power is primary, as in the stirring of the limb-wind.
In some cases the self-power is primary, as in the contraction and vibration of the bulb.
In some cases the <s>prāṇa</s>-power is primary, as is clear in the movement of <s>prāṇa</s> in the heart.
For attentive yogins, either all three or two may be primary.
Because of attention, an unseen factor, strength, or because of non-impulsion,
there may also be a reversal in the primacy of the powers of <s>prāṇa</s> and self.
<s>Vāmā</s>, mistress of those who transmigrate, is the ordaining lord-power.

children.text: jyeṣṭhā tu suprabuddhānāṃ bubhutsūnāṃ ca raudrikā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Jyeṣṭhā</s> belongs to the well-awakened, and <s>Raudrikā</s> to those who desire to know.
<s>Vāmā</s> is so called because she emits saṃsāra; <s>Jyeṣṭhā</s>, because she is made of <s>Śiva</s>.
<s>Raudrī</s> melts pains and restrains all actions.

children.text: sṛṣṭyāditattvam ajñātvā na mukto nāpi mocayet
children.translated_text: Without knowing the principle of creation and the rest, one is not liberated and does not liberate others.
And it is said in the venerable <s>Yogacāra</s>: liberation comes from the manifestation of everything.
Those yogins who do not know emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal
are not liberated, being solely conditioned by the bondage of ignorance of them.

children.text: sṛṣṭyādayaśca te sarve kālādhīnā na saṃśayaḥ
children.translated_text: And all those, creation and the rest, are dependent on time; there is no doubt.
And that time has <s>prāṇa</s> as its nature; therefore the articulation is clearly taught.
The movement of <s>prāṇa</s> from the heart to the nasal <s>dvādaśānta</s>
is thirty-six finger-breadths for every creature, according to the measure of its own fingers.

children.text: kṣodiṣṭhe vā mahiṣṭhe vā dehe tādṛśa eva hi
children.translated_text: Whether the body is very small or very large, it is just the same kind of measure.

children.text: vīryamojo balaṃ spandaḥ prāṇacāraḥ samaṃ tataḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore vigor, vital force, strength, vibration, and the movement of <s>prāṇa</s> are equal.
In the course of thirty-six finger-breadths, the pair consisting of going and coming
clearly contains here the aggregate of <s>nālikā</s>, lunar day, month, and year.
A <s>tuṭi</s> is joined with one and a quarter finger-breadths; sixteen of these make a <s>prāṇa</s> while breathing out
and breathing in; here, in each finger-breadth together with a fifth part, there is a <s>caṣaka</s>.
The <s>nālī</s> of inhalation and exhalation is declared to be a day and night.
At the nine-finger and four-<s>tuṭi</s> measure are the watches; those fours constitute the day.
At the going out, the inner night and the moon are present; at the junction of the two, in the half-<s>tuṭi</s>,
there is <s>Ketu</s> in the sun and <s>Rāhu</s> in the moon; Mars and the others have their shares in the weekdays.
For the other planets, their rising occurs at an interval of two <s>prahara</s>s;
attainment is far off, while liberation, hostile magic, and otherworldly results are involved.
Worldly accomplishment varies in its greater remoteness or nearness over the eight <s>prahara</s>s.
Midday and midnight, as <s>abhijit</s>, grant liberation and enjoyment.
The rising of the other <s>nakṣatra</s>s takes place successively from the middle.
The <s>Nāga</s>s, the forms of the world-lords, the lords of forms, the <s>Gaṇeśa</s>s, from the water-principle
up to <s>Pradhāna</s>, the leaders, and the presiding lords of the <s>vidyātattva</s> (principle of mantra-knowledge),
and likewise the <s>Bhairava</s>s beginning with <s>Sakala</s> and extending as far as the throat and lips,
the supreme <s>Śakti</s>s, the <s>Vāmeśa</s>s, and the hero-leaders,
all those, in groups of eight and eight, that thus partake of the status of pervaded and pervader,
gross and subtle in sequence, have their rising through the eight <s>prahara</s>s.
By day there are fierce rites, and by night gentle rites, without doubt.
But fierceness or gentleness has also been explained as depending on the intention.
At the end of day and night there is liberation through the yoga of meditation on pervasion.
And these were taught by the Supreme Lord in the revered <s>Vīrāvalīkula</s>:
White and black, long and short, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, day and night,

children.text: kṣīyete yadi taddīkṣā vyāptyā dhyānena yogataḥ
children.translated_text: if they are made to wane, then that initiation is accomplished through pervasion, meditation, and yoga.
The day-and-night has been described in the movement of <s>prāṇa</s>; now the month is stated.

children.text: dinaṃ kṛṣṇo niśā śuklaḥ pakṣau karmasu pūrvavat
children.translated_text: The dark fortnight is day and the bright fortnight is night; in rites the two fortnights are as before.
Among the sixteen <s>tithi</s>s that have been taught, those that are earlier and later
have repose in their respective halves; the <s>tithi</s>s are the fifteen and the other one.
The day-and-night is divided by a <s>tithi</s> of two and a quarter finger-breadths.
Because of manifestation and repose, those two indeed are day and night.
For consciousness at every instant is joined with manifestation and bliss.

children.text: tau kﾱptau yāvati tayā tāvatyeva dinakṣape
children.translated_text: For as much as those two are conceived by it, just so much are day and night.
For just as much as consciousness has arisen and is clearly manifest,

children.text: tāvāneva kṣaṇaḥ kalpo nimeṣo vā tadastvapi
children.translated_text: just that much is a moment, an aeon, or even a blink, whatever it may be.
As much as the arising of consciousness is intent on grasping a single object,
so much indeed is its setting, the savoring of the knower's own self.

children.text: vedye ca bahirantarvā dvaye vātha dvayojjhite ||
children.translated_text: With regard to the known, whether outside, inside, both, or free from both,
becoming wholly identical with that is day; abiding in the knower is night.
The cognizer is one who rests in the known, while the knower is the inward-facing state.
At first he deliberates; afterwards he has the form of mere being.
Waking is the condition of cognizing; dream is the prior state of being the knower.
The higher state is sleep; when night and day cease, the fourth state is nondual.
Sometimes, through an equality of resting in the object, there is savoring within the self;
that equality of known and knower is the equality of night and day.
When repose in the known is greater, that makes for the lengthening of day;
when repose in one's own self is less, and in the opposite case the reverse occurs.
For when eagerness toward one's own self has awakened, repose in the known is slight.
In just this way one should describe the sequence by which day and night are lesser or greater.
Just as among bodies the lesser and greater measures of day and night and the rest are not the same,
so too among cities or bodies; therefore it has not been stated according to each particular difference.
The sun in the wide sky of the venerable <s>Traiyambaka</s> lineage,
the venerable <s>Śambhu</s>, revealed to me the sequence of day and night in this way.
But the venerable lineage-teacher says: The station of the awakened and the unawakened,
beginning from the heart, is what divides night and day.
That is not correct, since in the bright fortnight there is a share in inward entry and expansion;
how could this very station of the unawakened be day?

children.text: alaṃ vānena nedaṃ vā mama prāṅmatamatsaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Enough of this; this is not jealousy toward my former teacher.
But when what is to be rejected has been shown, pupils become fixed on seeing the true path alone.
In the dark fortnight that has been explained, the moon moving in <s>prāṇa</s>
as the principle of nourishment should give up one <s>kalā</s> on each <s>tithi</s>.
And that fifteenth <s>tuṭi</s> near the <s>dvādaśānta</s>
is the new-moon point here; there the waned moon enters the sun of <s>prāṇa</s>.

children.text: uktaṃ śrīkāmikāyāṃ ca nordhve 'dhaḥ prakṛtiḥ parā
children.translated_text: And in the revered <s>Kāmikā</s> it is said: There is neither above nor below; <s>prakṛti</s> is supreme.
<s>Māyā</s>, divided in two and having the form of <s>Śiva</s>, moves in half and half.
As moon and sun, it fills the body and dissolves it.
The nectar in the form of the moon, twofold and again sixteenfold,

children.text: pibanti ca surāḥ sarve daśapañca parāḥ kalāḥ
children.translated_text: all the gods drink: the fifteen and the supreme <s>kalā</s>s.
<s>Amā</s>, abiding within the remaining cave, is <s>Amāvāsyā</s>, the satisfier of the universe.

children.text: evaṃ kalāḥ pañcadaśa kṣīyante śaśinaḥ kramāt
children.translated_text: Thus the fifteen <s>kalā</s>s of the moon wane in sequence.
But the sixteenth does not, because it is identical with the nourishing nectar-form.
There, that fifteenth <s>tuṭi</s> is the fully waned moon;
the half-<s>tuṭi</s> above it is called the junction of the fortnight.
Therefore, from the half-<s>tuṭi</s> of repose, the former half is new-moon,

children.text: paraṃ prātipadaṃ cārdhamiti saṃdhiḥ sa kalpyate ||
children.translated_text: and the latter half is the first lunar day; thus the junction is conceived.
There, on that first lunar day, within the half of half a <s>tuṭi</s>, the former half
should make the new-moon condition at the cutting of the <s>tithi</s>, as it enters the solar eclipse.
There, the moon dissolved in the solar disk trickles the honey which,
being heated, the son of <s>Siṃhikā</s>, born together with the moon, drinks.
The sun is <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), and the moon is the measurable; they are of the nature of knowledge and action.
<s>Rāhu</s> is the <s>māyā</s>-bound subject, skilled in covering them.
For that very reason he has the form of darkness and is unable to dissolve them.
From the collision of those two there is the chief surge of nonduality; the measurer is the dissolver.
From the collision of sun, moon, and <s>Rāhu</s>, the means of knowledge, the known, and the knower...
Therefore, by that nonduality, this great eclipse is auspicious.
Even apart from the new-moon day, if this conjunction occurs, it is a great eclipse,
as when the sun is in Aries, <s>Rāhu</s> stands in <s>Aśvinī</s>, and it is the day of <s>Aśvinī</s>.

children.text: āmāvāsyaṃ yadā tvardhaṃ līnaṃ prātipade dale
children.translated_text: But when one half of the new-moon tithi has merged into the portion of Pratipad,
and Pratipad is pure, that is the release, when the moon is far away.
Between the swallowing and the release, bathing, meditation, oblation, recitation, and the like
bring abundant worldly, non-worldly, and otherworldly fruit.
Entering for a moment when the disturbance of what is swallowed and what swallows has completely dissolved,
one who performs meditation, worship, and the like at an eclipse of the moon or sun becomes a sharer in liberation.
The cutting of a tithi is debt; coughing is increase; exhalation is wealth.
What arises without effort and what arises with effort come from expulsion and then from restraint.

children.text: evaṃ prāṇe viśati citsūrya induṃ sudhāmayam
children.translated_text: Thus, when <s>prāṇa</s> (breath) enters, the consciousness-sun enters the nectar-filled moon;
by meditating on each one, one should fill the ray of awakening with a lunar digit.
These fifteen <s>tuṭis</s> (instants), beautiful with the moon's nectar and rich in gradual filling,
are the tithis belonging to the bright fortnight.
At the last, the full-moon <s>tuṭi</s>, there is the junction of the fortnights as before,
and there is a lunar eclipse at the junction with Pratipad, because of the prior entry.
Here, at an eclipse, there is great fruit in this world for practitioners;
the rest is as before. This is the month; in the movement of breath it is called a year.
In each group of six aṅgulas, the sun, proceeding from the heart through Capricorn and the following signs,
stands and produces the group of six months beginning with Māgha; that is the northern course.
When three transitions have passed and eighteen aṅgulas have been traversed,
when the sun reaches Aries, the equinox is auspicious and has otherworldly fruit.
At the entry when the sun is in Libra, that too becomes the equinox;
and this, belonging thereafter to the southern course, grants accomplishment here in this world.
Embryonic state, the condition of being about to arise, then the wish to arise,
being about to come forth, the beginning of emergence, and the state of emergence,
birth, existence, maturation, growth, decline, and destruction occur in order.
Therefore the signs beginning with Capricorn produce here a ritual action whose fruit corresponds to them.
For otherworldly results, Pisces and Aquarius apply to the preliminary service of mantra and the like;
the fourfold set beginning with Pisces is said to be near, and each succeeding one nearer still.
At entry precisely there, an action adorned with pacification, nourishment, and the like
would be directed to this-worldly results; and its fruit is progressively more and more remote.
At exit there is an increase of day; when it is reversed, the result is the reverse.
In this year the tithis are five for each aṅgula: such is the sequence.
There too the rule of day and night applies; thus everything is as before.
In this year belonging to breath, with proper skill, among the months beginning with Kārttika,
there are twelve <s>Rudras</s> to arise here in front, ending with <s>Pitāmaha</s>.
The rise of the year in breath has been taught; now the rise of the twelve-year cycle is explained.
The tithis termed kharasā occur successively in each single aṅgula;
in the rise of the twelve-year cycle they are declared to be the twelve beginning with Caitra.
In Caitra the mantra arises; that too is now connected with the palate. But again,
the rise of Caitra is in the heart; therefore there too is indeed the arising of mantra.
When three hundred tithis are calculated for each aṅgula,
a year in breath occupies an aṅgula together with a fifth part; and again there is a sixty-year cycle.
Twenty-one thousand and six hundred: this
division belonging to breath is called the day-and-night of sixty years.
Wherever there is a division of watch, day and night, month, season, year, solar year, or sixty-year cycle,

children.text: yaśchedastatra yaḥ sandhiḥ sa puṇyo dhyānapūjane ||
children.translated_text: whatever junction occurs there is auspicious for meditation and worship.
Thus this time, arising in the emergence of breath, is an embodiment of the one <s>śakti</s> (power);
it abides within as the self of the universe. Its external form is now set forth.
Six breaths make one caṣaka; sixty of these are a nālī, and likewise
a tithi; by thirty of those there is a month, and twelve months make a year.
A year is a day and night for the ancestors, because of the northern and southern courses;
what is a year by the ancestors' own measure is called divine.
Here three hundred and sixty human years
are to be multiplied by twelve, and from that the number of months is obtained.
Multiplying that again by thirty, one should state the reckoning of days and nights;

children.text: hatvā tāṃ caikaviṃśatyā sahasraiḥ ṣaṭśatena ca ||
children.translated_text: and multiplying that by twenty-one thousand six hundred,
one should state the number of breaths there. Then the rise of years beginning with sixty
has been taught by the gurus in their own commentaries on the venerable <s>Raurava</s> and other scriptures.
That which is a day and night of the gods is a year for human beings;
by three hundred and sixty years of men there is a year of the gods.
And in the venerable <s>Svacchandaśāstra</s> the same view is seen;
after beginning with, 'That is the day and night of the ancestors,' subsequently
it concludes in unity: 'Thus is the divine day and night.'
Therefore those gurus who, from the two statements in the venerable <s>Svacchanda</s>,

children.text: pitryaṃ varṣaṃ divyadinamūcurbhrāntā hi te mudhā
children.translated_text: declared that the ancestral year is the divine day are simply mistaken.
In the yugas, beginning with the fourfold one, there are thousands of divine solar years;
with each one diminished by one, there are also that many hundreds, and in them there are eight junctions.
A <s>manvantara</s> consists of seventy-one <s>caturyugas</s>, and these are fourteen.
Within a day of <s>Brahmā</s>, fourteen <s>Indras</s> pass away in succession.
At the end of <s>Brahmā</s>'s day, a flame of the fire of Time, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas,
burns the three worlds and, by its smoke, puts another triad to sleep.
